tips.title: Store money as floating point and 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3
tips.keyPoint: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly. Store money as an integer count of the smallest unit (yen, cents) or in an exact decimal type (NUMERIC / DECIMAL), and decide where and in which direction you round.
tips.body: A program's `double` (a double-precision floating-point number) holds numbers in binary. Decimal 0.1 becomes the never-ending binary fraction 0.000110011…, so it is stored as the nearest value that fits. That is why `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004` in JavaScript, Java, and Python, and comparing it with `0.3` is false. One error is tiny, but add millions of values or branch on equality and you get totals that are a cent off the ledger, or discounts that never trigger. Store money as an integer in the smallest unit, such as yen or cents, or in a type that computes exactly in decimal (`NUMERIC` / `DECIMAL` in the database, `BigDecimal` in Java, and so on). Tax rates and splitting a bill produce fractions, so also decide up front where you round and in which direction (truncate, round half up, or banker's rounding).
tips.inDesign: It matters for payments, invoices, points, and unit prices, anywhere totals must match the books. A single float anywhere along the path (the database column, the API's JSON, an app variable) lets error in, so keep the type consistent across every boundary. In JSON, send amounts as integers in the smallest unit or as strings. Currencies differ in decimal places (yen has none, dollars have two), so keep each amount with its currency code.

tradeOffs.gain: Fast, exact, and the same value in every language and database
tradeOffs.cost: You must know each currency's decimal places and convert for display

tradeOffs.gain: Exact arithmetic with fractions, including fine-grained values like interest rates
tradeOffs.cost: Slower, and the app also needs a decimal type (such as BigDecimal)

tradeOffs.option: Not recommended for exact money calculations: round floats only for display
tradeOffs.gain: Simple to write and fast to compute
tradeOffs.cost: Totals, comparisons, and fractions will eventually disagree with the books

tips.title: UTF-8 uses 1–4 bytes per code point; one visible character may contain several
tips.keyPoint: Specify whether limits count grapheme clusters, code points, UTF-16 code units, or bytes. MySQL utf8mb3 cannot store supplementary-plane characters such as 😀; use utf8mb4.
tips.body: UTF-8 encodes a Unicode code point in 1–4 bytes. ASCII uses one, many hiragana and kanji use three, and 😀 uses four, but Japanese and emoji do not have one fixed size. The family emoji 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 is a grapheme cluster of code points joined by ZWJ: one visible character, 25 bytes. JavaScript length counts UTF-16 code units and returns 11. MySQL utf8mb3 cannot represent supplementary-plane characters; use utf8mb4. Align counting units and Unicode handling across UI, API, and DB.
tips.inDesign: It matters when setting length limits for usernames, posts, SMS, and push notifications, and when choosing column types, external API limits, and index key lengths. Write each limit together with how it counts, and use the same count in the UI, the API, and the database. When cutting a string, cut at the boundary of a visible character (a grapheme cluster), never mid-byte. Use utf8mb4 in MySQL and size index key lengths at 4 bytes per character.

tradeOffs.gain: Matches what users expect
tradeOffs.cost: Needs a library, and you must check every language counts the same way

tradeOffs.gain: Maps directly to database and API size limits
tradeOffs.cost: Japanese fits a third as much as English, and users cannot see why

tradeOffs.gain: Works in the browser with no extra code
tradeOffs.cost: Emoji count as 2 or more, and the count drifts from server-side languages

tips.title: Signed 32-bit sequential IDs exhaust their range after about 2.1 billion allocations
tips.keyPoint: INT (signed 32-bit) tops out at 2,147,483,647. Make the primary keys of ever-growing tables, and the foreign keys that reference them, BIGINT (64-bit) from the start. Changing the type later rewrites a large table.
tips.body: A signed 32-bit integer covers −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647, so an auto-increment primary key hits the ceiling after about 2.1 billion rows. Then the next ID cannot be generated, and every INSERT into that table fails. Deleting rows does not give numbers back, and failed INSERTs and rollbacks skip numbers too, so the limit arrives sooner than the row count suggests. Even with a BIGINT column, an app that reads IDs into a 32-bit integer (such as Java's `int`) overflows there and sees negative values. 2.1 billion sounds like a lot, but at 1,000 writes per second it lasts about 25 days.
tips.inDesign: It matters for tables that only grow: logs, events, notifications, likes. Make the primary key, the foreign key columns that reference it, the app's variables, and the API schema all 64-bit. For existing tables, compute when the current maximum ID plus daily growth reaches the limit, and monitor it. JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53, so consider returning IDs as strings in APIs.

tradeOffs.gain: Provides a larger ID range than INT; continue monitoring limits and allocation rates
tradeOffs.cost: Each row grows by 4 bytes in the column and again in each index

tradeOffs.option: Start with INT and change it near the limit
tradeOffs.gain: Slightly less storage while small
tradeOffs.cost: Changing the type of a large table rewrites it, and foreign keys and app types must change in step

tradeOffs.gain: No limit to worry about, and IDs can be generated outside the database
tradeOffs.cost: 16 bytes is large, and the IDs are hard for people to read and compare

tips.title: Loading related data per row turns one list into 1 + N queries (the N+1 problem)
tips.keyPoint: Touching an association while looping over an ORM list runs one query per row. Load associations together with a JOIN or an IN clause (eager loading), and measure queries per request to catch counts that grow with the list.
tips.body: Fetch a list of posts in one query, then reference `post.author.name` inside the loop, and the ORM loads each author the moment it is needed (lazy loading). A list of 100 posts takes 1 query for the list plus 100 for the authors: 101 queries. This is the N+1 problem. Even at 1 ms each, 100 extra round trips to the database add 100 ms. With a handful of rows in development nobody notices; it slows down in production once lists grow. Loading the authors together (one `WHERE id IN (...)` or a JOIN) takes two queries or one, however long the list is.
tips.inDesign: It shows up in list screens, list APIs, nested GraphQL fields, and loops in batch jobs. Use the ORM's eager loading (Rails `includes`, Django `select_related` / `prefetch_related`), and in GraphQL batch same-kind loads with DataLoader. Log queries per request in tests and development, and check the count does not grow when the list does.

tradeOffs.gain: A single round trip to the database
tradeOffs.cost: For one-to-many relations the parent row repeats once per child, transferring more data

tradeOffs.option: Load each association with an IN clause in later queries
tradeOffs.gain: No duplication, and it works for many-to-many relations
tradeOffs.cost: One more query per association, and large IN lists need splitting

tradeOffs.option: Keep lazy loading and cache the results
tradeOffs.gain: Faster after the first time with little code change
tradeOffs.cost: The first load stays slow, and you must handle cache invalidation

tips.title: Expressions on a column can prevent efficient range lookup in a plain B-tree
tips.keyPoint: A plain B-tree orders column values. Functions on the column and leading-wildcard LIKE often prevent a selective range lookup. Distinguish expression indexes and full index scans, and inspect EXPLAIN.
tips.body: A plain B-tree can locate a value range. A half-open timestamp range is often selective, whereas DATE(created_at) is a different expression from the indexed column. A matching expression index may support lookup; a plain index can still be used for a full or covering scan. No index use and no efficient selective range lookup are different claims. Prefix LIKE also depends on collation and operator class. Also inspect plans when implicit type conversion changes how the column is evaluated.
tips.inDesign: It matters for search and admin filters, per-day aggregates, and case-insensitive email lookups. For a slow query, check with EXPLAIN whether it uses the index or scans the whole table. Write conditions so the value being compared is transformed, not the column. If the column really must be transformed, create an expression index in PostgreSQL (`CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))`). If substring search is a requirement, consider full-text search or a trigram index.

tradeOffs.option: Rewrite conditions as ranges on the bare column
tradeOffs.gain: The existing index works as is, with no extra storage
tradeOffs.cost: The team must follow the rule, and some ORM idioms break it

tradeOffs.gain: Faster without changing the app's queries
tradeOffs.cost: The expression is computed on every write, and queries must match it exactly

tradeOffs.option: Use full-text search or a trigram index
tradeOffs.gain: Substring searches become fast too
tradeOffs.cost: The index is large, and writes get heavier

tips.title: Default isolation levels differ: PostgreSQL uses Read Committed, MySQL uses Repeatable Read
tips.keyPoint: Under Read Committed, reading the same row twice in one transaction can return different values (a non-repeatable read). The isolation level decides which read anomalies are allowed, and the default differs by database, so assumptions shift when you switch.
tips.body: The SQL standard lists read anomalies between concurrent transactions and defines four isolation levels by how many of them they prevent. A dirty read is seeing another transaction's change before it commits. A non-repeatable read is reading a row twice and finding a different value because someone else committed an update in between. A phantom read is running the same search twice and finding extra rows someone else inserted in between. PostgreSQL's default, Read Committed, reads the data committed as of each statement, so dirty reads cannot happen but non-repeatable and phantom reads can. MySQL (InnoDB)'s default, Repeatable Read, keeps reading the snapshot taken at the first read until the transaction ends. The same application code sees different values on a different database.
tips.inDesign: It matters for batch jobs that aggregate then write, code that checks a balance before updating it, and reports whose queries must agree with each other. Check whether a transaction assumes "what I read earlier is still the same"; if it does, raise the isolation level or lock the rows with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. A higher level makes some databases return update conflicts as errors, so build in retries too.

tradeOffs.option: Stay on Read Committed and lock only the rows you need
tradeOffs.gain: Little waiting and high concurrency
tradeOffs.cost: You must assume reads can change and pick the places to lock yourself

tradeOffs.gain: Values read within the transaction stay consistent
tradeOffs.cost: You keep reading an old snapshot, and update conflicts bring more errors or waiting

tradeOffs.gain: Results match running transactions one at a time
tradeOffs.cost: More conflict errors, and retries become mandatory

tips.title: Build SQL by string concatenation and input runs as SQL (SQL injection)
tips.keyPoint: Pass values through placeholders so the statement and the data travel separately. Placeholders cannot stand in for column names, table names, or sort direction, so pick those from an allowlist.
tips.body: Concatenate input into SQL, as in `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"`, and an input of `' OR '1'='1` makes the condition always true and returns every user. This is SQL injection. The root cause is that the database cannot tell where the SQL command ends and the data begins. Pass the value separately through a placeholder (`WHERE name = ?` or `$1`) and the database always treats it as data, so quotes in it never become commands. Placeholders only work in value positions, though, not for a column name in `ORDER BY` or a table name. Concatenate input there and the same hole remains.
tips.inDesign: It tends to happen wherever conditions are built dynamically: search, sorting, filtering, report aggregation. Use your ORM or query builder's standard API, and pass values through placeholders when writing raw SQL too. Pick sort columns and directions from an allowlist such as `{"new": "created_at DESC"}` and reject anything else. Do not rely on hand-rolled escaping of quotes, which leaks depending on character encoding and database settings. Give the database user only the permissions it needs (least privilege), so a breach can do less.

tradeOffs.gain: No character in a value can become a command
tradeOffs.cost: They cannot cover column names or SQL structure, which need another defense

tradeOffs.option: Leave it to the ORM or query builder
tradeOffs.gain: Its standard API uses placeholders automatically
tradeOffs.cost: Functions that embed raw SQL open the same hole

tradeOffs.option: Not recommended: concatenate SQL using hand-composed escaping
tradeOffs.gain: Keeps existing concatenation code mostly as it is
tradeOffs.cost: Leaks depending on encoding and database settings, and one miss is enough to break it

tips.title: In public-key cryptography, encrypt with the recipient's public key and sign with your own private key
tips.keyPoint: To keep something secret (encryption), encrypt with the recipient's public key so only their private key can undo it. To show who sent it (signing), sign with the sender's private key so anyone can check it with the public key. A private key never leaves its owner.
tips.body: Public and private keys form a pair, but encryption/decryption and signing/verification are distinct operations. Encryption protects data for a recipient’s public key and decryption uses the corresponding private key. Signing uses the signer’s private key; verification uses a public key obtained through a trusted channel. Signing is not private-key encryption followed by public-key decryption, and does not hide content. Algorithms support different uses; TLS establishes authenticated key material before encrypting application data symmetrically. How a digital signature uses a hash value depends on the scheme; key distribution also differs from symmetric-key cryptography.
tips.inDesign: It matters when designing JWT signatures (RS256, ES256), webhook signatures, commit and package signing, and encryption of data you hold for others. Give verifiers only the public key, and keep the private key in the one place that signs (ideally inside a KMS or HSM). Signing with a shared-key HMAC (HS256) lets every verifier sign too, so prefer a public-key scheme when there are many verifiers. Use separate keys per purpose, and never use one key pair for both encryption and signing.

tradeOffs.option: Sign with a public-key scheme (RS256, ES256)
tradeOffs.gain: Verifiers never receive a secret
tradeOffs.cost: Needs key distribution (such as JWKS) and rotation, and costs more computation

tradeOffs.gain: Fast and simple to implement
tradeOffs.cost: Every verifier can also sign, and the key can leak from more places

tradeOffs.option: Keep the private key in a KMS or HSM
tradeOffs.gain: Can sign without exporting private-key material, reducing exposure paths
tradeOffs.cost: Every signature is an API call, with latency, cost, and rate limits

tips.title: Raising a cache hit ratio from 90% to 99% cuts database reads to a tenth
tips.keyPoint: Only misses (1 − hit ratio) reach the DB. When every request checks the cache, mean time = lookup time + miss ratio × DB fetch time. Compare miss ratios to estimate DB load.
tips.body: Consider a lookup on every read, followed by a DB fetch on a miss. At 10,000 reads/s, a 90% hit ratio sends 1,000 reads/s to the DB; 99% sends 100. In a hypothetical calculation, each lookup takes 1ms and a miss adds a 20ms DB fetch: means are 1 + 0.1×20 = 3ms and 1 + 0.01×20 = 1.2ms. A miss takes 21ms total, distinct from its 20ms DB fetch. This simple model excludes load-dependent DB latency and request coalescing. This mean is called effective access time.
tips.inDesign: It matters when sizing the database on the assumption of a cache, when replacing or restarting cache nodes, and when changing cache key design. Size the database not for the normal hit ratio but for the misses when it drops (right after a restart, or when memory runs short and eviction rises). To raise the hit ratio, lengthen the TTL, drop elements that do not change the result from the cache key (unneeded query strings or headers), and add memory to reduce eviction.

tradeOffs.gain: Fewer misses and fewer database reads
tradeOffs.cost: Stale data is served until updates show up

tradeOffs.gain: Less eviction and a higher hit ratio
tradeOffs.cost: Costs more, and gains level off depending on how skewed access is

tradeOffs.option: Key the cache only on what changes the result
tradeOffs.gain: Identical results share one key, raising the hit ratio
tradeOffs.cost: Drop too much and you serve one person's result to another

tips.title: A DNS change does not reach everyone at once, so lower the TTL ahead of time
tips.keyPoint: Lower DNS TTL in advance and wait out the previous TTL before switching. This guides ordinary cache expiry; reused connections or custom caches mean it is not a deadline guaranteeing migration of every client.
tips.body: When a browser or server looks up a name, the query usually goes to a recursive resolver run by an ISP or the company network. The recursive resolver caches the answer from the authoritative DNS server for the record's TTL (in seconds) and does not ask the authoritative DNS server again until it expires. So if you change an A record's IP address but its TTL is 86,400 seconds (one day), users behind a resolver that looked it up just before can keep reaching the old IP address for up to a day. Lowering the TTL does not take effect either until the old, long TTL expires from caches. That is why you lower the TTL at least one old TTL's worth before the cutover. Operating systems and language runtimes may also cache names on their own, so some clients keep using the old address longer than the TTL.
tips.inDesign: It matters for server migrations, switching load balancers or CDNs, and DNS-based failover between regions. DNS failover is delayed by the TTL and client caching, so include that in your RTO (the recovery time objective). A short TTL switches faster but means more queries, higher DNS cost, and more time spent resolving. Keep it longer in normal times and shorten it only before a change. Do not shut down the old destination right after switching; wait until traffic to it stops.

tradeOffs.gain: Fewer queries, and name resolution is faster and cheaper
tradeOffs.cost: Cutovers and failovers take longer to move traffic

tradeOffs.gain: A cutover completes in about one TTL
tradeOffs.cost: More queries, higher DNS cost, and more time spent resolving names

tradeOffs.option: Switch at the load balancer instead of in DNS
tradeOffs.gain: Switches immediately, regardless of client DNS caches
tradeOffs.cost: Needs a fixed entry point in front (a load balancer or an anycast IP address)

tips.title: SQL NULL means unknown, and comparisons can silently exclude rows
tips.keyPoint: Ordinary comparisons with NULL yield unknown. Use IS NULL to find missing values and test nullable conditions explicitly.
tips.body: NULL represents an unknown or missing value, distinct from zero and an empty string. SQL uses three-valued logic: true, false, and unknown. WHERE retains only true rows. Thus `deleted_at = NULL` does not find undeleted rows; use `deleted_at IS NULL`. Likewise `status <> 'archived'` excludes rows whose status is NULL. If the requirement includes missing statuses, write `status <> 'archived' OR status IS NULL`. COALESCE substitutes a value, so use it only when treating missing data as that value is meaningful.
tips.inDesign: Use this when implementing optional fields, soft deletion, and filters. Define whether NULL means unknown or not applicable for each column; require NOT NULL for mandatory data. Test ordinary values, NULL, and empty strings separately.

tradeOffs.gain: Keeps missing data distinct from ordinary values
tradeOffs.cost: Requires explicit missing-value rules in filters and aggregates

tradeOffs.gain: The database rejects missing values for that column
tradeOffs.cost: Existing missing data needs repair and defaults need justification

tips.title: Separate an event instant from a business calendar date
tips.keyPoint: Represent creation time as a UTC instant and birthdays or billing dates as calendar dates. Define the business time zone for daily reports.
tips.body: An order creation time identifies one instant worldwide; a birthday is a calendar date that should not move to the previous day when displayed elsewhere. Send instants with an offset, such as `2026-10-25T00:30:00+09:00`, and normalize them to UTC internally. A time zone describes regional clock rules; an offset is the difference from UTC at a particular instant. A recurring 9 a.m. appointment also needs a region such as Asia/Tokyo. For daily reports, construct local midnight and the next local midnight, convert both to UTC, and query a half-open interval. A local day is not always 24 hours where daylight saving applies.
tips.inDesign: Choose types by meaning when designing created_at, birthdays, cutoff dates, and appointments. Require offsets for instant inputs and test month ends, date boundaries, and daylight saving transitions.

tradeOffs.option: Store event timestamps as UTC instants
tradeOffs.gain: The same event can be compared across regions
tradeOffs.cost: Display and daily reporting require regional conversion

tradeOffs.option: Store business dates as date values
tradeOffs.gain: Birthdays and billing dates do not shift with time zones
tradeOffs.cost: Time of day and event ordering need separate fields

sources.title: Python — Aware and Naive datetime Objects

tips.title: Memorize latency gaps by orders of magnitude
tips.keyPoint: Illustrative orders of magnitude: memory about 100ns, SSD tens–100µs, intra-DC RTT 0.5ms, intercontinental RTT 150ms. Hardware, route, load, and access size change these; update estimates with measurements.
tips.body: Latency changes by orders of magnitude depending on where the data lives. A main-memory read and a cross-continent round trip differ by more than a millionfold. Exact values depend on hardware, but a sense of the magnitudes lets you judge a design quickly. A cross-continent round trip is bounded below by the time light takes through optical fiber, so faster servers do not shorten it.
tips.inDesign: This table explains why caches sit in the same data center as the app and why synchronous cross-region replication slows writes. Counting sequential round trips per request is the core of latency estimation.

tradeOffs.option: Call several times in sequence (the plain approach)
tradeOffs.gain: Simple to write and to trace during incidents
tradeOffs.cost: Round trips add up directly; 150 ms each to a distant service

tradeOffs.gain: Fewer round trips; waiting approaches the slowest single call
tradeOffs.cost: APIs must accept batches, and partial failures need handling

tradeOffs.option: Copy data close to users (CDN, in-region replicas)
tradeOffs.gain: Removes the cross-continent round trip altogether
tradeOffs.cost: Copies can lag and serve stale data; storage and sync cost more

sources.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know

tips.title: Mean concurrency = arrival rate × mean time in system (Little’s law)
tips.keyPoint: In a stable system, mean count = mean arrival rate × mean time in system. For DB connections, use mean connection holding time rather than total API latency, then size headroom separately.
tips.body: In steady state, mean count L = mean arrival rate λ × mean residence time W (L = λW). Use the same observation interval and system boundary. At 500 req/s and mean residence time 100ms, 50 requests are in the system on average. API requests including queues, running threads, and occupied DB connections are different quantities. Estimate occupied connections from the acquisition rate and mean time from acquisition to release. Measure QPS and holding time over the same processing boundary.
tips.inDesign: Estimate the mean for a peak interval using mean arrival rate and mean holding time. Set variability and failure headroom separately through load testing. Substituting p99 latency does not produce p99 concurrency. A proxy can pool connections but does not add DB execution capacity.

tradeOffs.option: Allow high concurrency (large pools, many threads)
tradeOffs.gain: Keeps accepting requests for a while when a dependency slows
tradeOffs.cost: Puts heavy concurrent load on dependencies and uses more memory and connections; hides the slowdown and spreads the outage

tradeOffs.gain: Protects dependencies and memory, and rejects overflow early
tradeOffs.cost: A small rise in latency hits the cap and errors start

tradeOffs.option: Shorten the time per request (caching, better queries)
tradeOffs.gain: The same concurrency handles a higher arrival rate
tradeOffs.cost: Takes engineering effort, and the payoff depends on the bottleneck

tips.title: 90% utilization is not headroom; waiting time explodes
tips.keyPoint: For steady-state M/M/1, mean response time = mean service time ÷ (1 − utilization ρ). At ρ = 90% it is ten times service time; ρ is not interchangeable with measured CPU utilization.
tips.body: Arrivals are bursty, so queues form more often as utilization rises. In an M/M/1 model the mean response time is S / (1 − ρ): twice the service time at 50% utilization, 10x at 90%, and 20x at 95%. Even if average utilization looks low, a few peak minutes can push you to the steep end of this curve. The higher the utilization, the more often a new request arrives while earlier work is unfinished, so both the chance of waiting and the length of the wait grow. That is why waiting time rises along a steep curve rather than a straight line.
tips.inDesign: In capacity planning, set a utilization ceiling derived from the latency target, such as "size the fleet for 60–70% CPU". The most heavily utilized resource (database, workers, connection pool) becomes the bottleneck.

tradeOffs.gain: Fewest servers and lowest cost
tradeOffs.cost: Latency is erratic and spikes with small load increases; no slack for failures

tradeOffs.gain: Stable latency that absorbs peaks and a server failure
tradeOffs.cost: You pay for 30-50% of capacity sitting idle most of the time

tradeOffs.option: Defer work that can wait to a queue
tradeOffs.gain: Keeps online paths at low utilization while batch work soaks up the spare capacity
tradeOffs.cost: Results are not immediate, and the queue needs monitoring and operation

tips.title: Track p99 as well as the mean: fan-out that waits for every response inherits the slowest
tips.keyPoint: If delays are independent and all 100 responses are required, a 1% slow probability per server becomes about 63% overall. Correlated delays from shared failures require a different model.
tips.body: Measure tail latency such as p99 alongside the mean. Fan-out waiting for every response inherits any slow server. If each server is independently slow with probability p, the probability of at least one slow response among n servers is 1 − (1 − p)^n. At p = 1% and n = 100 this is about 63%, roughly six in ten. GC and retransmits cause delays; shared network failures or congestion introduce correlation, so check the independence assumption.
tips.inDesign: Define SLOs at p99 or p99.9, and combine mitigations: reduce fan-out, allow timeouts with partial results, and resend slow requests to another replica (hedged requests). If hedged requests are sent only for requests still pending past, say, p95, the extra load stays at a few percent.

tradeOffs.gain: Can assemble complete results if every response succeeds
tradeOffs.cost: The slowest server sets the latency of the whole request

tradeOffs.option: Cut off at a timeout and return partial results
tradeOffs.gain: Puts a ceiling on latency
tradeOffs.cost: Quality drops (some results missing), and callers must handle incomplete answers

tradeOffs.option: Hedged requests (resend only slow ones to another replica)
tradeOffs.gain: Cuts tail latency sharply
tradeOffs.cost: Adds duplicate request load. Restrict to side-effect-free requests or operations safe to duplicate

sources.title: Google Research — The Tail at Scale

tips.title: For one-AZ loss across three AZs, two-thirds of total capacity is a theoretical ceiling; add headroom
tips.keyPoint: When one AZ fails, the remaining AZs take all the traffic. Run enough capacity for after the failure before it happens.
tips.body: With load spread evenly over N availability zones (AZs), losing one sends its traffic to the other N−1, so each carries N/(N−1) times its normal load: 1.5x with three AZs, 2x with two. Adding servers by autoscaling after the failure takes minutes, and the same incident can slow down getting new servers at all.
tips.inDesign: With equal AZ capacities and even distribution, staying within capacity after one AZ fails requires a normal load fraction at most 2/3 for three AZs or 1/2 for two. At 100% after failure there is no room for queueing or imbalance. Size using safe per-server throughput that meets latency goals, with extra margin for failover imbalance and retries. This supports static stability.

tradeOffs.option: Always hold one AZ's worth of spare capacity (+50% across three AZs)
tradeOffs.gain: Keeps serving through a failure without doing anything (static stability)
tradeOffs.cost: A third of the fleet sits idle in normal times

tradeOffs.option: Add servers by autoscaling after the failure
tradeOffs.gain: Lowest cost in normal times
tradeOffs.cost: Overloaded for the minutes servers take to start, and the incident may block getting capacity at all

tradeOffs.option: Spread over more AZs (four or more)
tradeOffs.gain: Less spare capacity needed (+33% with four AZs)
tradeOffs.cost: More complex to run, with more cross-AZ traffic and cost

sources.title: AWS Builders' Library — Static stability using Availability Zones

tips.title: Interpret load tests with representative data, caches, skew, and duration
tips.keyPoint: When data size, cache state, access skew, or test length differ from production, a load test reports better numbers than reality.
tips.body: Load test environments tend to be smaller and cleaner than production. With little data, indexes and tables fit in memory, and hitting the same keys over and over pushes the cache hit rate near 100%. Replacing external APIs with a mock removes their latency and limits. A test of a few dozen minutes never surfaces problems that build over time, such as memory leaks, GC, LSM compaction, or growing logs. Reading from memory versus disk changes latency by orders of magnitude, so these differences are not rounding errors.
tips.inDesign: Before testing, list how the environment differs from production and close each gap: data size (production row counts and distribution, with personal data masked), starting with an empty cache, reproducing key skew (popular products or accounts), and using real dependencies or stubs that reproduce their limits and latency. Split tests by purpose: a soak test at expected peak for hours, a spike test for sudden surges, and a test that searches for the breaking point. Record results with their conditions: how many servers, under what conditions, and what p99.

tradeOffs.option: Test with production-like environments and data
tradeOffs.gain: Numbers close to production that you can plan capacity with
tradeOffs.cost: Preparing the environment and data costs time and money, and personal data must be masked

tradeOffs.option: Test in production (side-by-side runs, gradually increased load)
tradeOffs.gain: Real data, caches, and dependencies: the most accurate
tradeOffs.cost: Failures affect users, and writes and external side effects must be isolated

tradeOffs.option: Test a small environment and scale up by server count
tradeOffs.gain: Cheap, fast, and repeatable
tradeOffs.cost: Misses effects that change sharply with size, such as data no longer fitting in memory

tips.title: Estimate configured DB connection ceilings as instances × processes × pool limit
tips.keyPoint: Scaling the app out multiplies database connections by the pool size. Size against the autoscaling maximum, and if that exceeds the database's limit, shrink the pools or put a connection proxy in between.
tips.body: Each app instance keeps database connections in a connection pool and reuses them. From the database's side, the connection count is instances × processes per instance × pool size. When autoscaling quadruples the instances, connections quadruple too, and a rolling deploy adds more while old and new instances run side by side. Past the database's max_connections, new instances cannot connect and fail, at exactly the moment load is highest. Staying under the limit is not enough either: PostgreSQL uses a process and memory per connection, and once concurrently running queries far exceed the CPU cores, switching and contention slow everything down. A bigger pool is not a faster one.
tips.inDesign: Estimate connections at the autoscaling maximum and during deploys, not at normal load, and compare with the database's limit. Set a total budget from the database's cores and divide it by the instance count to get each pool's size. When instance counts swing widely, or on serverless, put a connection proxy such as PgBouncer or RDS Proxy in front so connections on the database side stay flat. Monitor how long requests wait for a free connection.

tradeOffs.gain: Caps database connections without adding parts
tradeOffs.cost: Each instance runs fewer queries at once, and requests wait for a free connection more often

tradeOffs.option: Funnel connections through PgBouncer or RDS Proxy
tradeOffs.gain: Database-side connections stay flat as instances grow
tradeOffs.cost: One more component and hop, and transaction pooling rules out session-level features

tradeOffs.gain: A settings change widens the limit right away
tradeOffs.cost: More memory per connection, and too many concurrent queries slow everything down

tips.title: Traffic between AZs is billed, and replication multiplies it
tips.keyPoint: Estimate cross-AZ volume from routes and replica destinations. Charges vary by service, direction, and region, with exceptions such as free internal replication; separate volume and price assumptions.
tips.body: AZ distribution can send replication and reads across boundaries. With independent uniformly distributed endpoints across three AZs, the cross-AZ fraction is 2/3. With replication factor three and the two follower copies in other AZs, the payload crosses twice. Traffic volume is not identical to billable volume: AWS services and routes have exceptions. With Topology Aware Routing or follower reads, also verify failure headroom and pricing conditions.
tips.inDesign: In capacity planning, estimate daily cross-AZ transfer alongside CPU and storage. Send readers to a follower or instance in their own AZ (a Kafka client's rack ID, Kubernetes Topology Aware Routing), so that only replication and failover cross AZs. Compress to send fewer bytes. Watch cross-AZ transfer per service in the billing breakdown.

tradeOffs.gain: Load spreads evenly across AZs, and the setup is simple
tradeOffs.cost: Every write and read pays transfer charges, multiplied by the number of copies

tradeOffs.option: Point readers at copies or instances in their own AZ
tradeOffs.gain: Lower transfer charges and latency
tradeOffs.cost: Load per AZ can skew, and followers may return slightly stale data

tradeOffs.gain: No cross-AZ charges
tradeOffs.cost: Losing that AZ takes everything down

sources.title: AWS Data Exports — Understanding data transfer charges
AWS Architecture Blog — Overview of Data Transfer Costs for Common Architectures

tips.title: Shorter timeouts downstream, and pass the remaining budget along
tips.keyPoint: Propagate deadlines and cancellation downstream, and make downstream work detect and honor them. Propagation alone does not automatically stop running work.
tips.body: A call without a timeout holds threads and connections while a stuck dependency hangs. And when downstream timeouts are longer than upstream ones, downstream services keep working on results nobody will receive after the caller gives up, adding load during an incident.
tips.inDesign: Hand out the time budget from the outside in (for example, client 3 s → API 2.5 s → each service 1 s → database 300 ms). Rather than hard-coding values everywhere, pass the request's deadline downstream and fail fast when too little time remains. Derive values from measured downstream latency, such as p99.9.

tradeOffs.option: Hard-code a timeout at each hop
tradeOffs.gain: Simple
tradeOffs.cost: The sum can exceed the caller's timeout, and downstream keeps working after the caller gives up

tradeOffs.gain: Work that cannot finish in the time left is never started
tradeOffs.cost: Every service and library must carry the deadline along

tradeOffs.gain: Stuck calls are abandoned early, freeing threads and connections
tradeOffs.cost: Slightly slow but healthy responses fail too; values must come from measurements

sources.title: AWS Builders' Library — Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

tips.title: Retries multiply across layers and amplify outages
tips.keyPoint: Retry at one layer only, with exponential backoff, jitter, and a retry budget.
tips.body: When every layer retries independently, attempts at the bottom layer are the product of each layer's attempts. The moment a dependency slows, load multiplies many times over and knocks down a service that was recovering (a retry storm). If every client retries on the same schedule, the load spikes line up.
tips.inDesign: Decide which single layer retries, and add random jitter to exponential backoff. Combine a retry budget (for example, at most 10% extra requests) or a circuit breaker that stops retrying when success rates drop. Retried operations must be idempotent.

tradeOffs.option: Every layer retries on its own
tradeOffs.gain: Each layer absorbs transient errors locally
tradeOffs.cost: Attempts multiply across layers during an outage

tradeOffs.gain: The maximum number of attempts is predictable
tradeOffs.cost: Every other layer must pass failures straight up

tradeOffs.option: Cap with a retry budget or circuit breaker
tradeOffs.gain: Retries shrink automatically during an outage
tradeOffs.cost: More settings and monitoring; bad thresholds give up on requests that would have succeeded

sources.title: AWS Builders' Library — Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

tips.title: Under overload, reject some requests quickly instead of serving all slowly
tips.keyPoint: Bound your queues and drop requests whose clients already timed out. Unbounded queues make everyone late.
tips.body: When requests exceed capacity, an unbounded queue keeps growing and every request waits longer. Eventually the server keeps working on requests whose clients have already timed out, so it is busy yet almost nothing succeeds. Rejecting early with 429 or 503 lets the accepted requests finish in time. Rejected requests can be retried a little later, and accepted ones succeed in time. That yields more successful responses overall than accepting everything and making everything late.
tips.inDesign: In interviews, volunteer what happens beyond peak. Combine bounded queues, priority-based shedding (keep payments, drop recommendations), discarding expired requests, and backpressure to upstream callers.

tradeOffs.gain: Never rejects anything in normal times
tradeOffs.cost: Under overload everyone is late, and resources go to requests that already timed out

tradeOffs.gain: Limits admission to preserve more requests within latency goals; not a guarantee of success
tradeOffs.cost: Some users get explicit errors, and clients need sane retry behavior

tradeOffs.gain: Protects critical work such as payments
tradeOffs.cost: Needs a priority scheme and agreement on what to drop

sources.title: AWS Builders' Library — Using load shedding to avoid overload

tips.title: An expiring hot key turns into a database stampede
tips.keyPoint: Collapse recomputation of a key into one request, and serve stale data or make the rest wait.
tips.body: When a key read thousands of times per second expires, every request at that moment misses and sends the same heavy query to the database at once (a cache stampede). Giving many keys the same TTL makes them expire together and causes the same effect.
tips.inDesign: Coalesce same-key work with single flight. Go’s singleflight.Group coordinates only callers sharing a Group in one process; fleet-wide coordination needs a distributed lock, lease, or another mechanism. Combine stale-while-revalidate, early refresh, and TTL jitter according to freshness needs. Coalescing suppresses duplicate work; it does not guarantee the latest value. A jittered TTL can spread expiry across multiple keys.

tradeOffs.option: Collapse recomputation into one and make others wait (single flight, locks)
tradeOffs.gain: Reduces duplicate recomputations within the coordination scope; freshness depends on the source and update policy
tradeOffs.cost: Waiting requests are slower, and the lock needs an expiry in case its holder dies

tradeOffs.option: Serve the stale value while refreshing in the background (stale-while-revalidate)
tradeOffs.gain: Readers never wait
tradeOffs.cost: A slightly old value shows until the refresh completes

tradeOffs.gain: Stops many keys from expiring at once
tradeOffs.cost: Does nothing for a single hot key, and expiry times vary

tips.title: Estimate required dependency availability with a product only under an independence model
tips.keyPoint: If dependency uptime is independent, requiring five 99.9% dependencies gives about 99.5%. With perfectly overlapping outages it is 99.9%, so the product is not a universal upper bound.
tips.body: Assume success requires every dependency to be available. Under independence, availability is the product; independent equivalent replicas can be estimated by 1 − (1 − a)^n. Shared regions, configuration changes, or identity systems create correlation. If all five dependencies have perfectly overlapping outages, overall availability remains 99.9%. Model common causes and degraded operation, and compare using the same observation interval and availability definition.
tips.inDesign: Start with an independence model, then examine critical path dependencies and shared failures when setting an SLO. Isolate optional dependencies through timeouts and graceful degradation. Connect error budgets and SLAs to measurements and operational decisions rather than treating the calculation as a guarantee.

tradeOffs.option: Add dependencies in series (success needs all of them)
tradeOffs.gain: Features can be built and run as separate parts
tradeOffs.cost: Falls as a product in the independent model; real impact depends on correlation and required success conditions

tradeOffs.gain: Core features keep working when they fail
tradeOffs.cost: Degraded behavior must be designed and tested, and some features go missing

tradeOffs.gain: Availability rises as 1 − (1 − a)^n
tradeOffs.cost: Costs more, and does nothing if the copies fail together

tips.title: Shrink the blast radius by design, before the outage
tips.keyPoint: When everyone shares one platform, one customer's bad request stops everyone. Cells and shuffle sharding limit who gets caught. Validate isolation including shared dependencies and configuration.
tips.body: Redundancy helps when one server fails, but not when the same failure hits every server. A request that crashes servers, a sudden surge from one customer, or a bad configuration push takes down every shared server. Adding servers does not help while everyone uses the same pool: everyone is still affected.
tips.inDesign: Split users or tenants into independent cells (small copies of the same environment) so a failure in one cell does not spread. Shuffle sharding goes further and gives each customer a different combination of servers. There are 28 ways to pick 2 servers out of 8, so only a small share of customers overlap a bad customer on both. Roll out configuration and deployments cell by cell, too, to limit the blast radius of changes themselves.

tradeOffs.gain: Most efficient use of resources and simplest to run
tradeOffs.cost: One customer's problem reaches everyone

tradeOffs.gain: Failures and bad deployments stay inside one cell
tradeOffs.cost: Each cell needs its own headroom, lowering efficiency, and routing plus cross-cell operations are needed

tradeOffs.gain: Even with few servers, very few customers share an exact combination
tradeOffs.cost: Assignments must be managed, and clients must be able to retry on the other server

sources.title: AWS Builders' Library — Workload isolation using shuffle-sharding

tips.title: Some outages do not end when the load drops (metastable failures)
tips.keyPoint: After the trigger is gone, retries or cold caches keep load above capacity. Getting out means deliberately pushing load well below capacity.
tips.body: Even a system with plenty of headroom can enter a bad state when a trigger such as a brief surge, a deployment, or a lost cache pushes it past capacity. Clients retry timed-out requests, and the retries cause more timeouts. A cold cache raises database load, and the slowed database keeps the cache from warming up. With such a self-sustaining loop, load stays above capacity after the trigger is gone, and the system does not recover by itself. This is called a metastable failure.
tips.inDesign: Think of an outage as a trigger plus a loop that sustains it, and break the loop by design. Cap retries with a retry budget and a circuit breaker, and reject load beyond capacity early (load shedding). Make sure you can throttle traffic to what the database can take with a cold cache. As a recovery procedure, decide and rehearse in advance how to throttle hard at the entry point and then ramp back up gradually.

tradeOffs.option: Cap retries with a retry budget and circuit breaker
tradeOffs.gain: Breaks the loop that keeps retries sustaining the load
tradeOffs.cost: More requests give up on transient errors, lowering the success rate a little

tradeOffs.option: Have a procedure to throttle the entry point and recover
tradeOffs.gain: Reliably gets out of the bad state
tradeOffs.cost: Some users are rejected on purpose during recovery, and how hard to throttle and how fast to ramp up are judgment calls

tradeOffs.gain: Absorbs the surges that act as triggers
tradeOffs.cost: Costs more, and a trigger beyond the headroom still leads into the same bad state

sources.title: USENIX OSDI '22 — Metastable Failures in the Wild

tips.title: Retries of non-idempotent writes need deduplication such as idempotency keys
tips.keyPoint: A request that timed out may still have finished on the server. The client creates one idempotency key per operation and sends the same key on every retry; the server stores the key with the result and returns the saved result for repeats.
tips.body: When the network fails, the client cannot tell "never processed" from "processed, but the response was lost." Retrying a read is harmless, but retrying a payment or an order as is can run it twice. An idempotency key makes the operation idempotent: a unique value the client creates for each operation and sends unchanged on every retry, never regenerated. The server stores the key, the request contents, and the result, and when the same key arrives again it skips the work and returns the saved result. Write the key in the same transaction as the operation's effect, and put a unique constraint on it so that only one of two simultaneous requests proceeds. A request that reuses a key with different contents is misuse and gets an error. Keep keys longer than the client may keep retrying. For external effects outside the DB transaction, combine provider-side idempotency, an outbox, and outcome queries as appropriate. A local key record alone cannot prevent both duplicate charges and lost work.
tips.inDesign: Let every externally called write API accept an idempotency key, and design it together with the retry policy. Keep keys longer than the longest time a client or queue might retry. If the same key arrives while the first request is still running, do not process it twice; answer "in progress" so the client retries later. Queue consumers and webhook receivers can treat the message ID as the idempotency key.

tradeOffs.gain: Prevents duplicate effects within a boundary that atomically couples the key record and the effect
tradeOffs.cost: Needs storage for keys and results, a retention period, and handling for duplicates that arrive mid-flight

tradeOffs.option: A unique constraint on a business key such as the order number
tradeOffs.gain: Little extra machinery; existing tables block duplicates
tradeOffs.cost: Does not work for operations without a natural key, and the second response has to be rebuilt by hand

tradeOffs.gain: Nothing runs twice
tradeOffs.cost: Transient failures become user-facing errors, and whether the write happened stays unknown

sources.title: IETF — The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field (Internet-Draft)

tips.title: Returning a timeout does not stop the work behind it
tips.keyPoint: Propagate request cancellation to database calls, HTTP calls, and loops. Cancellation does not undo completed writes.
tips.body: Even after a timeout response, database or external API work can continue occupying connections and CPU. In Go, derive a child context with a deadline from the request context and pass it to QueryContext and downstream HTTP requests. Loops and concurrent work must observe cancellation and exit; release cancellation functions, response bodies, and other resources. Stopping is cooperative and depends on drivers and downstream implementations, so it is not an immediate-stop guarantee. Cancellation does not roll back committed database writes or completed payments. Resolve uncertain writes through status checks and idempotency; use a durable job for work that must finish.
tips.inDesign: For search, aggregation, and external calls, decide whether work remains useful after the caller stops waiting. Cancel unnecessary work; persist accepted work that must finish as a managed job. Test connection and worker cleanup after disconnection and deadlines.

tradeOffs.gain: Reduces unnecessary work and resource retention
tradeOffs.cost: Needs support throughout the chain and handling for uncertain write outcomes

tradeOffs.option: Hand required work to a durable job
tradeOffs.gain: Work can finish and be tracked after caller disconnection
tradeOffs.cost: Requires durable acceptance, progress, retry, and deduplication design

tips.title: A timed-out write may have an unknown outcome rather than a failure
tips.keyPoint: An external side effect may finish without a response arriving. Represent unknown outcomes explicitly and use the same business operation identity for lookup, safe retries, and reconciliation.
tips.body: If a connection breaks immediately after an external payment succeeds, the caller cannot determine success or failure from that observation alone. Recording failure locally and creating another payment can double-charge. An idempotency key suppresses duplicates within the provider’s API and retention contract; it does not guarantee an immediate final outcome. Retain the unresolved operation, look up the provider operation ID or mapped business ID, and resolve it through verified notifications or periodic reconciliation. Without a provider guarantee for safe retries, do not automatically repeat the side effect.
tips.inDesign: Ask: what if the provider succeeds but we stop before storing the result? Persist the operation ID, submitted parameters, and attempt history, and expose a pending-confirmation state. Retry the same operation with the same key within its guarantee window; reconcile after that window. Handle duplicate and out-of-order notifications. Drop only the response after a side effect, then check for duplicate execution and abandoned unknown outcomes.

tradeOffs.option: Return pending confirmation and resolve through notifications or lookups
tradeOffs.gain: Keep responses short while exposing uncertainty honestly
tradeOffs.cost: Provide user-visible states, authenticate notifications, and handle duplication and ordering

tradeOffs.option: Add periodic reconciliation and manual review for unresolved operations
tradeOffs.gain: Catch missing notifications and operations left unresolved
tradeOffs.cost: Require lookup capacity and operational ownership, with delayed final confirmation

sources.title: AWS Builders’ Library — Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

tips.title: In a composite index, put equality columns first and range columns last
tips.keyPoint: In a multicolumn B-tree, leading equality conditions followed by a range condition usually restrict the scan well. Searches without the leading condition may use skip scan or other plans; check the product, version, and plan.
tips.body: A multicolumn B-tree sorts by the left column, then by the next within equal values. (tenant_id, created_at) can read a tenant’s date range contiguously. Reversing the order may be less efficient. PostgreSQL 18 also supports skip scan, repeatedly probing distinct leading values, so a missing leading condition can still be useful. Selectivity, distinct counts, and statistics affect the plan; inspect scan scope and returned rows.
tips.inDesign: Choose the column order from the `WHERE` and `ORDER BY` of your most frequent queries. Put equality condition columns (`=`) first and range condition columns (`>`, `BETWEEN`) or the `ORDER BY` column last. Every index is updated on every write, so before adding several similar ones, check whether one can serve multiple queries. Use `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` to compare rows read from the index with rows returned.

tradeOffs.option: Build one composite index for the frequent query
tradeOffs.gain: Reads only the needed rows and skips the sort
tradeOffs.cost: Queries needing another order may be less efficient; inspect plans

tradeOffs.gain: Every query gets fast
tradeOffs.cost: Every write updates every index, so writes slow down and storage grows

tradeOffs.option: Use single-column indexes and let the database combine them
tradeOffs.gain: Fewer indexes that work for many conditions
tradeOffs.cost: Reads more than a composite index and cannot serve the `ORDER BY` sort

tips.title: PostgreSQL does not index the referencing side of a foreign key for you
tips.keyPoint: When you add a foreign key, also index the column on the child table, so deleting a parent does not read the whole child table.
tips.body: With a foreign key, every time a parent row is deleted or its key changes, the database checks for child rows that still reference it. The parent's primary key has a unique index, but PostgreSQL does not automatically index the referencing column on the child table (such as `user_id`). Without one, each parent delete reads the entire child table (a sequential scan), and deletes slow down as the child table grows. ON DELETE CASCADE runs the same full scan to find the child rows to remove.
tips.inDesign: It matters wherever parents get deleted: account closures, organization deletion, bulk cleanup of old data. Create the child table's column index in the same migration as the foreign key (a composite index with that column leftmost, such as `(user_id, created_at)`, also works). On an existing database, list foreign key columns without an index and fix them. MySQL (InnoDB) requires an index on foreign key columns and creates one if missing, so this is easy to miss when moving databases.

tradeOffs.gain: Restricts referencing-row lookup; large cascades and lock waits still cost time
tradeOffs.cost: Every child write updates one more index, and storage grows

tradeOffs.option: Soft-delete parents (`deleted_at`) instead of deleting them
tradeOffs.gain: No child table check on each delete
tradeOffs.cost: Child rows stay forever, and every query needs a condition to exclude deleted rows

tradeOffs.option: Skip the foreign key and enforce integrity in the app
tradeOffs.gain: No check on delete, and tables are easier to split across databases
tradeOffs.cost: Bugs or manual fixes can leave rows pointing at parents that no longer exist

tips.title: Read, compute, write back, and a concurrent update disappears (lost update)
tips.keyPoint: Compute stock or balance changes in the database, as in `UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1`, or detect conflicts with a version column.
tips.body: When two requests each read a value, compute in the app, and write the result back (read-modify-write), the later write overwrites the earlier one and one update silently disappears (a lost update). PostgreSQL's default Read Committed only makes writes to the same row wait their turn; it does not notice that the value you read went stale. Even under the same name, Repeatable Read, PostgreSQL fails the later writer, while MySQL (InnoDB) applies updates to the latest row and lets the overwrite through. Check your own database's behavior rather than trusting the isolation level's name.
tips.inDesign: For updates that are additions or subtractions, such as stock, balances, points, or like counts, compute in the database. For updates you cannot express that way, such as editing a form and saving it, keep the `version` you read and write with `UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?`; if zero rows change, re-read and retry (optimistic locking). For heavily contended rows, lock at read time with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. Duplicate decrements on retries are a separate issue; design order-level idempotency and outcome checks too.

tradeOffs.option: Compute in the database (`SET stock = stock - 1`)
tradeOffs.gain: Prevents arithmetic lost updates in one statement; deadlock and communication-failure handling remain necessary
tradeOffs.cost: Only works for updates you can write as an expression, like additions

tradeOffs.option: Detect conflicts with a version column (optimistic locking)
tradeOffs.gain: Works for any computation or form edit, with no lock waits
tradeOffs.cost: Retries pile up under contention, and you must handle zero-row updates

tradeOffs.option: Lock at read time with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
tradeOffs.gain: Processes one at a time reliably even under heavy contention
tradeOffs.cost: Requests wait on locks, and a wrong lock order causes deadlocks

tips.title: Snapshot isolation still lets writes to different rows break invariants
tips.keyPoint: Guard "read a condition, write a different row" logic with Serializable or explicit locks.
tips.body: When two transactions read the same data to check a condition and then update different rows, no conflict is detected because they never write the same row. Each decision is correct alone, yet together they break an invariant such as "at least one doctor on call" (write skew). PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation and does not prevent it. Snapshot isolation detects only concurrent writes to the same row, not another transaction changing rows you read.
tips.inDesign: It appears in double bookings, constraints spanning balances, and username uniqueness. State whether you use Serializable (SSI in PostgreSQL) with retries on serialization errors, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the rows behind the decision, or unique and exclusion constraints enforced by the database.

tradeOffs.gain: Keeps implemented checks and updates equivalent to serial execution; does not supply omitted business checks
tradeOffs.cost: More serialization failures, retries are mandatory, and throughput drops under contention

tradeOffs.option: Lock the rows the decision reads with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
tradeOffs.gain: Targeted and reliable
tradeOffs.cost: You must pick the right rows, waits and deadlocks can occur, and rows that do not exist yet (a booking about to be made) cannot be locked

tradeOffs.option: Let unique or exclusion constraints enforce it
tradeOffs.gain: Most reliable, even against application bugs
tradeOffs.cost: Only works for conditions a constraint can express

tips.title: Lock rows in different orders and you get deadlocks
tips.keyPoint: When updating several rows, have every transaction lock them in the same order, such as by ascending ID, and make deadlock errors retryable.
tips.body: When a transfer from account 1 to 2 and one from 2 to 1 run at once, one takes the row lock on account 1 first and the other on account 2, and each waits for the other's row. The database detects this wait cycle and aborts one transaction, which can only start over. The cause is a lock order that differs between code paths: if everyone locks in the same order, a later transaction simply waits for the earlier one, and no cycle can form.
tips.inDesign: For transfers or multi-item reservations, use the same immutable ID order on every path. For example, sort target IDs and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE each row before updating. An IN clause alone does not define acquisition order. Other tables and foreign-key locks can still matter, so support whole-transaction retries for PostgreSQL 40P01 or MySQL 1213.

tradeOffs.option: Sort the rows by ID before updating
tradeOffs.gain: The wait cycle cannot form at all
tradeOffs.cost: You need to know every row to update up front

tradeOffs.option: Acquire SELECT ... FOR UPDATE row locks one by one in ID order first
tradeOffs.gain: Avoids cycles on these row locks among paths following the same order
tradeOffs.cost: Locks are held longer, so other work waits more

tradeOffs.option: Accept deadlocks and retry the error
tradeOffs.gain: Simple to build and enough when deadlocks are rare
tradeOffs.cost: Detection delay (1 s by default in PostgreSQL) plus the redo adds latency, and frequent deadlocks cut throughput

sources.title: MySQL — How to minimize and handle deadlocks

tips.title: Waiting for an external API after updating or locking rows prolongs row-lock holding
tips.keyPoint: Keep transactions to database reads and writes and close them quickly; move external API calls before or after the commit.
tips.body: Row locks taken by a transaction's updates stay until commit or rollback. Call a payment or notification API in between, and the time spent waiting for the response becomes time spent holding the lock, so every other request that wants to update that row waits. When the API slows down, the waiting requests use up the connection pool and unrelated pages stall too. On top of that, while a transaction stays open, PostgreSQL's VACUUM cannot remove old row versions it might see, and MySQL (InnoDB) cannot discard its undo log, so storage grows in both.
tips.inDesign: Move payments, email, HTTP calls to other services, and file uploads outside the transaction. Write a "processing" state in one short transaction, call the external API, then record the result in another short transaction. For a message that must go out exactly when the commit happens, write it to an outbox table in the same transaction. In PostgreSQL, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` closes connections left idle with a transaction open.

tradeOffs.option: Move the API call outside and write state in two steps
tradeOffs.gain: Locks are held only while SQL runs
tradeOffs.cost: You need a job that finds and cleans up orders stuck in "processing"

tradeOffs.option: Write to an outbox and let another process call the API after commit
tradeOffs.gain: Commits and API calls never drift apart, and calls can be retried
tradeOffs.cost: The result is asynchronous, so the page cannot show it right away

tradeOffs.option: Call it inside the transaction with a short timeout
tradeOffs.gain: Minimal code change
tradeOffs.cost: API latency still becomes lock time

tips.title: An ALTER TABLE waiting for its lock blocks every query that arrives after it
tips.keyPoint: Set `lock_timeout` to a few seconds for schema changes, and if the lock is not granted, give up and retry after a pause.
tips.body: Most forms of PostgreSQL's `ALTER TABLE` take an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. That lock conflicts even with a plain SELECT, so if a long query or transaction is using the table, the ALTER waits for it to finish. The trouble is that SELECTs and UPDATEs arriving after the waiting ALTER cannot jump ahead of it and join the lock queue behind it. Even a change that finishes instantly, like adding a column, stops all access to the table for as long as one long query in front of it runs.
tips.inDesign: In migrations, cap the wait with something like `SET lock_timeout = '3s'`, fail if the lock is not granted, and retry after a pause. Do no slow work, such as rewriting every row or validating a constraint, while holding the lock. Build indexes with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, and add foreign keys or CHECK constraints as NOT VALID before checking them with `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`. Before running, also check for long-running queries or transactions.

tradeOffs.gain: Limits blockage from lock acquisition waits; holding time after acquisition needs separate control
tradeOffs.cost: At busy times it may keep failing, and the migration drags on

tradeOffs.option: Stop long-running queries before running it
tradeOffs.gain: The ALTER gets its lock immediately
tradeOffs.cost: Analytics or batch jobs get interrupted

tradeOffs.option: Run it as maintenance during quiet hours
tradeOffs.gain: Fewer people are affected if it waits
tradeOffs.cost: Releases become less frequent, and it is not an option for services busy around the clock

tips.title: Checking before INSERT does not prevent duplicates; enforce a database constraint
tips.keyPoint: A pre-insert SELECT can race. Use UNIQUE for uniqueness, NOT NULL for required values, and CHECK for row-level rules.
tips.body: Two concurrent signup requests can both SELECT and conclude that an email is absent. Like form validation, that check can improve feedback but cannot guarantee consistency. Put a unique constraint in the database and handle a conflicting INSERT. For per-tenant uniqueness, use `UNIQUE (tenant_id, normalized_email)` with both columns NOT NULL; choose normalization rules for the business. A quantity column might use `quantity integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0)`. In PostgreSQL a CHECK expression yielding NULL passes, so CHECK alone does not make a field mandatory.
tips.inDesign: Use this for signup, membership IDs, order numbers, and relational schemas. Encode invariants so batch jobs and administrative tools follow them too. Map constraint violations to identifiable application errors without returning raw SQL or submitted data.

tradeOffs.option: Combine database constraints with application validation
tradeOffs.gain: Combines concurrency safety with useful feedback
tradeOffs.cost: Needs translation from database violations to application errors

tradeOffs.option: Not recommended: prevent duplicates with SELECT alone
tradeOffs.gain: Sequential code is easy to write
tradeOffs.cost: Concurrent requests and other write paths can insert duplicates

tips.title: Put the expected state in UPDATE instead of checking and then writing
tips.keyPoint: For order cancellation or claiming work, include the key and expected state in WHERE and check affected rows. Do not silently treat zero rows as success.
tips.body: After reading pending and deciding cancellation is allowed, another request may change the order to shipped. SELECT and UPDATE occur at different instants. Use a conditional update such as `UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'pending' RETURNING id`. Under PostgreSQL Read Committed, a conflicting updater waits and re-evaluates WHERE against the updated row. For this single-row transition, one returned row means success; zero means absence or a state conflict. Enforce authorization in the same scope and follow the API’s disclosure rules on a miss. This does not make external shipping or payment atomic.
tips.inDesign: For approval, cancellation, publishing, or claiming work, list permitted state transitions first. Check affected rows or RETURNING and define whether a conflict triggers a reread, 409, or an already-completed result. Multi-row invariants need additional transaction design.

tradeOffs.option: Use a conditional write for a single row
tradeOffs.gain: Detects races between reading and writing
tradeOffs.cost: Requires defined handling for zero rows and conflicts

tradeOffs.option: Lock the row within a transaction
tradeOffs.gain: Makes multiple operations based on a read easier to coordinate
tradeOffs.cost: Needs control of lock duration, order, and waiting

tips.title: Separate DB updates and message sends can succeed independently
tips.keyPoint: Record business data and the event in one DB transaction using an outbox. Provide retention, relay recovery, and retries, and monitor unsent-event backlog.
tips.body: "Save to the database, then publish" loses the event if the process dies in between, while "publish, then save" emits events for orders that never existed. Distributed transactions spanning a database and a message broker are unavailable or too heavy in most setups. Recording within the DB can be atomic while external delivery remains a separate stage.
tips.inDesign: With a transactional outbox, business data and the event are written in one database transaction, and a relay or CDC reads the outbox and publishes. Delivery becomes at-least-once, so consumers deduplicate by event ID. Expect interviewers to probe consistency between writes and events. Recover unsent events after relay restarts and do not delete them before delivery confirmation. Monitor oldest-unsent age and retry failures.

tradeOffs.option: Save to the database, then publish directly
tradeOffs.gain: Simplest and lowest latency
tradeOffs.cost: A crash in between loses the event

tradeOffs.gain: Data and event are always written together
tradeOffs.cost: An outbox table and relay to operate, slightly delayed publishing, and duplicate deliveries that consumers must remove

tradeOffs.option: CDC (publish from the database's change log)
tradeOffs.gain: No publishing code in the application
tradeOffs.cost: A CDC pipeline to run, and table structure tends to leak into the event format

tips.title: Reading from async replicas can hide your own writes
tips.keyPoint: After a user writes, read their data from the leader or a caught-up replica (read-your-writes).
tips.body: With asynchronous replication, replicas trail the leader by milliseconds to seconds, and the gap widens under load or during incidents. Reading from a replica right after an update can return the old value, and values may flip back and forth between reloads (a monotonic-read violation).
tips.inDesign: When offloading reads to replicas, decide which screens need which guarantees. Read a user's own data from the leader for a while after they write, remember the write position (LSN) and use only replicas that have caught up, or pin each user to one replica.

tradeOffs.gain: Always sees the latest value
tradeOffs.cost: All load lands on the leader, and reads cannot be spread

tradeOffs.option: Read from the leader only after a user's recent write
tradeOffs.gain: Users see their own changes while other reads stay on replicas
tradeOffs.cost: You must define what counts as recent, and lag beyond that window still shows

tradeOffs.option: Remember the write position (LSN) and use only replicas that have caught up
tradeOffs.gain: Correct no matter how long the lag
tradeOffs.cost: The position must travel with the session, and with no caught-up replica you wait or go to the leader

tips.title: Compare LSM and B-tree write, read, and amplification costs under real workloads
tips.keyPoint: LSM trees batch and append to speed up writes, paying for it in reads and compaction.
tips.body: B-trees update pages in place, giving consistently fast reads. LSM trees buffer writes in memory, flush them as sorted files, and later merge files (compaction). Writes become fast sequential I/O, but reads may need to check several files. B-tree databases also buffer updates and group WAL persistence, so one logical update is not one physical random write.
tips.inDesign: Write-heavy data such as logs, metrics, and messages suits LSM-based stores like Cassandra or RocksDB. Bloom filters and caches keep read amplification in check. Conversely, data that mixes reads and updates and needs range queries and steady reads, such as users or orders, suits B-trees as in PostgreSQL or MySQL (InnoDB). With LSM, compaction keeps using disk and CPU, so budget headroom for it.

tradeOffs.gain: Fast sequential writes that also compress well
tradeOffs.cost: Reads may check several files, and compaction uses disk and CPU in the background, causing latency spikes

tradeOffs.gain: Fast, steady reads and good range queries
tradeOffs.cost: Low-locality updates outside cache increase page I/O; actual I/O also depends on buffering and WAL

tips.title: Replicas alone do not protect against accidental deletion; verify backups by restoring them
tips.keyPoint: A mistaken delete reaches replicas within seconds. Keep backups you can restore to a point in time, and measure how long restoring actually takes.
tips.body: Replication protects against hardware and AZ failures, but it faithfully copies application bugs, a broken migration, and an operator's `DELETE`. Backups have their own surprises: you often learn during the incident that they were failing or that restoring takes many times longer than expected.
tips.inDesign: Decide RPO (how much data you may lose) and RTO (how long recovery may take) first, then pick the mechanism. Use point-in-time recovery to go back to just before a mistake, and copy backups to another account or region. Run a restore test regularly and measure the time against data size to confirm you meet the RTO. Restores usually create a new database, so plan how to switch connections or write back only the missing rows.

tradeOffs.gain: Fast failover and resilience to hardware faults
tradeOffs.cost: Mistaken deletes and bugs replicate within seconds and cannot be undone

tradeOffs.gain: Can go back to just before a mistake
tradeOffs.cost: Storage costs money, and restores take longer as the database grows

tradeOffs.option: Copies in another account or region
tradeOffs.gain: Survive an account compromise or a region outage
tradeOffs.cost: More transfer and storage cost, and more restore steps

sources.title: GitLab — Postmortem of database outage of January 31

tips.title: Chain work across services with compensating steps (a saga)
tips.keyPoint: Commit each service's local transaction in turn, and if a step fails, undo the completed steps in reverse order with compensating transactions.
tips.body: When orders, payments, and inventory each have their own service and database, one database transaction cannot commit them together. Distributed transactions such as two-phase commit need every database and service to support them, and if the coordinator fails everyone waits. A saga commits each step as that service's own transaction, and when a later step fails, it runs compensating transactions that cancel out the completed steps. Unlike a database rollback, though, intermediate states (payment held but inventory not yet reserved) are visible to other work.
tips.inDesign: Make each step and compensation idempotent, persist state, and support resumption. Idempotency does not guarantee success: monitor failed compensations and define retry limits, manual reruns, and human resolution. Expose intermediate states such as held credit as pending. Define the pivot and irreversible operations, and track progress through orchestration or choreography.

tradeOffs.gain: Everyone commits together, and no intermediate state is visible
tradeOffs.cost: Every participant must support it, everyone waits if the coordinator fails, and it is slow and couples services tightly

tradeOffs.gain: The flow lives in one place, easy to follow and change
tradeOffs.cost: The coordinator is one more service to run, and knowledge of the flow concentrates there

tradeOffs.gain: No center; services are loosely linked by events
tradeOffs.cost: The overall flow is written nowhere and hard to follow, and event cycles are easy to miss as steps grow

tips.title: Run big updates and deletes in small, throttled batches
tips.keyPoint: One giant UPDATE stalls production through locks and replica lag. Small batches can still block or overshoot lag thresholds; they do not guarantee a ceiling.
tips.body: Changing tens of millions of rows in one UPDATE or DELETE holds locks for a long time and makes other writes wait. The flood of changes also hits replicas at once, widening replica lag. If it fails midway, the whole thing rolls back, which also takes a long time.
tips.inDesign: Split by primary key ranges into batches of 1,000–10,000 rows and commit each batch. Watch replica lag and database load, and pause when they cross a threshold. Record progress so the job can resume, and make it safe to run more than once.

tradeOffs.gain: Done in one go, simple to write
tradeOffs.cost: Locks and replica lag stall production, and a failure means a long rollback

tradeOffs.gain: Runs during the day without stalling production
tradeOffs.cost: Takes longer, and the application must handle a half-updated state

tradeOffs.option: Stop the service and run it in a maintenance window
tradeOffs.gain: Simple procedure
tradeOffs.cost: Downtime, and big tables may not finish within the window

tips.title: CAP forces a choice only during a network partition
tips.keyPoint: During a partition, choose consistency or availability; even without one, latency trades off against consistency.
tips.body: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition you cannot both return the latest value on every response (consistency) and answer every request (availability). PACELC adds that even without a partition, waiting for replicas to sync raises latency. A partition is when the nodes are running but the network between them is cut, so neither side knows the other's state. Accepting writes on one side then makes the sides diverge.
tips.inDesign: Rather than "pick two of CAP", decide partition behavior per feature. A strong answer: balances favor consistency and reject writes, while like counts favor availability and converge later.

tradeOffs.gain: Never returns stale or conflicting values
tradeOffs.cost: One side of the partition rejects writes or reads with errors

tradeOffs.gain: Both sides keep responding
tradeOffs.cost: Stale values for a while, plus a way to reconcile conflicts later (merging)

tradeOffs.option: Wait for synchronization even in normal times (EC in PACELC)
tradeOffs.gain: Can preserve read/write order within the chosen consistency protocol’s guarantees
tradeOffs.cost: Each write is slower by a round trip to the replicas

tips.title: R + W > N guarantees intersecting read/write sets within the same replica set
