tips.keyPoint: Within the same N replicas, a completed write’s W acknowledgers and R readers intersect when R + W > N. This alone does not guarantee concurrent write ordering or linearizability.
tips.body: W writers and R readers chosen from the same N replicas share at least one replica when R + W > N. A read can recover a preceding completed write if there are no later or concurrent writes and version selection recognizes it as newer. Concurrent and partially failed writes, timestamp ordering, sloppy quorum, and membership changes need separate handling. Intersection alone is not linearizability. R + W > N expresses this same-set condition.
tips.inDesign: For Dynamo- or Cassandra-style consistency levels, check the data-center and replica scope. N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 can retain intersection with one replica unavailable, but freshness and conflict resolution depend on product semantics. Choose a suitable protocol when strict serialization is required.

tradeOffs.gain: Fastest reads
tradeOffs.cost: A single node failure blocks writes

tradeOffs.gain: Can obtain two responses despite one replica failure and intersect read/write sets in the same replica set
tradeOffs.cost: Both wait for two responses, slower than asking one node

tradeOffs.gain: Fastest, and works with two nodes down
tradeOffs.cost: May read stale values, and needs later repair (read repair)

tips.title: hash mod N moves almost every key when you add one node
tips.keyPoint: With balanced placement, adding one node moves an expected fraction about 1/(N + 1). Actual movement depends on ring and key distribution; removing one node instead has a rough fraction of 1/N.
tips.body: Assigning nodes with `hash(key) % N` reassigns most keys the moment N changes. Consistent hashing places keys and nodes on the same ring and assigns each key to the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node affects only a neighboring range. Virtual nodes also even out the load.
tips.inDesign: When you grow a cache cluster or shard set, it avoids mass cache misses and bulk data movement. When discussing sharding in interviews, explain how you will rebalance, too.

tradeOffs.gain: Simple and evenly distributed
tradeOffs.cost: Changing the node count moves almost every key

tradeOffs.gain: Balanced placement limits expected movement to about 1/(N + 1) on addition and 1/N on removal
tradeOffs.cost: The ring must be managed, and too few virtual nodes skew the load

tradeOffs.option: Range partitioning with an assignment table
tradeOffs.gain: Fine control over what moves, and range queries work
tradeOffs.cost: Needs a metadata service holding the assignments, which must stay available too

tips.title: Adding shards never spreads a single hot key
tips.keyPoint: One key always lands on one shard. Split the key itself or replicate its reads.
tips.body: Hash partitioning evens out load across many keys, but all traffic to one key hits the shard that owns it. Skew is normal in real traffic: celebrity posts, items on sale, global counters.
tips.inDesign: Split write-hot keys into N keys with suffixes and sum them when reading (write sharding). Absorb read-hot keys with local caches or replicas. In feeds, merge posts from accounts with huge followings at read time instead of fanning out on write.

tradeOffs.option: Split the key into N suffixed keys (write sharding)
tradeOffs.gain: Distributes writes when subkeys map across shards; N keys do not guarantee N distinct servers
tradeOffs.cost: Reads must sum N keys, which is slower and more complex

tradeOffs.option: Serve reads from copies or local caches
tradeOffs.gain: Absorbs concentrated reads
tradeOffs.cost: Does not help concentrated writes, and copies may be stale

tradeOffs.gain: Fewer writes reach the database
tradeOffs.cost: Updates in the buffer are lost on a crash, and changes show up later

tips.title: A distributed lock cannot stop a client that missed its expiry
tips.keyPoint: Attach a monotonically increasing fencing token to writes and have storage reject stale ones.
tips.body: If a process holding a leased lock stalls for a long GC pause or network delay, the lease can expire and another process can take the lock. The first process resumes believing it still holds the lock and writes, colliding with the new holder. Checking right before writing does not help if the pause falls between the check and the write.
tips.inDesign: Distinguish locks for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work) from locks for correctness. When correctness depends on it, have the storage verify monotonically increasing tokens issued by the lock service. Leader election works the same way: reject writes from old leaders by epoch number.

tradeOffs.gain: Simple, and enough for avoiding duplicate work
tradeOffs.cost: Cannot stop a long-paused process from writing, so correctness is not guaranteed

tradeOffs.gain: The store reliably rejects writes from a stale holder
tradeOffs.cost: The store must be able to check tokens, which not every storage system can

tradeOffs.gain: Issues monotonically increasing numbers correctly
tradeOffs.cost: Another cluster to operate, and acquiring locks is slower

sources.title: Martin Kleppmann — How to do distributed locking

tips.title: Machine clocks drift; don't rely on wall time for order or duration
tips.keyPoint: Measure durations with a monotonic clock; order events with sequence numbers or logical clocks.
tips.body: Wall-clock time can jump forward or back when NTP syncs, and machines can disagree by milliseconds or more. "Last timestamp wins" can therefore let a write from a skewed clock erase a correct update. Monotonic clocks never go backward, so use them for timeouts and durations.
tips.inDesign: With Last-Write-Wins, clock skew can discard updates. Lamport clocks preserve causal order, but numerical order does not imply causality and cannot detect concurrent updates. Version vectors can detect concurrency. DB sequence allocation order also differs from commit order; specify whether arrival, causal, or commit order is required.

tradeOffs.gain: Simple, and any node can decide
tradeOffs.cost: Clock skew can let an older update overwrite the correct one

tradeOffs.option: Have one leader or database assign sequence numbers
tradeOffs.gain: Provides an allocation order; for a DB, check how it differs from commit order
tradeOffs.cost: The single numbering point can become a bottleneck or single point of failure

tradeOffs.gain: Lamport clocks preserve causal order; version vectors also help detect concurrent updates
tradeOffs.cost: Complex, and the application must resolve the conflicts it detects

sources.title: Lamport — Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events

tips.title: A queue does not remove overload; it defers it, and the debt comes due
tips.keyPoint: While arrivals exceed processing, the backlog keeps growing. Monitor the age of the oldest message, not the count, and estimate how long draining takes.
tips.body: A queue smooths a temporary peak, but backlog grows by the excess arrival rate. With positive constant spare capacity, drain time = backlog ÷ (processing rate − arrival rate). Large spare capacity can drain it faster than the peak lasted; small spare capacity takes longer. Processing expired work delays new work too, so define deadlines and overload behavior.
tips.inDesign: Estimate consumer capacity and how long the backlog takes to drain after a peak. Monitor the age of the oldest message (consumer lag) rather than the count. Give queues a cap or retention period, and beyond it reject new work or drop old work. Give time-sensitive work a deadline, and when the backlog is large serve newest first (LIFO) or split queues per customer so one customer's flood does not delay everyone.

tradeOffs.option: Queue without limit and process everything in order
tradeOffs.gain: Never drops a message
tradeOffs.cost: Everyone gets later as the backlog grows, and expired work still consumes resources

tradeOffs.option: Cap the queue or set a retention period, rejecting or dropping beyond it
tradeOffs.gain: Puts a ceiling on delay
tradeOffs.cost: Rejected or dropped work needs handling (resending, telling users)

tradeOffs.option: Serve newest first (LIFO) or split queues per customer
tradeOffs.gain: Work that still matters finishes first, and one customer's flood does not delay others
tradeOffs.cost: Old work waits even longer, and there are more queues to run

sources.title: AWS Builders' Library — Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs

tips.title: Effects outside an exactly-once guarantee need their own deduplication
tips.keyPoint: Distinguish delivery count, processing results, and external effects when checking the guarantee boundary. Deduplicate external DB updates or charges with idempotency keys or records in the same transaction.
tips.body: A sender cannot tell whether a message never arrived or arrived and only the reply was lost. The only way not to lose it is to resend, and resending can create duplicates. A queue consumer that crashes after processing but before committing its offset (how far it has read) processes the same message again after restarting. Kafka transactions give exactly-once results for reading from and writing to Kafka, but they do not cover side effects outside it, such as calling a payment API or writing to another database.
tips.inDesign: Deliver at-least-once and decide how to remove duplicates for each side effect. When writing to your own database, record the processed message ID in the same transaction and do nothing if it is already there. When calling an external API, pass a business ID such as the order ID as the idempotency key. Resends that arrive after the key's retention period (say, 24 hours) are not caught, so keep keys longer than resends can continue.

tradeOffs.gain: Nothing is processed twice
tradeOffs.cost: Messages in flight when the consumer crashes are lost

tradeOffs.gain: Nothing is lost, and the result is effectively once
tradeOffs.cost: Each side effect needs its own duplicate removal (recorded IDs, idempotency keys), with retention to manage

tradeOffs.gain: Reads and writes inside Kafka happen exactly once
tradeOffs.cost: No protection for side effects outside Kafka, higher write latency, and readers must use read_committed

sources.title: Confluent — Exactly-once Semantics Are Possible: Here's How Kafka Does It

tips.title: Moving a failed message aside does not complete the business operation
tips.keyPoint: A dead-letter queue (DLQ) isolates failed messages. Assign ownership, monitoring, retention deadlines, safe replay, and business-result reconciliation to recover unfinished work.
tips.body: A dead-letter queue reduces disruption from repeatedly failing messages, but shipping, notification, or other work remains unfinished. Redriving everything without fixing the cause repeats the failure. Replaying a partly successful operation can duplicate side effects. Preserve the original business operation ID and inspect duplicate protection and current business state before replay. Expired requests and order-sensitive operations cannot always be processed like fresh messages.
tips.inDesign: Ask: can the normal queue be empty while orders remain unshipped? Detect DLQ arrivals, assign an investigator, and decide what to do before messages expire. After fixing the cause, redrive a small sample and increase the rate without overwhelming normal work. Inject failure after the side effect and verify that replay avoids duplicates and matches the business completion records.

tradeOffs.option: Redrive at a limited rate after repairing and validating the cause
tradeOffs.gain: Recover unfinished work without overwhelming normal traffic
tradeOffs.cost: Implement duplicate, ordering, expiry, and stop-condition handling

tradeOffs.option: Individually reconcile uncertain side effects and expired requests
tradeOffs.gain: Reduce duplicate or inappropriate actions from automatic replay
tradeOffs.cost: Require operator work and audit records, slowing recovery

sources.title: Amazon SQS — Configuring dead-letter queue redrive

tips.title: "Safe" and "idempotent" HTTP methods are what retries and automated clients rely on (RFC 9110)
tips.keyPoint: RFC 9110 safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) do not request state changes in their semantics. Incidental effects such as logging are allowed. Safe methods plus PUT and DELETE are idempotent; this does not require identical responses.
tips.body: Safety concerns the semantics requested by the client. It allows incidental server effects such as access logs or accounting records. Implementing deletion or unsubscribe on GET can let crawlers or prefetchers trigger it unintentionally. Idempotency means repeated requests have the same intended effect as one, not identical status codes. Retrying a non-idempotent POST requires separately establishing safe retry semantics.
tips.inDesign: Use POST, PUT, or DELETE, never GET, for operations that change state. Make PUT and DELETE genuinely idempotent. If POSTs need retrying, accept an idempotency key. Check which methods your proxies' and clients' retry settings will resend. Keep semantics safe under automated prefetching too.

tradeOffs.option: Use POST, PUT, or DELETE for state changes
tradeOffs.gain: Automated GETs do nothing, and retries behave as the spec expects
tradeOffs.cost: No one-click links; a confirmation step is needed

tradeOffs.option: Add idempotency keys so POSTs can be retried
tradeOffs.gain: POSTs can be retried safely too
tradeOffs.cost: Keys and results must be stored and expired

tradeOffs.option: Complete the operation with a single GET link
tradeOffs.gain: The least effort for users
tradeOffs.cost: Scanners, prefetchers, and crawlers trigger it on their own

sources.title: RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics, Section 9.2 Common Method Properties

tips.title: Paginate lists with cursors, not OFFSET
tips.keyPoint: OFFSET slows down on deep pages and duplicates or skips rows when data changes.
tips.body: With `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000`, the database counts 100,020 rows from the start and throws away 100,000. Deeper pages get slower. And if new rows are inserted at the top while someone pages through, rows they already saw reappear on the next page.
tips.inDesign: Return the sort key of the last row (such as created_at and id) as a cursor, and fetch the next page with `WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20`. It walks the index directly, so every page is equally fast. You lose "jump to page 100", which suits infinite scroll and "next" buttons. This assumes unique immutable sort keys. Updates that move rows across the cursor can still duplicate or omit them; use a separate snapshot strategy when a consistent point-in-time listing is required.

tradeOffs.gain: Simple, and can jump to any page
tradeOffs.cost: Deep pages are slow, and inserts or deletes cause duplicates or gaps

tradeOffs.gain: With unique immutable sort keys and a suitable index, leading inserts do not shift position and deep OFFSET scans are avoided
tradeOffs.cost: Cannot jump to an arbitrary page; the sort key must include a unique column (id) and be indexed

tips.title: Without Cache-Control, caches guess how long to keep a response (RFC 9111)
tips.keyPoint: Under RFC 9111, caches may store a response without an explicit expiry by assigning a heuristic one. CDNs store with their default TTL, and some settings even override private. Mark per-user responses private or no-store, and check that CDN settings do not override them.
tips.body: HTTP caching follows the response's Cache-Control. Even without it, RFC 9111 lets a cache assign a heuristic expiration, with 10% of the time since Last-Modified given as a typical setting. A shared cache such as a CDN must not store a response marked private, and no-store forbids every cache from storing it. Shared caches also do not reuse responses to requests carrying an Authorization header unless explicitly allowed. That protection does not apply to APIs authenticated by cookie, though. And CDNs can let their own settings win over the origin's. Add a "cache everything" setting to responses with no Cache-Control, and one user's response can be served to another.
tips.inDesign: Set the intended Cache-Control on every response explicitly. Make per-user responses private or no-store, with middleware that does so by default. Give static files names containing a hash of their content and a long max-age. Check that CDN minimum TTLs and "cache everything" rules do not override the origin.

tradeOffs.option: Set Cache-Control explicitly on every response
tradeOffs.gain: Caching behavior is predictable
tradeOffs.cost: Needs a mechanism, such as default middleware, to prevent omissions

tradeOffs.gain: Prohibits storage by caches honoring the header; also check CDN overrides to prevent exposure
tradeOffs.cost: No caching benefit, so the origin carries more load

tradeOffs.gain: Takes effect right away without touching the origin
tradeOffs.cost: Overrides per-response directives and can store per-user responses

tips.title: Large integers in JSON get silently rounded in JavaScript (RFC 8259)
tips.keyPoint: RFC 8259 leaves numeric range and precision to implementations, and only integers within ±(2^53−1) are guaranteed to agree. Return a 64-bit ID as a JSON number and JavaScript changes its last digits. Send 64-bit integers as strings.
tips.body: The JSON spec sets no limit on the size or precision of numbers and lets implementations impose their own. Most use double-precision floating point, which represents integers exactly only from -(2^53−1) to 2^53−1; in JavaScript that ceiling is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (9007199254740991). 64-bit integer IDs such as Snowflake IDs run to 19 digits, far beyond it. JSON.parse raises no error; it silently rounds to the nearest representable value, so IDs turn into other IDs or two IDs collide. Server languages handle them correctly, so tests rarely catch it. Decimals such as money cannot be represented exactly in binary either, so send them as integers in the smallest unit or as strings.
tips.inDesign: Return 64-bit integers as strings in JSON, write that into the API spec from the start, and accept both numbers and strings. Send money as integers in the smallest unit or as decimal strings. When designing new IDs, consider whether clients need to treat them as numbers.

tradeOffs.gain: No language changes the digits
tradeOffs.cost: Comparing or sorting them as numbers needs conversion

tradeOffs.option: Generate IDs that fit in 53 bits
tradeOffs.gain: Safe as plain numbers everywhere
tradeOffs.cost: A smaller ID space and more constraints on ID design

tradeOffs.option: Use a BigInt-aware parser on clients
tradeOffs.gain: Exact values while keeping numbers
tradeOffs.cost: No guarantee every client uses it

sources.title: RFC 8259 — The JSON Data Interchange Format, Section 6 Numbers

tips.title: Random UUIDv4 primary keys scatter writes across the index (RFC 9562)
tips.keyPoint: UUIDv4 is random, so consecutive values land far apart in an index. As a B-tree primary key, every insert touches a different page, which slows down once the index no longer fits in memory. RFC 9562's UUIDv7 starts with a millisecond timestamp, so new values gather at the end of the index.
tips.body: RFC 9562 points out that UUIDv4 has poor database-index locality: values created in succession do not sit near each other. Inserting random values into a B-tree index reads and writes some page anywhere in the index on every insert. While the index fits in memory this hardly shows, but once it outgrows memory, each insert reads from disk and page splits increase. UUIDv7 puts a 48-bit Unix timestamp in milliseconds at the front, so new values arrive roughly in time order and only recent pages need to stay in memory. RFC 9562 recommends UUIDv7 over v1 and v6. Note, though, that a v7 ID reveals its creation time, and in distributed databases that split by key range, new values tend to pile onto the last range.
tips.inDesign: If a database with B-tree indexes uses UUID primary keys, choose UUIDv7. For external IDs whose creation time should stay hidden, keep a v4 in a separate column. In distributed databases that split by range, check that time-ordered keys do not concentrate writes in one place.

tradeOffs.gain: No creation time leaks, and writes never pile onto one spot
tradeOffs.cost: Writes scatter across the B-tree index and slow down as it grows

tradeOffs.gain: New values gather at the end, which suits indexes
tradeOffs.cost: IDs reveal creation time, and range-split databases see writes pile onto the end

tradeOffs.gain: Small and fast
tradeOffs.cost: Needs central ID assignment, and outsiders can infer counts and order

tips.title: Requests sent in TLS 1.3 0-RTT can be replayed by an attacker (RFC 8446, RFC 8470)
tips.keyPoint: 0-RTT saves one round trip on reconnect, but the data sent first is not protected against replay across connections. Accept only requests that change nothing in 0-RTT, and answer the rest with 425 Too Early so they are resent after the handshake.
tips.body: With TLS 1.3 0-RTT, a client uses a key from an earlier connection to send its first request (early data) without waiting for the handshake to finish. Saving a round trip helps on high-latency links such as mobile. But RFC 8446 says early data is not forward secret and carries no guarantee of non-replay between connections. An attacker who copies the traffic and sends the same data again can get the server to process a legitimate request twice. RFC 8470 has intermediaries that forward a request before the handshake completes add an Early-Data: 1 header, and lets servers unwilling to risk replay return 425 Too Early. Some GET handlers have side effects, so the method alone does not prove a request is safe.
tips.inDesign: If you enable 0-RTT, have the origin return 425 for state-changing requests that arrive with Early-Data: 1. Decide explicitly which endpoints may accept early data. When enabling it on a CDN or load balancer, confirm the Early-Data header reaches the origin.

tradeOffs.gain: Avoids the TLS early-data replay path; application retries still need separate handling
tradeOffs.cost: One extra round trip on every reconnect

tradeOffs.option: Accept only requests that change nothing in 0-RTT
tradeOffs.gain: Faster reads with little risk
tradeOffs.cost: You must verify which endpoints truly have no side effects

tradeOffs.option: Detect replays on the server and accept each once
tradeOffs.gain: Even state-changing requests can use 0-RTT
tradeOffs.cost: Needs a shared record of accepted requests across servers

sources.title: RFC 8470 — Using Early Data in HTTP
RFC 8446 — The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

tips.title: HTTP/2 and gRPC bundle requests onto one connection, so L4 load balancers skew load (RFC 9113)
tips.keyPoint: Under RFC 9113, a client keeps one connection to a given server and sends many requests over it at once. An L4 load balancer that picks a target per connection sends everything to whichever backend the connection reached. Balance per request with an L7 proxy, or on the client.
tips.body: With HTTP/1.1, clients opened many short connections, so balancing per connection spread load fairly evenly. With HTTP/2, connections stay open, and clients should not open more than one connection to the same host and port. Many requests are multiplexed over that single connection, and gRPC runs on top of HTTP/2. An L4 load balancer such as a Kubernetes Service chooses a target only when the connection opens, so every later request goes to the same Pod. Adding replicas does not help existing clients, which keep using their connections to the original Pods, so new Pods get no traffic.
tips.inDesign: Route gRPC and HTTP/2 traffic through an L7 proxy or service mesh that balances per request, or have clients know every backend and balance themselves. Set a maximum connection age on servers and use GOAWAY to make clients reconnect periodically, which also fixes skew after scaling. After scaling out, check that new Pods actually receive requests.

tradeOffs.option: Route through an L7 proxy or service mesh
tradeOffs.gain: Even balancing per request
tradeOffs.cost: One more hop, adding latency and operational work

tradeOffs.gain: No extra hop and low latency
tradeOffs.cost: Client implementation and configuration for each language

tradeOffs.option: Shorten connection lifetimes to force reconnects
tradeOffs.gain: Settings alone gradually fix the skew
tradeOffs.cost: Reconnection overhead, and a lag before balance returns

tips.title: Validate again at the API boundary, even when the form validates
tips.keyPoint: Validate types, presence, ranges, and relationships such as start before end on the server. Valid input still requires authorization.
tips.body: Browser validation helps users, but clients can call an API directly. Before business processing, input validation should check JSON types, required fields, string lengths, numeric ranges, enumerations, and array counts. Then check business rules such as end after start. Use an allowlist of writable fields instead of copying the entire request into a persistence model; profile updates must not set role or owner_id. Validation does not replace parameterized SQL or authorization. A valid account ID does not prove that the caller owns the account.
tips.inDesign: Define request types and enforce validation before business logic. Document whether unknown properties are rejected or ignored, and restrict writable fields either way. Test ordinary values, boundaries, cross-field contradictions, and tampering.

tradeOffs.option: Define dedicated request types and writable fields
tradeOffs.gain: Protects administrative persistence fields from unintended writes
tradeOffs.cost: Requires maintaining mappings to the business model

tradeOffs.gain: Detects typos and contract mismatches early
tradeOffs.cost: Needs care when evolving clients and servers independently

tips.title: Return an HTTP status and a stable error type instead of branching on prose
tips.keyPoint: Separate human explanations from machine identifiers. Represent failures with appropriate HTTP statuses so clients can decide whether to fix input, sign in, or wait.
tips.body: A client that matches the exact text “insufficient balance” breaks when wording or language changes. Use HTTP status for the broad outcome and a stable error type for business decisions. In Problem Details (RFC 9457), type identifies the problem while title and detail explain it to people. If you add a custom code, document its meaning and stability too. For example, consistently use 400 for malformed input and 409 for conflicts with current state. A 5xx response may leave a write outcome uncertain; status alone does not justify automatically retrying POST. Keep internal exceptions, SQL, and secrets out of responses, and use a reference ID to find safe diagnostic logs.
tips.inDesign: Define errors alongside successful API responses. Explain how callers can recover, provide a client fallback for unknown types, and connect reference IDs to access-controlled diagnostic logs.

tradeOffs.gain: Uses a shared format and available library support
tradeOffs.cost: Business problem types and client handling still need definition

tradeOffs.option: Keep an existing custom error format
tradeOffs.gain: Preserves existing client compatibility
tradeOffs.cost: Requires documenting types, extensions, and HTTP mappings

sources.title: ASP.NET Core — Handle Errors in APIs
RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs

tips.title: Distinguish omitted, null, zero, false, and empty strings in partial updates
tips.keyPoint: A partial update must preserve whether each field was sent. The PATCH method alone does not define what null means.
tips.body: Updating a display name should not reset an omitted notification setting to false. That bug occurs when decoding collapses field absence into a zero value. Preserve field presence: omitted means unchanged; false and zero are explicit values to apply. Define whether null clears a value, represents missing data, or is rejected. JSON Merge Patch uses null to remove a member and replaces arrays as a whole, so it may not suit APIs that must set literal null values. JSON Patch expresses operations such as replace and remove explicitly. Either format still requires checking writable fields and validating the resulting business state.
tips.inDesign: Use this for settings, profiles, and administrative partial updates. Verify whether decoding distinguishes omission from null; use presence flags or operation lists if needed. Test omission, null, false, zero, and empty strings separately.

tradeOffs.gain: Makes object updates concise
tradeOffs.cost: Unsuitable for setting literal nulls or editing individual array elements

tradeOffs.gain: Expresses removal, replacement, and preconditions explicitly
tradeOffs.cost: Requires per-operation validation and writable-path restrictions

sources.title: Kubernetes — Update API Objects with kubectl patch

tips.title: Limit work per request as well as the number of requests
tips.keyPoint: Bound body bytes, array items, page size, and concurrent work. Rate limiting alone cannot contain one oversized request.
tips.body: Ten requests a minute can still overwhelm memory and the database if one request reads a million records. Bound both the incoming body and expanded work: array items, query range, page size, and concurrent operations. Enforce a byte limit while reading instead of trusting Content-Length alone. If compression is accepted, limit decompressed size too. Set default and maximum page sizes and document whether excessive values are rejected or clamped. Limiting batch length does not prevent a burst of downstream calls if every item runs at once, so bound concurrency separately.
tips.inDesign: Use this for list, search, import, and batch endpoints. Choose limits from expected workloads and measured memory and execution time. Reject oversized bodies early with 413 and use a documented input error for item-count violations. Provide pagination or asynchronous jobs for legitimate bulk work.

tradeOffs.option: Limit synchronous request size and item counts
tradeOffs.gain: Makes resource use per ordinary request more predictable
tradeOffs.cost: Bulk callers must split their work

tradeOffs.option: Use asynchronous jobs for bulk work
tradeOffs.gain: Allows controlled scheduling and concurrency
tradeOffs.cost: Needs progress tracking, retries, and stored results

tips.title: CPU limits can throttle work; exceeding memory limits can lead to OOM termination
tips.keyPoint: requests reserve capacity for placement; limits are ceilings. At the CPU limit a container is paused until the next period (throttling) and latency grows; past the memory limit it is OOM killed. Match the runtime's thread count to the container's limit too.
tips.body: The Kubernetes scheduler places a Pod on a node by looking at its containers' requests, and a container may use more than its requests when the node has room. limits are ceilings, and they behave differently for CPU and memory. A CPU limit is enforced as a quota per Linux period (100 ms by default); once the quota is spent, the container is paused for the rest of the period. When a process with many threads runs them all at once, it can burn the quota early even at low average utilization, and the paused time lands directly in p99. Exceed the memory limit and the kernel ends the container with an OOM kill, losing in-flight requests. Older runtimes size their thread pools from the node's CPU count rather than the container's limit, which makes throttling more likely.
tips.inDesign: Set memory requests for placement and limits for runtime separately. Equal values do not prevent OOM when the app exceeds its limit. Allow headroom for peak use, GC, and native allocations. If applying CPU limits, measure throttling and check GOMAXPROCS or JVM settings against container limits and runtime version.

tradeOffs.gain: Protects other Pods on the node, and usage is predictable
tradeOffs.cost: Throttling can stretch p99 even with plenty of average headroom

tradeOffs.option: Set CPU requests only, no limit
tradeOffs.gain: Uses spare node capacity, with no throttling
tradeOffs.cost: Competes with neighbors for CPU, so performance depends on how busy the node is

tradeOffs.option: Set memory requests equal to limits
tradeOffs.gain: Accounts for limit-sized capacity during placement; does not prevent OOM from exceeding the limit
tradeOffs.cost: Reserves for the peak, holding memory that usually sits unused

tips.title: Autoscaling takes effect minutes after the load arrives
tips.keyPoint: After HPA decisions, metric delays, node provisioning, image pulls, and startup still take time. Scheduled scaling acts before demand; queue-length scaling reacts to backlog after arrival. Distinguish these and retain headroom.
tips.body: Metric collection, HPA control loops, node provisioning, image pulls, and startup add delay before new Pods accept work. Periods and scaling policies depend on configuration and version. Queue length grows after work arrives: it is not predictive, though it can represent backlog more directly than CPU. Separate pre-scaling by schedule or forecast from faster reactive scaling. Allow forecast error when using a predictive signal.
tips.inDesign: Measure the time a spike takes, broken down from metrics to Pod readiness. Scale ahead of predictable spikes on a schedule. Scale queue workers on queue length rather than CPU, with KEDA or similar. Keep spare node capacity, and shrink images to start faster. Scale in more slowly than you scale out.

tradeOffs.gain: Easy to set up, and works for any service
tradeOffs.cost: Scales only after the load arrives, so capacity falls short until Pods are ready

tradeOffs.option: Pre-scale on schedules; react to arrived backlog using queue length
tradeOffs.gain: Schedules can provision ahead of time; queue length can reveal waiting not visible in CPU
tradeOffs.cost: Needs well-designed signals or schedules, and a wrong guess pays for idle Pods

tradeOffs.gain: Absorbs spikes before any scaling
tradeOffs.cost: Pays for unused capacity all the time

tips.title: Serverless pays a startup cost on the first request (cold starts)
tips.keyPoint: New execution environments add startup and initialization latency, affecting the mean too. Their frequency and duration determine effects on p95 and p99. Provision warm capacity where needed and reduce initialization work.
tips.body: In serverless, when no idle execution environment is available, a new one is created, and the first request waits for initialization: starting the runtime, loading libraries, creating clients and database connections. That is a cold start, and depending on the language and framework it can take seconds. Warm environments are reused, so the average is fast, but during quiet hours and sudden spikes many requests hit cold starts. Each new environment also opens its own database connections, so connection counts jump during spikes. The remedy is to prepare initialized environments in advance with provisioned concurrency or minimum instances, which are billed even while idle. The mean changes with the warm/cold mixture. Rare cold starts may not appear in a particular percentile, so measure their frequency and latency distribution together.
tips.inDesign: Keep warm environments only for work with latency requirements, sized to peak concurrency and adjusted by schedule or utilization. Initialize once outside the handler, and defer initializing features until they are needed. Track the share of cold starts and initialization time as metrics.

tradeOffs.gain: Pay only for use, with no cost for waiting
tradeOffs.cost: p99 grows in quiet hours and during spikes

tradeOffs.gain: Stable latency
tradeOffs.cost: Billed while idle, and the count needs tuning

tradeOffs.gain: Shorter cold starts without extra cost
tradeOffs.cost: May require trimming dependencies or rethinking the language or framework

sources.title: AWS Lambda — Understanding the Lambda execution environment lifecycle

tips.title: Errors on every deploy? Check your shutdown
tips.keyPoint: On SIGTERM, stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests, then exit.
tips.body: If a process exits as soon as it receives SIGTERM, in-flight requests are cut off. And for the few seconds before the load balancer removes the pod, new requests keep arriving and fail to connect. A trickle of 502s on every deploy or scale-in usually comes from this.
tips.inDesign: Fix the shutdown order: (1) wait to be removed from the load balancer (in Kubernetes, sleep a few seconds in preStop), (2) stop accepting new work, (3) finish in-flight requests and jobs, (4) close database connections and exit. Keep the total under the grace period before a forced kill (terminationGracePeriodSeconds).

tradeOffs.gain: Fast shutdown
tradeOffs.cost: In-flight requests and those arriving before removal from the load balancer fail

tradeOffs.gain: Waiting for routing propagation and draining can reduce shutdown-related errors
tradeOffs.cost: Deployments and scale-in take longer by the wait

tradeOffs.gain: Work that outlasts the grace period is not lost
tradeOffs.cost: Progress must be saved and resume logic written

sources.title: Kubernetes — Pod lifecycle: termination of Pods

tips.title: Health checks that are too shallow or too deep both make outages worse
tips.keyPoint: Checking a shared dependency takes every server out when that dependency is merely slow. Restart decisions should depend only on the process itself; watch dependencies separately.
tips.body: A shallow health check that only sees whether the process responds misses servers that run but cannot work correctly: a full disk, a config that failed to load, expired database credentials. A deep health check that also tests a shared dependency such as the database fails on every server at once when that dependency slows down. A load balancer then removes every server, and a Kubernetes liveness probe restarts every pod, turning a temporary slowdown into a full outage.
tips.inDesign: A liveness probe (restart on failure) should check, inside the process, only states that a restart alone can fix, such as a deadlock. A readiness probe (remove from routing on failure) may include dependencies specific to that server, but a failure of a dependency every server shares must not remove them all. Configure the load balancer to fail open: when every server is unhealthy, send traffic to all of them. Watch shared dependencies with monitoring and alerts, not with removal decisions.

tradeOffs.gain: A shared dependency's outage never removes every server at once
tradeOffs.cost: Misses servers that run but cannot work correctly

tradeOffs.gain: Removes a single broken server, such as one with a bad config or expired credentials
tradeOffs.cost: A merely slow shared dependency fails every server at once, removing or restarting them all

tradeOffs.option: Deep health check plus fail open
tradeOffs.gain: Removes single broken servers yet keeps traffic flowing when all fail
tradeOffs.cost: Sends traffic even when every server really is broken, and the behavior is complex and hard to test

sources.title: AWS Builders' Library — Implementing health checks

tips.title: Without a PodDisruptionBudget, a node upgrade can stop a service's Pods all at once
tips.keyPoint: Cluster upgrades and node replacements are planned Pod evictions (voluntary disruptions). Without a PodDisruptionBudget limiting how many may stop at once, a service's Pods can be evicted together. Set that number to zero, though, and evictions never proceed, stalling the upgrade.
tips.body: Kubernetes separates disruptions it cannot prevent, such as hardware failure, from planned voluntary disruptions such as a drain for an upgrade or repair. A drain evicts Pods through the Eviction API, which honors PodDisruptionBudgets. A PDB sets how many of an application's Pods may be down at once from voluntary disruptions. Without one, a service's Pods sitting on the same node are evicted together, and the remaining ones take all the load. Conversely, a PDB demanding as many available Pods as there are replicas keeps rejecting evictions, and the drain cannot proceed. Managed services eventually lose patience and evict by force, so everything stops together anyway. A PDB does not prevent involuntary disruptions, but they count against its budget.
tips.inDesign: Give multi-replica services a PDB such as maxUnavailable: 1, and spread their Pods across zones and nodes. For single-replica services, add replicas or plan the downtime instead of blocking evictions with a PDB. Even with a PDB, make sure evicted Pods shut down cleanly, with proper termination handling and readiness.

tradeOffs.gain: Cluster upgrades move quickly
tradeOffs.cost: A service's Pods can all stop together

tradeOffs.gain: Bounds voluntary Eviction API disruptions by the budget; separately provide capacity and graceful shutdown
tradeOffs.cost: Upgrades take longer when there are many replicas

tradeOffs.gain: Planned disruptions never reduce Pods
tradeOffs.cost: Evictions stall, so the upgrade stops or times out into forced eviction

sources.title: Kubernetes — Specifying a Disruption Budget for your Application

tips.title: Use spot instances assuming they will be taken away
tips.keyPoint: Spot capacity is cheaper but interruptible. AWS’s roughly two-minute warning for stop/termination is best effort; hibernation may begin immediately. Support external state and checkpoint recovery without relying on warnings.
tips.body: Spot instances sell a cloud's spare capacity cheaply, and the cloud takes them back when it needs them. On AWS, an interruption notice appears in EventBridge and instance metadata two minutes before the stop, on a best-effort basis. Google Cloud Spot VMs get no advance notice by default, and the grace period before shutdown is at most 30 seconds, also best effort. So a job that runs for tens of minutes without saving progress starts over every time it is reclaimed. Instances of the same type tend to be reclaimed together. A web server must leave the load balancer on notice and finish in-flight requests before stopping.
tips.inDesign: Use spot for work whose state lives elsewhere and that can resume from a checkpoint. On an interruption notice, stop accepting new work and save state. Spread across several instance types and zones so a mass reclaim does not stop everything. Keep the minimum capacity you always need on on-demand instances.

tradeOffs.gain: Avoids Spot-specific reclamation; ordinary failures and maintenance still need handling
tradeOffs.cost: Expensive

tradeOffs.gain: Much lower cost
tradeOffs.cost: Needs resumable design, and work slows when reclaims are frequent

tradeOffs.option: An on-demand base topped up with spot
tradeOffs.gain: Cheaper while protecting minimum capacity
tradeOffs.cost: Two kinds of capacity to balance and manage

sources.title: Amazon EC2 — Best practices for EC2 Spot

tips.title: Page on SLO burn rate and complement it with preventive capacity alerts
tips.keyPoint: Alert on user impact through error-budget burn rate. Also warn before impact for risks such as disk exhaustion that need advance response.
tips.body: Alerting on causes like CPU or disk usage wakes people at night when users are fine, and stays silent when they are not. With an SLO, the speed at which you spend the allowed failures (the error budget) tells you whether action is needed now.
tips.inDesign: For a 30-day SLO, burn rate 14.4 for one hour spends 2% of the budget in a time-based or constant-traffic model. With request-based SLIs and variable traffic, count actual consumed requests. Route fast burn to pages and slower burn to tickets, combining long and short windows. Use CPU for diagnosis and retain preventive alerts for disk exhaustion or certificate expiry.

tradeOffs.gain: Early warning, with a hint at the cause
tradeOffs.cost: Fires when users are fine and stays silent when they are not

tradeOffs.gain: Pages match user impact and urgency
tradeOffs.cost: The SLO and its measurement must be designed first, and early signs with little impact are missed

tradeOffs.option: Require both a long and a short window
tradeOffs.gain: Ignores brief spikes and resets quickly after recovery
tradeOffs.cost: More complex conditions that take effort to understand

sources.title: Google SRE Workbook — Alerting on SLOs

tips.title: Carry one trace ID across services so logs connect
tips.keyPoint: Assign an ID at the edge, pass it downstream in headers, and log it everywhere.
tips.body: With microservices, one user action passes through several services, queues, and databases. If each service logs on its own, you cannot trace which request an error belongs to, or at which step it happened.
tips.inDesign: Generate a trace ID at the edge (load balancer or API) and pass it downstream in the W3C Trace Context `traceparent` header. Attach it to queue messages as an attribute too. Use structured (JSON) logs that always include the trace ID, and show the same ID on error pages so a support request leads straight to the logs. Do not reuse a fixed traceparent: share trace-id, and when creating a new span, set the outgoing parent-id to that sending span’s ID.

tradeOffs.gain: No extra work
tradeOffs.cost: Cannot tell apart requests at the same moment, and machine clocks drift

tradeOffs.option: Propagate a trace ID and log it
tradeOffs.gain: One search finds every service's logs
tradeOffs.cost: Every service, queue, and library must carry the ID, by convention and code

tradeOffs.option: Record every hop's timing with distributed tracing
tradeOffs.gain: Shows which hop is slow
tradeOffs.cost: Recording and storage cost money, so usually only a sample is kept

tips.title: Put user IDs in metric labels and the time series explode
tips.keyPoint: Every combination of label values is a separate time series. Unbounded values such as user IDs or URLs with IDs in them multiply storage and cost until the monitoring system falls over. Keep individual values in logs and traces.
tips.body: A metric creates a series for each observed name/label combination. Fifty endpoints, five statuses, and twenty Pods allow up to 5,000 combinations. Ten thousand user IDs raise the ceiling to 50 million, but actual series are fewer unless every combination occurs. Cardinality increases storage, memory, and query load. Classic histograms add bucket and related series; pricing depends on the monitoring service. Put individual IDs in logs or traces.
tips.inDesign: Use only labels whose values are bounded, such as endpoint templates (/orders/{id}) or statuses. Keep per-user and per-request values in logs and traces and investigate there. Cap the number of series you ingest, and monitor the series count itself.

tradeOffs.gain: Slice finely using metrics alone
tradeOffs.cost: Series and cost multiply, and the monitoring system can fall over

tradeOffs.option: Only bounded labels; individual values in logs and traces
tradeOffs.gain: Predictable monitoring cost and load
tradeOffs.cost: Per-user breakdowns are not possible in metrics and need logs or traces

tradeOffs.gain: An explosion does not take down monitoring
tradeOffs.cost: Data beyond the cap is dropped

tips.title: Adding application instances can overload a shared database or API
tips.keyPoint: Autoscaling increases application capacity without necessarily increasing shared dependency capacity. Budget total concurrency, request rate, and instance counts from downstream limits.
tips.body: If each instance can send 20 requests per second to an external API, ten instances can send 200 and forty can send 800. A shared API key limited to 300 requests per second becomes easier to overload as instances multiply. Per-instance rate limits and connection pools are not fleet-wide limits. Budget shared database, external API, and connection-path capacity across normal traffic, retries, batches, and overlapping releases. Even below a rate limit, slower responses increase in-flight work, so concurrency and waiting time need limits too.
tips.inDesign: Ask: if instance count quadruples, which downstream request rates can quadruple? Use shared rate control or conservative per-instance budgets and instance limits. Bound waiting time or reject work that cannot fit. Slow the dependency during load tests and verify that scaling does not exceed downstream capacity or let retries consume the entire budget.

tradeOffs.option: Manage a shared fleet-wide sending budget
tradeOffs.gain: Control aggregate downstream rate as instance counts change
tradeOffs.cost: Require a reliable control mechanism, window and burst rules, and budget allocation

tradeOffs.option: Conservatively cap instance counts and per-instance budgets
tradeOffs.gain: Bound expected load without adding distributed budget coordination
tradeOffs.cost: Leave capacity unused and verify assumptions including overlapping releases or temporary instance-count overshoot

sources.title: Google Cloud Run — Autoscaling impact on backing services
Google Cloud SQL — Manage database connections

tips.title: Build the image once and promote that same image to production
tips.keyPoint: Rebuilding per environment means what you tested is not what runs in production. Build once, and pass what differs between environments as configuration at runtime.
tips.body: If staging and production each run their own build, newer dependency versions or base image updates can slip in between the two. What you verified in staging is then a different image from what runs in production. And once you bake API URLs or feature switches into the build, you are forced to build per environment.
tips.inDesign: Build the image once in CI and promote its digest from staging to production. Pass values that change by environment (endpoints, credentials, feature flags) at runtime through environment variables or a ConfigMap. Even frontends, which tend to bake values into the bundle, can read a config file at startup. Keep deployment records that show which image runs in which environment.

tradeOffs.gain: Environment values can be baked into the build, and the setup is simple
tradeOffs.cost: No guarantee that what you tested is what runs in production

tradeOffs.gain: What you verified in staging is exactly what runs in production
tradeOffs.cost: The app must be changed to read environment values at runtime

sources.title: The Twelve-Factor App — V. Build, release, run

tips.title: Tags can be overwritten. Pin production images by digest
tips.keyPoint: Push to the same tag again and its content changes. Different nodes run different code, and a "rollback" can run the new version. Reference production images by digest and block tag overwrites in the registry.
tips.body: A tag such as `:latest` or `:v1` can be pushed again with a different image. With Kubernetes' pull policy IfNotPresent, nodes that already have the image start the old content while new nodes pull the new content, so one Deployment runs a mix of code. Rolling back to the previous tag does nothing if that tag has already been overwritten.
tips.inDesign: Write the image as `name@sha256:…` in the manifest, with CI filling in the digest of the build. Keep a tag alongside for humans to read. Block tag overwrites in the registry and never use `:latest` in production. To roll back, point at the digest that was running before.

tradeOffs.gain: Easy to update, and the same definition picks up new versions
tradeOffs.cost: Unclear what content is running and what to roll back to

tradeOffs.gain: Every node runs the same content and the rollback target is exact
tradeOffs.cost: Without CI updating the manifest, people end up handling long hashes

tradeOffs.option: Block tag overwrites in the registry
tradeOffs.gain: Prevents a tag from silently meaning different content
tradeOffs.cost: No re-pushing, so every fix needs a new tag

tips.title: When a shell is PID 1, check that SIGTERM reaches the application
tips.keyPoint: With a shell form ENTRYPOINT, the shell becomes PID 1 and SIGTERM never reaches the app. The app skips cleanup and is killed when the grace period ends. Use the exec form, or a tiny init that forwards signals.
tips.body: Write `ENTRYPOINT node server.js` in shell form and the container's first process (PID 1) is `/bin/sh`, with the app as its child. On shutdown SIGTERM goes only to PID 1, and the shell does not forward it. The app never starts its shutdown, and SIGKILL stops it once the grace period runs out. In-flight requests are cut off, and each pod adds a full grace period to every deploy.
tips.inDesign: Write ENTRYPOINT and CMD in exec form (`["node", "server.js"]`) so the app itself is PID 1. If you need a startup script, end it with `exec` to replace the shell with the app. PID 1 ignores signals it has no handler for, so register a SIGTERM handler in the app. For apps that spawn child processes, make a tiny init such as tini PID 1 to forward signals and reap zombie processes. Measure the time from SIGTERM to exit in your deploy tests.

tradeOffs.gain: Shell features such as variable expansion just work
tradeOffs.cost: SIGTERM never arrives, so every stop ends in a forced kill

tradeOffs.option: Use exec form so the app is PID 1
tradeOffs.gain: Signals arrive directly and shutdown starts at once
tradeOffs.cost: PID 1 ignores SIGTERM without a handler, so the app must register one

tradeOffs.option: Put an init such as tini in front
tradeOffs.gain: Signal forwarding and zombie reaping are handled for you
tradeOffs.cost: One more component to ship in the image

tips.title: Kubernetes Secrets are not encrypted by default
tips.keyPoint: By default Secrets sit unencrypted in etcd, and anyone who can create pods in the namespace can read them. Turn on encryption at rest, narrow permissions, and keep the source of truth in an external secrets manager. Values passed as environment variables stay stale after rotation until a restart.
tips.body: A Secret is only Base64-encoded, which is not encryption. By default it is stored unencrypted in etcd behind the API server. Even without permission to read Secrets, anyone who can create a Pod or Deployment in the namespace can start a container that mounts the Secret and read it. And when values are passed as environment variables, a running container keeps using the old password after rotation until it restarts.
tips.inDesign: Enable encryption at rest for etcd (backed by a KMS), and guard the right to create pods in a namespace as tightly as the right to read its Secrets. Keep the source of truth in an external secrets manager such as AWS Secrets Manager and rotate there. Hand values to the app as a volume it rereads, or have it fetch them after startup. During rotation, accept both the old and new values for a while before retiring the old one. Never put values in images or Git.

tradeOffs.option: Use Secrets alone, passed as env vars
tradeOffs.gain: Simple, and no app changes
tradeOffs.cost: Easy to leak without separately configured encryption and permissions, and every rotation needs a restart

tradeOffs.option: Keep the truth in a secrets manager, mount as a volume
tradeOffs.gain: Rotation and auditing in one place, and new values arrive without a restart
tradeOffs.cost: Another external dependency, and the app must reread values

tradeOffs.option: Have the app fetch values at startup and periodically
tradeOffs.gain: Always current, and no copy stays in Kubernetes
tradeOffs.cost: You must decide how startup and caching behave when the service is down

sources.title: Kubernetes — ConfigMaps (values consumed as environment variables)

tips.title: Hand-fix production and the next sync undoes it, or the drift lingers
tips.keyPoint: With GitOps or IaC, the definition in Git is the truth. A manual change is either erased by automatic sync or left behind as unrecorded drift. Route emergency changes through Git too, and detect drift regularly.
tips.body: Change settings directly with `kubectl scale` or the cloud console during an incident and Git no longer matches reality: drift. With Argo CD's self-heal on, the change is reverted to the definition within seconds and your fix disappears. With it off, the drift goes unnoticed until another change syncs and overwrites the manual values all at once.
tips.inDesign: Give people a procedure and permissions to ship emergency changes as small Git commits (an emergency path with a shorter review). If you must change something by hand, put the same change in Git right away. Let a sync tool such as Argo CD show drift at all times, and run Terraform's `plan -refresh-only` on a schedule to catch changes made outside the code. Do not hand out rights to change production manually by default.

tradeOffs.option: Always revert to the definition with self-heal
tradeOffs.gain: No manual changes or drift survive, and Git tells you what production looks like
tradeOffs.cost: Manual fixes during an incident are erased within seconds

tradeOffs.gain: Leaves room to fix things by hand in an emergency
tradeOffs.cost: Forgotten drift gets overwritten all at once by the next sync

tradeOffs.option: Route emergency changes through Git too
tradeOffs.gain: Changes are recorded and never fight the sync
tradeOffs.cost: A few minutes slower than a manual change, and the path must be kept ready to use

tips.title: IaC replacement creates a different resource: check data restoration and retention settings
tips.keyPoint: Change an attribute that cannot be updated in place and IaC deletes and recreates the resource. Miss the replacement in the plan and the data is gone. Protect data-holding resources from deletion, and stop plans that include replacement in CI.
tips.body: In Terraform or CloudFormation, changing an attribute that cannot change after creation, such as a database engine or storage encryption, triggers a replacement rather than an in-place update. Terraform deletes the old resource before creating the new one by default; CloudFormation creates the new one first and then deletes the old. Either way, unless you say otherwise, the data in the old resource is not kept. The plan shows this as a single marker (in Terraform, `-/+`).
tips.inDesign: Terraform prevent_destroy rejects destructive plans while the resource configuration remains; removing its block also removes that protection. Combine it with cloud deletion protection and CI plan checks. CloudFormation DeletionPolicy controls deletion and UpdateReplacePolicy controls old resources during replacement. Use supported Retain or Snapshot policies, rehearse restoration and migration, and split state to narrow routine changes.

tradeOffs.gain: No tooling needed, so you can start now
tradeOffs.cost: A single replacement line in a long diff gets missed

tradeOffs.option: Stop plans with replacements or deletions in CI
tradeOffs.gain: Even a missed line cannot delete production resources
tradeOffs.cost: Every intentional rebuild needs an approval step

tradeOffs.option: Separate data-holding resources into their own state and block deletion
tradeOffs.gain: Everyday changes never touch the database
tradeOffs.cost: Values must be passed across states, and there are more units to manage

tips.title: If the app starts before its sidecar proxy, its first calls fail
tips.keyPoint: Ordinary containers do not wait for each other’s readiness. Even native sidecar process startup differs from usable connectivity; gate application startup with a startupProbe that checks the required connection or an equivalent mechanism.
tips.body: Run a service mesh proxy or a database connection proxy as a regular container next to the app, and Kubernetes starts them without waiting for each to be ready. If the app fetches config or connects to the database right at startup, it fails because the proxy is not listening yet, and the app may restart repeatedly. In a Job it is the reverse: the app finishes but the proxy keeps running, so the Job never completes.
tips.inDesign: On Kubernetes 1.29 and later (stable in 1.33), declare the proxy as an init container with `restartPolicy: Always`, a native sidecar. The app starts only after the sidecar has started (and its startupProbe has passed, if it has one), and on shutdown the sidecar stops after the app. In Istio, `holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts` holds the app until the proxy is ready. In the app, also retry early outbound connections briefly. Without a startupProbe, a running process can allow startup to proceed. Explicitly probe the required connectivity when it must be ready first.

tradeOffs.option: Run it as a regular container
tradeOffs.gain: Works on any Kubernetes version
tradeOffs.cost: No start or stop order, so problems appear at startup and when Jobs finish

tradeOffs.gain: Manages process order and, with a suitable startupProbe, waits for required connectivity
tradeOffs.cost: Needs 1.29 or later, and your mesh and tooling must support it

tradeOffs.gain: No reliance on ordering, and more robust to other transient failures
tradeOffs.cost: Slightly slower startup, and retries must be added for every dependency

tips.title: The longer a branch lives, the more integration pain you pay all at once later
tips.keyPoint: Merge branches back to trunk within hours, a day at most. The longer a branch drifts, the more merge conflicts and rework pile up, until you need a freeze just to integrate. Hide unfinished features behind feature flags, not on branches.
tips.body: While a development branch lives on, trunk and every other branch keep moving. The diff at merge time grows from your changes and everyone else's, and conflict resolution, retesting, and redoing work all arrive together. Some teams set an integration day and declare a code freeze, but nobody can ship during the freeze. In trunk-based development, everyone merges to trunk at least once a day and keeps trunk releasable at all times. That takes splitting changes small, letting CI's automated tests confirm nothing broke before merging, and landing unfinished features on trunk switched off behind a feature flag. In DORA's research, teams with three or fewer active branches, daily merges to trunk, and no code freezes delivered both faster and more reliably.
tips.inDesign: In design review, ask how many weeks a feature will be built on a branch. If the answer is more than a few days, split it into pieces that can land on trunk without changing behavior, such as a schema addition, an internal API, or the back of a screen, and put only the user-visible switch behind a feature flag. Keep CI to around 10 minutes so a broken trunk gets fixed fast.

tradeOffs.option: Build each feature on a long-lived branch
tradeOffs.gain: Unfinished code stays off trunk, and the whole feature is reviewed together
tradeOffs.cost: Integration is deferred, so conflicts and retesting all arrive just before release

tradeOffs.gain: Daily integration keeps conflicts small, and trunk can ship at any time
tradeOffs.cost: Takes effort to split changes small, and to track flags and remove them later

tradeOffs.gain: Stabilizes a release without stopping work on trunk
tradeOffs.cost: As cherry picks into both branches grow, fixes get missed

sources.title: Martin Fowler — Patterns for Managing Source Code Branches

tips.title: Big changes wait longer for review and get reviewed less carefully
tips.keyPoint: Aim for one purpose per change, small enough for reviewers to follow. About 100 lines is a heuristic; generated files and change type affect useful size. Measure both mean wait time and a tail measure such as P75.
tips.body: Reading a 1,000-line change takes a block of time, so it waits until the reviewer's calendar opens up. Once they start, the volume makes details hard to follow, comments drift toward surface style, and design problems slip through. Meanwhile the author has moved on, and by the time comments come back the context is gone. Split the change small and a reviewer can read it in a few minutes between meetings, and the author can fix it the same day. You can split by building the next change on top of the previous one (stacking), by groups of files that need different reviewers, by layer, or by slicing a small feature vertically. Keep refactoring apart from behavior changes too; mixed together, the reader cannot tell what actually changed.
tips.inDesign: Once the design is settled, lay the implementation out as a series of small changes that each land on trunk without changing behavior, then start. As a team, measure how long a pull request waits for its first review at P75, and flag the ones that have waited long. Check that the faster turnaround has not come from rubber-stamping by watching how much time reviewers actually spend reading.

tradeOffs.option: Ship a feature as one big change
tradeOffs.gain: Reviewers see the whole thing at once, with no intermediate states to think about
tradeOffs.cost: Review comes later and shallower, and a revert takes everything with it

tradeOffs.gain: Reviews come sooner and closer, and you can revert only the change at fault
tradeOffs.cost: Takes effort to split so every intermediate state works, and to manage the order of changes

tradeOffs.option: Pair program so review happens while writing
tradeOffs.gain: No review wait, and design questions are settled on the spot
tradeOffs.cost: Ties up two people at once, and leaves less of a record for later readers

sources.title: Google Engineering Practices — Speed of Code Reviews

tips.title: Check service compatibility early with contracts and retain key end-to-end tests
tips.keyPoint: End-to-end tests start every service together, so they are slow, brittle, and hard to diagnose. Write the requests and responses a consumer relies on as a contract, and have the provider verify it in isolation; you find compatibility breaks sooner and more reliably.
tips.body: Rely on end-to-end tests that put every service and database in one environment to check how microservices fit together, and a run takes tens of minutes, the environment is locked to one suite at a time, and a hiccup in any one service fails the whole thing. When it fails, finding which service's change caused it takes a while, and soon nobody believes the failures. With contract tests, the consumer's tests write out the requests it sends and the responses it expects as a contract. The provider replays that contract in its own tests and checks that its responses satisfy it. Neither side needs the other running, and the provider is free to change fields no consumer uses. Check before deploying that the contracts with the versions already in the target environment have been verified, and changes that break compatibility stop before they reach production. Keep end-to-end tests, but only a few, for the main user journeys.
tips.inDesign: Once you draw a service boundary, keep a contract for each one recording who the consumers are and which fields they use. Verify every consumer's contract in the provider's CI, and before deploying, confirm compatibility with the versions in the target environment. Cut end-to-end tests to a handful of main journeys, and cover the rest with contract tests and each service's own tests.

tradeOffs.option: End-to-end tests with every service running
tradeOffs.gain: Checks that the whole journey works in a production-like setup
tradeOffs.cost: Slow and brittle, and tracing a failure to its cause takes time

tradeOffs.gain: Run in minutes without the other side, and show at once which change broke compatibility
tradeOffs.cost: Contracts take effort to write and maintain, and behavior or data combinations outside them go unchecked

tradeOffs.option: Check schema compatibility only, such as OpenAPI
tradeOffs.gain: Easy to adopt, and catches type changes and removed fields right away
tradeOffs.cost: Misses changes in what values mean, or in behavior consumers depend on, even when the types match

sources.title: Martin Fowler — Consumer-Driven Contracts: A Service Evolution Pattern

tips.title: If 500 tests fail independently with probability 0.1%, about 40% of CI runs fail
tips.keyPoint: Each flaky test may fail only rarely, but with enough of them, some test fails on every run. If failures are simply retried until green, nobody trusts a red build and real bugs slip through. Record tests that pass on a retry as flaky, then quarantine and fix them. The roughly 40% figure assumes independence; measure correlations such as shared-environment failures separately.
tips.body: With 500 tests that each fail independently 0.1% of the time, the chance all of them pass is 0.999 to the 500th power, about 61%. About 40% of CI runs go red even when the code is fine. Developers start rerunning red builds out of habit, and when a real bug fails a test, they rerun that until it passes too. Most flakiness comes from how tests are written: fixed sleeps instead of waiting for a condition, dependence on test order or shared data, dependence on the clock or random numbers, or calls to outside services. Sometimes, though, a race condition in the code itself shows up as flakiness. Use a retry to find flaky tests, not to erase failures. Record tests that passed on a retry, quarantine the ones over your threshold by removing them from the checks that block merging, and give each an owner to fix it.
tips.inDesign: Store CI results per test and measure how often each one both passes and fails on the same code. Quarantine tests whose flakiness rate crosses your threshold, and set a deadline to fix or delete them. Before adding a new test, run it a few dozen times in a row to confirm it is stable.

tradeOffs.option: Retry failures automatically until they pass
tradeOffs.gain: CI turns green quickly and work keeps flowing
tradeOffs.cost: Flakiness goes unrecorded, and real bugs hide behind the retries

tradeOffs.option: Record tests that pass on a retry and quarantine them
tradeOffs.gain: A green build can be trusted, and the tests to fix are listed
tradeOffs.cost: What the test covered is less protected while it is quarantined, and fixing it needs people and time

tradeOffs.gain: The noise disappears right away
tradeOffs.cost: The behavior that test protected is no longer checked by anything

sources.title: Google Testing Blog — Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them
Martin Fowler — Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests

tips.title: Roll out changes gradually, and keep rollback instant
tips.keyPoint: Canary, widen in steps, then everyone. Stop and roll back when metrics worsen.
tips.body: Many outages start with a code or config change. Ship to every server at once and, by the time you notice, every user is affected. Shipping to a slice first and comparing old with new finds problems while the blast radius is small. Check rollback boundaries before exposure, since some data changes cannot be undone.
tips.inDesign: Define stages such as 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% of traffic and compare error rate and latency with the old version at each stage. Separate deploy from release with feature flags so turning a flag off is the rollback. Ship hard-to-reverse changes, like schema changes, ahead of time in a backward-compatible form.

tradeOffs.gain: Fast and simple
tradeOffs.cost: Any problem hits every user

tradeOffs.gain: Problems surface while impact stays small
tradeOffs.cost: Takes longer to reach everyone, and needs monitoring and automation that compare versions

tradeOffs.option: Separate release from deploy with feature flags
tradeOffs.gain: Roll back in seconds without a deploy
tradeOffs.cost: Flag branches pile up in code and need cleanup, and some changes (database changes) cannot be undone by a flag

tips.title: A feature flag you are done with stays a live branch in production until you delete it
tips.keyPoint: Give each type of feature flag a lifetime, and once a release flag is on for everyone, delete it from both the code and the configuration. Leftover flags multiply combinations and keep old, untested code paths callable in production. Never repurpose a flag for a new meaning.
tips.body: A feature flag helps separate deploying from releasing, but each one adds a branch in the code. Ten flags make 1,024 combinations in theory, and almost none of them have been tested. A release flag has done its job once it is on for everyone, yet removing it tends to slip, leaving the old path behind as code that can still be called but is never used. Flags that pile up this way become technical debt. At Knight Capital in 2012, a flag for a feature unused for years was repurposed to turn on new functionality. One of eight servers did not get the new code, and on that server the flag ran the old code instead, leading to 4 million executions in about 45 minutes and a $460 million loss. Some flags, such as release, experiment, and operational flags, are meant to be removed, while kill switches and permission flags are meant to stay. Give each type a lifetime, and find and delete the ones past their date.
tips.inDesign: When you create a flag, record its type, its owner, and the date it should be removed, and open the cleanup ticket at the same time. Remove a release flag's code branch and configuration within a few weeks of turning it on for everyone. For flags meant to stay, such as kill switches, test both the on and off states regularly. Never reuse a flag's name or meaning.

tradeOffs.gain: You can switch back to the old behavior at any time
tradeOffs.cost: Branches and combinations multiply, leaving untested paths in production

tradeOffs.option: Delete the code once everyone has the feature
tradeOffs.gain: The code gets simpler, and old paths can no longer be triggered by mistake
tradeOffs.cost: The removal needs its own review and deploy, and going back means redeploying

tradeOffs.option: Set a lifetime and owner, with automatic reminders when it expires
tradeOffs.gain: Forgotten flags show up in a list, and cleanup becomes routine
tradeOffs.cost: Needs flag management tooling and the discipline to honor the dates

sources.title: Martin Fowler — Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags)

tips.title: Ship schema changes as expand, migrate, contract
tips.keyPoint: During a rolling deploy, old and new code run together. Change things in an order neither version breaks on.
tips.body: For the minutes a rolling deploy takes, old and new versions of the app share one database. Renaming or dropping a column in a single release makes old instances query a column that no longer exists. Adding an index to a large table can also block writes for a long time, depending on how it is done. Release a backward-compatible version first.
tips.inDesign: ① Add the column (expand). ② Move all writers, including old applications and jobs, to dual writes. ③ Backfill in small conditional batches without overwriting concurrent newer values. ④ Validate and switch reads. ⑤ Remove the old column (contract) only after the rollback window closes and old references are gone. After deletion, an old app cannot be rolled back on its own; prepare restoration or migration steps. Check this boundary with online schema changes too.

tradeOffs.gain: Few steps, done quickly
tradeOffs.cost: Old versions still running mid-deploy break, and rolling back is hard

tradeOffs.gain: Supports staged compatibility checks; old-version rollback can be prepared before removing the old column
tradeOffs.cost: Four or five releases over days or weeks, and the complexity of writing both forms for a while

tradeOffs.gain: Simple and certain
tradeOffs.cost: The service stops, which is not an option at some scales

sources.title: Martin Fowler — Parallel change (expand and contract)

tips.title: Record design decisions with the rejected options and the way back
tips.keyPoint: Spend time on decisions that are hard to reverse and decide easy-to-reverse ones quickly. Record the reasons for both so the assumptions can be traced later.
tips.body: A year later, the most useful part of a design doc is not the chosen option but the constraints at the time, the alternatives compared, and why they lost. Without that, successors cannot tell whether the assumptions changed, so they either repeat the debate or break a constraint that existed for a reason. And treating every decision with the same care slows down small decisions that could easily be undone.
tips.inDesign: For each decision, briefly write the context and constraints (numeric requirements), the chosen option, the alternatives and trade-offs, how to reverse it and at what cost, and when to revisit it (an ADR). Review hard-to-reverse decisions such as data models, public APIs, and where data lives in depth; let the owner decide easy-to-reverse ones such as library choices or features behind a feature flag quickly.

tradeOffs.option: Review every decision with the whole team
tradeOffs.gain: Fewer oversights
tradeOffs.cost: Even small, reversible decisions slow down

tradeOffs.option: The owner decides quickly and records it
tradeOffs.gain: Fast progress
tradeOffs.cost: Applied to hard-to-reverse decisions, it can force a big migration later

tradeOffs.gain: No writing effort
tradeOffs.cost: The reasons are lost, leading to repeated debates or broken constraints that existed for a reason

tips.title: Delivery speed and stability are not a trade-off; measure them together as a set
tips.keyPoint: Measure delivery performance with five metrics: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate, and deployment rework rate. Business outcomes and overall development value require other perspectives too.
tips.body: Output measures such as lines, tickets, and velocity are easy to inflate and say nothing about whether value reached users. DORA measures software delivery along two dimensions: throughput and instability. Throughput covers lead time from commit to running in production, deployment frequency, and recovery time from a failed deployment. Instability covers the change fail rate, the share of deployments that needed immediate intervention, and the share of unplanned deployments made because of an incident. DORA's position is that speed and stability are not trade-offs. Teams that ship small changes often can find the cause quickly and roll back fast when something fails, because each change is small. Bundle deploys into one a month out of fear of failure, and each change grows larger, and both the change fail rate and recovery time tend to get worse. Use the metrics to track one team's change over time, not to rank teams against each other.
tips.inDesign: Connect deployment records to incident records and collect the metrics automatically from CI and incident management. When you pick one metric to improve, watch its counterpart too; to deploy more often, for example, check that the change fail rate is not getting worse. Do not use these metrics to evaluate individuals, since that rewards moving the numbers instead of the work.

tradeOffs.gain: Easy to collect, and shows day-to-day progress
tradeOffs.cost: Says nothing about whether value was delivered, and invites inflating the numbers

tradeOffs.gain: Shows speed and stability as one set, and where delivery is stuck
tradeOffs.cost: Needs deployment and incident records linked, and the numbers wobble if the definition of an incident does

tradeOffs.option: Assign metric targets to teams or individuals
tradeOffs.gain: Makes the improvement goal explicit
tradeOffs.cost: Once a metric becomes a target, people move the number instead, for example by not recording incidents

tips.title: Passing mocks do not prove SQL and transaction behavior
