tips.keyPoint: Use unit tests for business rules and real-database integration tests for SQL, constraints, and commit boundaries. Control connections and ordering in concurrency tests.
tips.body: A mock returns the values you programmed, but does not establish that SQL runs, a unique constraint holds, or another connection sees a committed write. Use fast unit tests for input rules and business branches, then integration tests where database behavior is part of the contract. Apply migrations to a disposable database of the production engine and a compatible version; verify constraint violations and rollback as well as success. Concurrency tests need multiple connections and explicit synchronization points. Sleeps that hope to create a race, or wrapping the whole test in one transaction, may not reproduce commit and conflict behavior.
tips.inDesign: Use this for signup, inventory writes, idempotency keys, and outbox behavior. Focus real-database tests on important boundaries and isolate test data. Report unavailable integration tests as skipped rather than treating mock success as database verification.

tradeOffs.gain: Fast execution and focused failure diagnosis
tradeOffs.cost: Does not verify SQL, constraints, or locking

tradeOffs.gain: Exercises migrations, constraints, and commits
tradeOffs.cost: Adds startup time, data isolation, and connection management

sources.title: Testcontainers for Go — PostgreSQL Integration Tests

tips.title: Catch invalid configuration at startup before the first user does
tips.keyPoint: Validate required settings, types, ranges, and relationships at startup. Keep secrets out of logs and avoid unsafe production defaults.
tips.body: Environment variables are strings; being present does not make them valid. A timeout may be -1, concurrency zero, or a URL a relative path. Parse typed configuration at startup and validate required fields, permitted ranges, and combinations such as an enabled feature requiring an endpoint. This fail-fast approach stops a misconfigured instance before it becomes ready. Report field names and safe reasons rather than dumping configuration or exceptions containing secrets. A temporary downstream outage differs from invalid configuration and needs connection retries or readiness handling.
tips.inDesign: Use this in API and worker startup. Restrict development authentication and dummy endpoints to explicit development modes. An optional feature may be disabled, but enabling it requires complete configuration. Check missing values, invalid ranges, and contradictory combinations before deployment.

tradeOffs.option: Stop startup on invalid required configuration
tradeOffs.gain: Keeps misconfigured instances from serving users
tradeOffs.cost: Needs visibility into failed rollout reasons

tradeOffs.option: Allow explicit disabling of optional features
tradeOffs.gain: Lets core features run where an optional dependency is unnecessary
tradeOffs.cost: Requires defined disabled behavior and enablement rules

tips.title: Rolling back code does not undo data written by the new version
tips.keyPoint: Verify that the rollback target can handle data and messages left by the new version. Separate reader preparation from activating new writes, and name the versions you can return to.
tips.body: Restoring an older application image leaves database and queue contents in place. If only the new version understands a format, enum value, or event, older readers can fail or misinterpret it. Check compatibility across readers and writers: deploy support for reading the new format everywhere before enabling writes. The prepared version may be a safe rollback target while earlier versions are not. Restoring an old backup also discards later valid updates, so it is not equivalent to a normal code rollback.
tips.inDesign: Ask: after the new version writes real data, how far back can we roll? Include batch jobs, consumers, and historical event replay as readers. Confirm their readiness before activating the new format, and record rollback targets and conditions that invalidate them. Test reading and updating new-version data with the rollback target, checking for information loss as well as read errors.

tradeOffs.option: Separate reader preparation from activating new writes
tradeOffs.gain: Verify compatibility and rollback targets at each stage
tradeOffs.cost: Require multiple releases, fleet-wide readiness checks, and support for both formats during migration

tradeOffs.option: For irreversible changes, restrict writes and recover with a forward fix or data conversion
tradeOffs.gain: Provide a recovery path when compatibility cannot be maintained
tradeOffs.cost: May require downtime or limited functionality and rehearsed conversion, validation, and resumption procedures

sources.title: AWS Builders’ Library — Ensuring rollback safety during deployments

tips.title: Service ownership needs coverage, authority, and a backup
tips.keyPoint: Development and operations share service quality. Define who detects, decides, and restores service, and when; naming one person does not cover absence or missing permissions.
tips.body: DevOps connects changes to operational feedback through shared responsibility, beyond installing CI/CD tools. A service owner makes quality and improvement decisions; on-call responders handle initial response during agreed coverage. These may be different people. Record notification routes, coverage, a backup responder, authorized actions, and escalation. Around-the-clock coverage requires a sustainable rotation rather than continuously paging everyone.
tips.inDesign: Link each service to its accountable team, dependencies, dashboards, and recovery instructions. Exercise notifications including an unavailable primary, and verify that responders can follow procedures with the necessary least privilege.

tradeOffs.gain: Implementation knowledge informs recovery and prevention
tradeOffs.cost: Requires training, workload allocation, and suitable permissions

tradeOffs.option: Share duties with a central operations team
tradeOffs.gain: Shares specialist knowledge and responder coverage
tradeOffs.cost: Requires agreed recovery authority and a route for development improvements

tips.title: Measure CI feedback from queue entry to actionable results
tips.keyPoint: Return fast checks early and require deeper checks at the appropriate gate. Faster individual tests do not remove runner queues or serial dependencies.
tips.body: CI feedback time includes runner queues, setup, checks, and notification. Trace the critical path and parallelize independent checks. Cache keys should reflect dependency and tool versions, and verification must remain correct on a cache miss. Separate quick type and unit checks from deeper database and end-to-end checks while retaining required validation before release.
tips.inDesign: Measure time to the first useful result separately from time to all required release checks. Isolate test data or environments if parallel jobs contend for a shared database.

tradeOffs.gain: Can reduce elapsed time to complete checks
tradeOffs.cost: Requires resources and test-data isolation

tradeOffs.option: Stage quick checks and deeper release validation
tradeOffs.gain: Finds early errors sooner
tradeOffs.cost: Requires mandatory gates so late failures are not ignored

tips.title: Serialize deployment writes and guard against stale arrivals
tips.keyPoint: Coordinate writers to each service and environment and recheck the intended revision before mutation. Canceling CI does not guarantee cancellation of a submitted deployment request.
tips.body: Builds can run in parallel, but competing environment mutations can finish out of order and restore an older revision. Scope mutual exclusion to the service and environment being changed. GitHub Actions concurrency groups coordinate runs within a repository but do not guarantee dispatch order. At the final mutation boundary, coordinate external API and manual paths too, compare the desired revision, and use a conditional update checking the generation number where needed to reject stale requests.
tips.inDesign: Record artifact digest, request generation, and applied revision. An intentional rollback selects an older artifact in a new generation. Exercise an old operation continuing after its lock expires.

tradeOffs.option: Serialize runs for the same target in CI
tradeOffs.gain: Reduces routine deployment races
tradeOffs.cost: Other repositories, manual paths, and delayed external work need coordination

tradeOffs.option: Validate generation and desired revision at deployment
tradeOffs.gain: Can reject stale mutations that arrive late
tradeOffs.cost: Requires atomic validation and a shared generation scheme

tips.title: During incidents, assign recovery work, coordination, and communication
tips.keyPoint: Share who is changing what to avoid conflicting recovery actions. Organize diagnosis alongside mitigation of user impact.
tips.body: Uncoordinated configuration changes can obscure what helped and cause further failures. An incident commander coordinates priorities and roles; operations responders apply coordinated changes; communicators report impact and the next update time. Small teams may combine roles while keeping ownership explicit. Maintain an incident record of timestamps, observations, actions, and results, and confirm acceptance when handing over.
tips.inDesign: Agree severity, mobilization rules, contacts, and a shared record in advance. Evaluate mitigation such as stopping a rollout or reverting before the root cause is certain, then verify recovery from the user perspective.

tradeOffs.option: Combine roles in a small team
tradeOffs.gain: Allows an immediate response
tradeOffs.cost: Requires handing off communication or recording as workload grows

tradeOffs.gain: Maintains communication while recovery work proceeds
tradeOffs.cost: Requires shared state and explicit role handovers

tips.title: Close postmortems with system changes and verification
tips.keyPoint: Encourage facts without blame and investigate the information and system available at the time. Turn improvements into work with owners, deadlines, and verifiable completion criteria.
tips.body: A postmortem records impact, timeline, conditions delaying detection or mitigation, and safeguards that worked. Attributing an incident only to insufficient care leaves the same failure path open to others. Tie action items to the observed path, such as validation, staged rollout, or stopping on anomalies. Prioritize by benefit and cost and verify completion through tests or observation. Publishing the record is different from proving the fix works.
tips.inDesign: Agree postmortem triggers in advance. Put actions into the development plan and review implementation and effectiveness later. Keep secrets and personal information out of shared records.

tradeOffs.option: Add validation for the observed failure path
tradeOffs.gain: Stops similar invalid inputs earlier
tradeOffs.cost: May require maintaining validation and migrating existing settings

tradeOffs.gain: Can limit impact from unanticipated causes
tradeOffs.cost: Requires tuning alerts and stopping conditions

tips.title: Prioritize repetitive operations by hands-on time and automation upkeep
tips.keyPoint: Measure repetitive manual work and compare removal, self-service, and automation. Include failure recovery and maintenance, beyond writing a script.
tips.body: Toil is operational work that is repetitive, automatable, leaves no lasting improvement, and tends to grow with service size. Not every meeting or investigation is toil. Estimate frequency times hands-on time, alongside interruption and failure impact. Preserve approval, permissions, duplicate-execution safeguards, and result reconciliation in automation. Machine runtime is different from human time if no one needs to wait.
tips.inDesign: Check whether frequent reprocessing or account setup can be eliminated entirely. Assign ownership and a failure-support route, then measure changes in hands-on time, failures, and support demand.

tradeOffs.option: Remove the need for the task
tradeOffs.gain: Can reduce both execution and upkeep
tradeOffs.cost: Requires business or upstream design changes

tradeOffs.gain: Reduces repetitive hands-on work
tradeOffs.cost: Permissions, recovery, and maintenance remain ongoing costs

tips.title: Assess team autonomy by independent validation and delivery
tips.keyPoint: Splitting ownership only by frontend, API, and database can turn small business changes into handoffs. Align business capabilities with data ownership to reduce coordination.
tips.body: Using only employees does not remove dependencies if every change waits for another team to implement or release. Consider team boundaries around business capabilities delivered to users. Independent deployment also needs compatible APIs, data-write ownership, and suitable test environments. Separate services still require coordination when multiple teams freely change the same tables in a shared database. In a small organization, a modular monolith may preserve boundaries with less operational overhead.
tips.inDesign: Trace recent changes and inspect waits for other teams and reasons for synchronized releases. Improve API and data boundaries incrementally alongside organizational changes. The goal is not to eliminate all communication.

tradeOffs.gain: Reduces handoffs for small business changes
tradeOffs.cost: Requires multiple skills and clear data boundaries

tradeOffs.gain: Shares scarce expertise across teams
tradeOffs.cost: Needs a support model that avoids ticket queues for routine changes

tips.title: Verify knowledge transfer by having the receiving team deliver a change
tips.keyPoint: Beyond receiving code and documentation, have the internal team build, validate, deploy, and recover. Retain the ability to make decisions and improve with external partners.
tips.body: In-house development does not mean employees must implement everything. Internal staff need the capability to decide priorities and acceptance and keep changing the service. Knowledge transfer should include pairing and work led by the receiving team, beyond a final presentation. Verify administration and renewal procedures for repositories, cloud accounts, certificates, and delivery systems. Remove build dependencies that exist only on an individual laptop or supplier environment, then verify transfer and remove unneeded access at the end of the engagement.
tips.inDesign: Allocate receiving staff and learning time, then have them lead a representative small change into a test environment. Exercise recovery and fix gaps in procedures and permissions.

tradeOffs.gain: Connects context to practical work
tradeOffs.cost: Requires time from both parties and a transfer plan

tradeOffs.option: Require exercises led by the receiving team
tradeOffs.gain: Reveals gaps in procedures, permissions, and implicit dependencies
tradeOffs.cost: Requires a safe environment and an available support period

sources.title: GOV.UK — Working with contractors or third parties

tips.title: Start legacy replacement with a switchable boundary and a source of truth
tips.keyPoint: For incremental replacement, define routing, write ownership, comparison, and rollback conditions first. Switching the interface alone does not complete data migration.
tips.body: The strangler fig pattern routes traffic at a boundary between legacy and replacement systems and replaces capabilities incrementally. Define switching units by capability or user scope, with explicit sources of truth and write ownership. Uncoordinated dual writes can succeed on only one side; design synchronization, lag handling, reconciliation, and failure behavior. Routing back alone cannot recover if the old implementation cannot read newly written data. Check the routing boundary for availability and capacity too.
tips.inDesign: Exercise comparison, switching, and recovery on a small scope. Define completion and retirement criteria for each step so compatibility layers do not remain indefinitely. Compare with a complete replacement for small systems.

tradeOffs.gain: Limits scope while enabling learning during migration
tradeOffs.cost: Requires synchronization, compatibility layers, and monitoring during coexistence

tradeOffs.option: Switch a small system as a whole
tradeOffs.gain: Can shorten coexistence
tradeOffs.cost: Requires validating complete data migration and rollback together

sources.title: AWS Prescriptive Guidance — Strangler fig pattern

tips.title: Design the update path alongside internal project templates
tips.keyPoint: Provide a safe default path for common workloads, with a way to update generated projects and clear ownership for exceptions.
tips.body: A golden path connects development, validation, deployment, and observability for common workloads. Shared CI and permission defaults reduce repeated setup work. A copied template does not automatically receive later fixes, so plan component versioning, installed-version visibility, update notifications, and migration instructions. Separate mandatory safeguards from recommended implementations and provide an exception path with ownership and validation for workloads outside the standard.
tips.inDesign: Choose one frequent workload and pilot it with a few teams. Test both initial delivery and an upgrade to the next version performed by users, then fix friction.

tradeOffs.gain: Makes shared fixes easier to manage
tradeOffs.cost: Requires compatibility management and validation of consumer upgrades

tradeOffs.gain: Allows workload-specific changes
tradeOffs.cost: Requires distributing fixes and tracking adoption

tips.title: Measure internal platform value through user friction and waiting
tips.keyPoint: Treat an internal platform as a product and iterate with users. Assess completion time, failures, support demand, and continued use alongside adoption.
tips.body: An internal platform serves development teams. More portal features do not remove waiting if fulfillment still requires manual work. Use user research to find frequent tasks and friction, then pilot a minimal capability together. Adoption rate means different things when use is mandatory versus chosen. Track satisfaction, completion time, and failures for comparable tasks, and check whether support requests merely moved to another channel.
tips.inDesign: Choose tasks with clear start and completion, such as preparing a service or provisioning a database. Observe users and measure how much they can complete without a manual request to the platform team.

tradeOffs.option: Iterate with a few partner teams
tradeOffs.gain: Finds concrete friction early
tradeOffs.cost: Needs later validation for other workloads

tradeOffs.gain: Makes baseline safeguards more consistent
tradeOffs.cost: Requires exception support and visibility into user burden

tips.title: Compare build and buy through maintenance and exit, beyond setup
tips.keyPoint: Separate capabilities central to business differentiation from commodity maintenance. Buying retains integration and operational duties; building retains dependencies and upkeep.
tips.body: Compare business fit, change speed, security, staffing, integration, and migration on equivalent scope. Total cost of ownership includes upgrades, incident response, training, and migration alongside setup and usage fees. Evaluate provider dependence against value and an exit plan rather than pursuing zero lock-in. Data export alone may not preserve semantics, history, or permissions. Define triggers for reevaluation as pricing or requirements change.
tips.inDesign: Try equivalent business cases in each option and compare required capabilities and operational responsibilities. Exercise exporting and reimporting important data on a small scale and record assumptions and unknowns.

tradeOffs.gain: Gives control over business-specific changes
tradeOffs.cost: Retains ongoing maintenance, operations, and staffing duties

tradeOffs.option: Buy or use a managed commodity capability
tradeOffs.gain: Delegates common implementation and some operations
tradeOffs.cost: Retains integration, usage management, pricing, and exit planning

sources.title: GOV.UK — Managing technical lock-in in the cloud

tips.title: Trace a code path from its entry point to the revision running in production
tips.keyPoint: Choose a representative operation and verify its code, data, build, and deployment path with evidence. Documentation alone does not establish the currently running path.
tips.body: When supporting an existing team, start by tracing a representative request instead of reading every file. Connect routing, authorization, business logic, writes, and asynchronous work through code and configuration. Identify which commit produced each artifact and where it was deployed, then compare deployment records with the running revision. Distinguish confirmed from unconfirmed paths in the map and omit credential values.
tips.inDesign: Ask: which CI run built the latest change, and where did it go? Inspect run records, artifact identifiers, and runtime revisions. Follow a small test-environment change through to telemetry to find undocumented manual steps.

tradeOffs.gain: Builds understanding grounded in real changes and operations
tradeOffs.cost: Requires follow-up for other paths and exceptions

tradeOffs.gain: Helps identify missing components and dependencies
tradeOffs.cost: An inventory alone does not establish actual execution paths

tips.title: Verify development setup by starting from a clean environment
tips.keyPoint: Define tool versions, seed data, external connections, shutdown, and reset. Test in a fresh workspace so prior caches and manual setup do not hide missing steps.
tips.body: Onboarding instructions should include runtime and database versions, sample configuration, migrations, initial data, and a verification step. Dev Container or Compose can codify shared setup, but host OS, CPU architecture, ports, and external permissions remain relevant. Separate development settings from production secrets. Scope reset procedures to development resources and verify targets before deleting data.
tips.inDesign: Ask whether a recent joiner can run the first test without verbal instructions. Preserve existing environments and test with a new directory and development data volume, then fix gaps in the instructions.

tradeOffs.gain: Helps align tool and service setup
tradeOffs.cost: Requires managing host differences, resources, and image updates

tradeOffs.option: Install pinned tools on the host
tradeOffs.gain: Integrates directly with host tools
tradeOffs.cost: Requires OS-specific instructions and version-drift management

sources.title: Dev Containers — Images, Dockerfiles, and Docker Compose

tips.title: Build test data from the conditions under test without copying personal data
tips.keyPoint: Synthetic data still needs appropriate volume, skew, relationships, and edge cases. Pin generator version, random seed, and reference time for reproducibility.
tips.body: A fixture establishes test preconditions. Include relationships, nulls, distinct orders with equal amounts, month boundaries, and long strings rather than just random names. A fixed random seed is insufficient when generator versions or reference times for relative dates change. Removing names from production copies can leave identifying free text or IDs. Prefer synthetic properties; production-derived data needs separately designed access, transformation, and retention.
tips.inDesign: Ask which minimal dataset reproduces the defect and which dataset tests performance. Separate small regression fixtures from larger load datasets, record generation conditions, and test regeneration.

tradeOffs.gain: Makes causes and expected results easier to understand
tradeOffs.cost: Volume and skew performance need separate checks

tradeOffs.gain: Enables volume and skew experiments
tradeOffs.cost: Requires managing generation cost, storage, and reproducibility

tips.title: Isolate preview data and external effects alongside preview URLs
tips.keyPoint: Separate databases, queues, storage, permissions, and outbound actions by test scope. Names or Kubernetes namespaces alone do not prevent shared-data races or real notifications.
tips.body: A preview environment per PR can still share database or queue state. Namespaces help organize resources and scope permissions but do not themselves block traffic. Configure network enforcement supported by the implementation and separate external database credentials. For an email or payment side effect, use test-only endpoints and permissions, beyond application flags. Cleanup must cover external data and queued jobs, with detection when expiry-based cleanup fails.
tips.inDesign: Ask whether resetting or sending mail from one of two simultaneous previews can affect the other or production. Exercise separate run IDs and data areas, with a test-only sink for outbound messages.

tradeOffs.gain: Makes data collisions easier to avoid
tradeOffs.cost: Requires cost, startup, and cleanup management

tradeOffs.option: Partition shared resources with scoped access
tradeOffs.gain: Can reduce resource cost
tradeOffs.cost: Requires validation of boundaries in every read, write, and cleanup path

tips.title: Align dependencies with a lockfile and validate upgrades as explicit changes
tips.keyPoint: Share an application dependency resolution and prevent silent CI rewrites. Align runtime and install settings; pinned versions still require upgrades and security review.
tips.body: A lockfile records resolved direct dependencies and each transitive dependency. npm ci fails on inconsistencies with package.json without updating the lockfile. Settings affecting dependency-tree shape must match those used to create the lock. The lock alone does not fully pin runtimes, OS behavior, native components, install scripts, or external downloads. Pinning supports reproducibility but does not justify leaving vulnerable versions unchanged. Review upgrade diffs and verify important behavior.
tips.inDesign: Ask whether a fresh CI runner resolves the same dependencies for the same commit. Check the lockfile and settings, then install and build without relying on a warm cache. Published libraries additionally need compatibility checks against supported consumer combinations.

tradeOffs.option: Pin application installation to a lockfile
tradeOffs.gain: Makes dependency drift easier to diagnose
tradeOffs.cost: Requires ongoing version maintenance and upgrades

tradeOffs.gain: Helps discover and advance outdated dependencies
tradeOffs.cost: Requires ownership of compatibility and behavior checks

tips.title: Enforce module boundaries with dependency checks alongside diagrams
tips.keyPoint: Define exposed entry points and prohibited dependency directions and enforce detectable rules in CI. Inventory existing violations and reduce them incrementally while preventing new ones.
tips.body: Modules in one repository can still become tightly coupled through internal classes or direct table access. Express dependency rules such as orders using only the payment public interface, and check for a dependency cycle. Architecture tests detect code dependencies but do not automatically guarantee dynamic calls or runtime data contracts. If existing violations form a baseline, review baseline changes so new violations are not silently accepted.
tips.inDesign: Ask why a change requires edits to unrelated module internals. Inspect real dependencies and exposed entry points, then introduce checks at one frequently changed boundary.

tradeOffs.gain: Finds boundary deterioration early
tradeOffs.cost: Requires managing detection scope and baseline changes

tradeOffs.option: Refine one boundary at a time and expand checks
tradeOffs.gain: Connects improvements to real change work
tradeOffs.cost: Requires tracking problems remaining in unchecked boundaries

tips.title: Capture current behavior before changing poorly understood legacy code
tips.keyPoint: Capture representative inputs, outputs, and mutations to detect accidental changes. Tests recording current behavior do not prove that behavior is correct for the business.
tips.body: A characterization test records what existing code does. Snapshots can cover larger outputs, but accepting diffs requires checking their meaning. Control or normalize nondeterministic timestamps and IDs without hiding important differences such as money or order. Separate refactoring from behavior changes; document the rationale and new expected result when fixing an existing defect. Existing behavior does not justify unsafe behavior.
tips.inDesign: Ask which behaviors must remain unchanged and who depends on them. Record normal and boundary cases safely, make a small structural change, and compare with identical inputs.

tradeOffs.option: Record and compare a larger output
tradeOffs.gain: Helps detect broad changes before the code is fully understood
tradeOffs.cost: Requires diff review and control of unstable values

tradeOffs.option: Test important rules with focused assertions
tradeOffs.gain: Makes failures and business intent clearer
tradeOffs.cost: Requires understanding intended behavior and designing cases

tips.title: Rehearse database migrations with volume, invalid data, and concurrent work
tips.keyPoint: Validate locks, scan duration, storage, partial failure, and restart beyond SQL success. A small test database does not establish production behavior or duration.
tips.body: Migration behavior depends on database version, row count, distribution, indexes, and active transactions. PostgreSQL 18 allows adding a CHECK constraint as NOT VALID to separate existing-row validation, but adding it still requires locking. It applies to subsequent inserts and updates. VALIDATE CONSTRAINT checks existing rows and fails if violations remain. Rehearse each stage and observe locks, scans, normal workload impact, and state after interruption.
tips.inDesign: Ask which stage waits under representative volume and long transactions. Use safe data to exercise contention, timeouts, retries, and post-migration consistency.

tradeOffs.gain: Separates longer validation from constraint addition
tradeOffs.cost: Requires checking supported constraint types and stage-specific locks

tradeOffs.gain: Finds procedural errors early
tradeOffs.cost: Representative production volume and contention still need testing

tips.title: Investigate active work before clearing a Terraform state lock
tips.keyPoint: Use a locking-capable backend to protect writes to the same state. Do not disable locking or unlock active work merely to avoid waiting.
tips.body: A Terraform state file maps configuration to managed resources. With supported backends, operations that write state acquire a state lock and stop if it cannot be acquired. This protects the same state, not resources mistakenly managed by different states. Force unlock is for a lock left by your own operation after automatic release fails; verify the operation has ended and the lock ID matches. Manual cloud changes and alternate delivery paths need separate coordination.
tips.inDesign: Ask which execution owns the lock and whether another state also manages the resources. Compare CI activity with the backend, inspect termination and partial changes, then plan resumption.

tradeOffs.gain: Prevents concurrent writers to the same state
tradeOffs.cost: Requires permissions, recovery procedures, and wait monitoring

tradeOffs.gain: Allows unrelated updates to proceed independently
tradeOffs.cost: Requires avoiding duplicate resource ownership and managing cross-state dependencies

tips.title: Keep production mutation privileges away from jobs executing PR code
tips.keyPoint: Separate untrusted code execution from privileged delivery. Short-lived tokens or approval screens do not protect a privileged job that executes attacker-controlled code.
tips.body: CI executes code through install scripts and tests too. Checking out and running PR code in a privileged context such as pull_request_target can expose secrets or write permissions. Enforce this trust boundary by running validation with minimal permissions and isolated runners; perform delivery separately using verified trusted references and artifacts. Do not blindly execute or unpack untrusted artifacts or caches in a privileged job. Restrict conditions for obtaining deployment credentials to the intended repository and environment.
tips.inDesign: Ask who can change a job input and what it executes under which permissions. Trace triggers, checkout targets, reusable workflows, artifacts, and runner reuse to verify an unprivileged validation path.

tradeOffs.gain: Limits privileges exposed to untrusted code
tradeOffs.cost: Requires validating artifacts and trust conditions between jobs

tradeOffs.gain: Reduces residual state passed to later jobs
tradeOffs.cost: Requires startup, cleanup, and external-access controls

tips.title: Scope development secrets separately from production
tips.keyPoint: Provide development endpoints and limited credentials rather than distributing production keys. Keep values out of sample configuration and document revocation and reissue.
tips.body: Make development accessible by enabling required actions in the right environment, rather than sharing every secret. Issue development credentials and test credentials with least privilege separately from production secret access. Individual or workload identities help with revocation and investigation. Environment variables can still leak through logs, process inspection, or debugging. Design issuance, storage, use, renewal, and deletion as one lifecycle.
tips.inDesign: Ask whether a new developer can test required behavior without connecting to production. Inspect examples, secret retrieval, destinations, and permissions, then test offboarding using test credentials.

tradeOffs.gain: Supports scoped revocation and attribution
tradeOffs.cost: Requires issuance, renewal, and access management

tradeOffs.option: Combine local substitutes with external test environments
tradeOffs.gain: Reduces routine dependence on external secrets
tradeOffs.cost: Real authentication and integration still need separate validation

tips.title: Include the ability to identify failing behavior and revisions in completion criteria
tips.keyPoint: Exercise representative success and failure and identify service, environment, and revision from telemetry. Existing logs alone do not prove operational diagnosability.
tips.body: Instrumentation adds logs, metrics, and traces to an implementation. Service identity and running revision help connect errors with a release. Telemetry acceptance criteria should include following a representative failure from its user-visible result to relevant logs. Sampling may omit requests, and instrumentation alone does not complete alerting or recovery. Avoid recording full inputs or secrets and avoid unbounded per-request IDs on metrics.
tips.inDesign: Ask whether another engineer can identify the revision and path of a test failure. Exercise it in a test environment, let them use the identifiers and search steps, and add the missing information.

tradeOffs.option: Align common attributes and investigation steps
tradeOffs.gain: Makes investigation easier across responders
tradeOffs.cost: Requires maintaining identifiers and instrumentation

tradeOffs.gain: Focuses telemetry where needed within a cost budget
tradeOffs.cost: Requires recognizing uninstrumented and sampled-out paths

tips.title: Use reviews to share rationale and verification alongside fixes
tips.keyPoint: Separate behavioral and design issues from preference. Support required changes with concrete cases and verification, enabling the author to explain the decision.
tips.body: For knowledge-sharing code reviews, go beyond prescribing edits. Explain the failing case, relevant assumptions, and how to verify it. Distinguish required corrections from optional suggestions and avoid delaying useful improvements over preference. Let authors make and test changes and explain similar decisions later. Preserve concise rationale in comments or design records so internal colleagues can review each other.
tips.inDesign: Ask whether the team can make the same judgment on a later PR without the advisor. Review a recent change together and have the author explain the failure condition and test so the reasoning can be reused.

tradeOffs.option: Have the author fix and explain
tradeOffs.gain: Connects reasoning with implementation knowledge
tradeOffs.cost: Requires time for explanation and verification

tradeOffs.option: Have an advisor fix urgently, then review together
tradeOffs.gain: Can mitigate immediate impact quickly
tradeOffs.cost: Skipping follow-up understanding and validation leaves dependency

sources.title: Google Engineering Practices — The Standard of Code Review

tips.title: Validate shared-library changes through consumer behavior, beyond version numbers
tips.keyPoint: Define the public API and supported environments, then validate representative consumers. Unchanged signatures can still hide breaking changes in exceptions, defaults, or semantics.
tips.body: Shared libraries reduce duplication but can spread change impact to every consuming application. Semantic versioning communicates changes to a declared public API; it does not replace validation. Include consumer-dependent exceptions and default behavior in the API contract. Define supported version and environment combinations and test representative consumers before release. For breaking changes, plan old-version support and migration rather than assuming simultaneous upgrades.
tips.inDesign: Ask what changes for which consumers. Inventory consumers and versions and exercise normal, edge, and failure cases against the candidate. Assign responsibility for validating consumer upgrades.

tradeOffs.option: Keep a small stable public API
tradeOffs.gain: Makes consumer impact easier to understand
tradeOffs.cost: Requires separating public capabilities from internal implementation

tradeOffs.option: Release breaking changes in a new major version
tradeOffs.gain: Allows necessary design improvements
tradeOffs.cost: Requires migration support and old-version upkeep

tips.title: Prioritize technical debt through observed change and incident costs
tips.keyPoint: Investigate change frequency, rework, incidents, and change propagation rather than choosing a rewrite based on age or preference. Tie small improvements to upcoming business changes.
tips.body: Technical debt interest can be observed as recurring extra effort in understanding, changes, validation, and recovery. A stable rarely changed component differs from one causing change propagation across modules repeatedly. Compare history, incidents, and upcoming work rather than ranking only by complexity scores or line count. Protect behavior with validation and improve boundaries or duplication through small diffs. Check comparable later changes for reduced rework and revisit ineffective interventions.
tips.inDesign: Ask which recent change required extra work because of this design. Record examples and impact and select improvements fitting upcoming work. Do not postpone a dangerous defect by labeling it debt.

tradeOffs.option: Improve the area alongside upcoming work
tradeOffs.gain: Connects improvement to real friction
tradeOffs.cost: Requires separating behavior changes from structural changes and their validation

tradeOffs.option: Reserve time for a cross-cutting improvement
tradeOffs.gain: Allows focus on problems blocking many changes
tradeOffs.cost: Requires bounded scope and continued effect measurement

tips.title: Make password hashing slow on purpose, and put that slowness in your login capacity plan
tips.keyPoint: Fast general-purpose hashing alone is unsafe for password storage. Prefer Argon2id for new implementations; measure CPU time, elapsed time, memory, and parallelism to size login capacity and rate limits.
tips.body: Even with a salt, fast general-purpose SHA-256 alone is not suitable for password storage. Prefer Argon2id for new implementations; review requirements and migration for existing bcrypt systems. Deliberate CPU and memory cost makes offline guessing expensive. Attacker GPU speed ratios do not necessarily equal server elapsed-time ratios. A verification using 100ms CPU time at 100/s consumes 10 CPU-seconds/s, but elapsed time including waits alone cannot determine core demand.
tips.inDesign: Benchmark production-like concurrency, recording CPU time, elapsed time, memory per verification, and parallelism. First-order CPU demand is verifications/s × CPU-seconds/verification; memory depends on concurrent verifications × per-verification use. Add queueing headroom separately. Rate-limit before hashing, cap concurrency, store algorithm parameters, and rehash incrementally on successful login.

tradeOffs.option: Unsafe / not recommended: store passwords with a general-purpose hash alone
tradeOffs.gain: Low CPU use, but lacks required resistance to password guessing
tradeOffs.cost: Once leaked, it is brute-forced quickly offline

tradeOffs.option: Slow it down with Argon2id or bcrypt
tradeOffs.gain: Even after a leak, cracking each account takes time
tradeOffs.cost: More CPU and memory per login, so capacity and rate limits need planning

tradeOffs.option: Delegate to an external identity service
tradeOffs.gain: Someone else chooses and migrates the hashes
tradeOffs.cost: Fees, plus dependence on that service's outages and behavior

tips.title: Reused leaked passwords slip past both per-IP limits and account lockout
tips.keyPoint: Credential stuffing tries username and password pairs leaked from other services, once per account, from many IPs. That rarely trips per-IP limits or account lockout, so layer checks against leaked passwords, multi-factor authentication, and monitoring of the service-wide login failure rate.
tips.body: Brute force throws many guesses at one account, so a per-account failure count stops it. Credential stuffing is different. The attacker holds millions of email and password pairs leaked from other services and tries each account once, with a pair that may well be right. Anyone who reused their password is in on the first try. The attempts come from a botnet spread over tens of thousands of IPs, so per-IP limits rarely fire either. Seen from one account or one IP, it looks like ordinary failures; a sudden rise in the service-wide login failure rate is the quicker signal.
tips.inDesign: Reject passwords found in leaked-password lists when they are set or changed. Monitor login success and failure rates across the whole service, and when failures spike, widen the set of logins that must pass an extra check (a CAPTCHA or multi-factor authentication). Require multi-factor authentication for logins from new devices or locations, and offer methods with nothing to reuse, such as passkeys.

tradeOffs.option: Only per-IP and per-account rate limits
tradeOffs.gain: Simple to build, and it stops brute force
tradeOffs.cost: One-attempt-per-account traffic spread across many IPs passes through

tradeOffs.option: Check against leaked passwords and watch the overall failure rate
tradeOffs.gain: Cuts reuse at the door and spots distributed attacks
tradeOffs.cost: Requires building the check and the logic to tighten verification during an attack

tradeOffs.gain: A correct password alone is not enough to get in
tradeOffs.cost: More friction at enrollment and on lost devices, raising drop-off and support load

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4 — Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management

tips.title: SPAs and mobile apps cannot keep secrets: bind the authorization code to the requesting app with PKCE
tips.keyPoint: A client secret embedded in an app that runs in a browser or on a device can be extracted by anyone. Skip the implicit flow, which hands over tokens directly, and use the authorization code flow with PKCE so an intercepted authorization code cannot be exchanged.
tips.body: In the OAuth authorization code flow, after login the authorization server sends the app a short-lived authorization code, which the app exchanges for tokens. An app running on a server uses its client secret in that exchange, so a stolen authorization code alone is useless. SPAs and mobile apps, however, ship their contents to users, so any secret inside can be extracted; they cannot hold a client secret. Such apps are called public clients. On mobile, another app registered for the same custom URL scheme can intercept the authorization code on its redirect. With PKCE, the app makes a random code_verifier each time and sends only its hash (the code_challenge) with the first request. Only the app that started the request can present the code_verifier at exchange time, so an intercepted authorization code is worthless. The implicit flow once used by SPAs returns tokens directly in the URL, which leaks easily, and current guidance (RFC 9700) says not to use it.
tips.inDesign: Build SPAs and mobile apps on the authorization code flow with PKCE (S256), and never embed a client secret in the app. Register redirect URIs for exact matching, and on mobile prefer App Links and universal links, which only the domain owner's app can receive, over custom URL schemes. Add PKCE to server-side apps as well.

tradeOffs.option: Not recommended for new implementations: implicit flow
tradeOffs.gain: No exchange step, so it is simple to build
tradeOffs.cost: Tokens travel in the URL and leak through history and referrers

tradeOffs.gain: An intercepted authorization code cannot be exchanged
tradeOffs.cost: Extra steps to make and keep the code_verifier, and older libraries may need updates

tradeOffs.gain: No tokens stored in the browser
tradeOffs.cost: More server and session management, plus CSRF defenses

sources.title: RFC 9700 — Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
RFC 7636 — Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients

tips.title: A token with a valid signature is not necessarily meant for you: check aud and iss
tips.keyPoint: Tokens from the same auth server are signed with the same key, whichever app they were issued for. An API that checks only signature and expiry accepts tokens meant for other apps. Always check that aud names you and iss is the issuer you expect.
tips.body: One IdP issues tokens to many apps and APIs, all signed with the same key. A valid signature shows only that this IdP issued the token, not that it was issued for your API. The intended recipient is in the aud claim, and the issuer in the iss claim. If the API skips these checks, a token obtained by logging in to another app on the same IdP passes as is, even one the attacker registered themselves. Inside a company, a token meant for a low-privilege service can call a high-privilege API. On an IdP shared by many organizations, tokens issued in other organizations carry the same signature, so check iss and the organization ID too.
tips.inDesign: Beyond signature and expiry, the API checks that aud matches its own identifier and that iss exactly matches the expected issuer, and rejects the token otherwise. Fix the accepted signing algorithms in configuration rather than following the token header. Issue tokens with a distinct aud per service, so no single token can call every API.

tradeOffs.option: Unsafe example: accept using only signature and expiry
tradeOffs.gain: Less implementation, but omits required audience and issuer validation
tradeOffs.cost: Tokens meant for other apps get through

tradeOffs.gain: Only tokens addressed to you are accepted
tradeOffs.cost: Each service registers its aud, and callers fetch a token per destination

tradeOffs.gain: One consistent place to verify
tradeOffs.cost: Internal paths that bypass the gateway stay unprotected unless each service verifies too

sources.title: RFC 8725 — JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

tips.title: Self-contained JWT verification alone does not learn about later revocation
tips.keyPoint: A JWT checked only for signature and expiry keeps working after logout or account suspension until it expires. Keep access tokens short-lived, revoke through refresh tokens, and check revocation on the server only for sensitive operations.
tips.body: JWTs carry signatures and claims and can be checked locally for signature, expiry, iss, aud, and other requirements. That setup alone does not learn of later revocation; JWTs are not inherently impossible to revoke. A denylist, user-state check, or session-version lookup can reject them before expiry. Short access-token lifetimes and refresh-token revocation reduce residual exposure but do not automatically reject already-issued access tokens immediately.
tips.inDesign: Set the access token lifetime from how long it may be used after you stop someone. Have a procedure that revokes refresh tokens on account suspension or password change. For sensitive operations such as transfers or permission changes, check revocation on the server even at the cost of a lookup.

tradeOffs.gain: Few renewals and little load on the auth server
tradeOffs.cost: A stolen token works until expiry, even after you stop the user

tradeOffs.gain: Less time for misuse after you stop someone
tradeOffs.cost: More renewals and a stronger dependency on the auth server's availability

tradeOffs.option: Check revocation on the server every time
tradeOffs.gain: Revocation takes effect immediately
tradeOffs.cost: A lookup per request adds latency and a point of failure

tips.title: Rotate refresh tokens on every use, and revoke the whole set when a used one comes back
tips.keyPoint: A refresh token stolen from a browser or device lets an attacker keep minting new access tokens. Replace it on every use (rotation), and when an already-used one arrives, treat it as stolen and revoke everything descended from that login.
tips.body: Short access token lifetimes do not help if the refresh token is stolen: the attacker simply renews each time one expires. For public clients that cannot keep secrets, such as SPAs and mobile apps, RFC 9700 requires refresh tokens to be either sender-constrained or rotated. With rotation, each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the one just used. Since both the thief and the legitimate app try to use the same token, one of them eventually presents a used one. The auth server cannot tell which is the attacker, so it revokes the whole chain from that login (the token family) and forces a fresh login. The trap is when the legitimate app itself sends a used token. If several tabs refresh at once, or the connection drops before the new token arrives, users get logged out with nothing stolen.
tips.inDesign: Rotate refresh tokens for public clients, and on reuse revoke the family and log the event. In the app, funnel refreshes through one place so multiple tabs or parallel requests never refresh at the same moment. Decide whether to allow a grace period of tens of seconds for dropped connections by weighing it against the window it gives a stolen token.

tradeOffs.option: Unsafe example: reuse an unbound refresh token indefinitely
tradeOffs.gain: Concurrent refreshes and dropped connections cause no trouble
tradeOffs.cost: A stolen token keeps renewing until someone notices

tradeOffs.gain: Theft is detected and the whole set can be stopped
tradeOffs.cost: Concurrent refreshes or dropped connections can log out legitimate users

tradeOffs.gain: Fewer false alarms from dropped connections and concurrent refreshes
tradeOffs.cost: During the grace period, a stolen old token still works

sources.title: RFC 9700 — Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security

tips.title: Hard-to-guess IDs are not a substitute for authorization
tips.keyPoint: Knowing someone is logged in does not mean they may see that record. Check ownership in every handler that takes an ID, and do not let tenant filtering depend on every query remembering it.
tips.body: Authentication establishes who someone is; authorization decides whether that person may touch this data. If an API takes an ID like /invoices/1002 and only checks that the caller is logged in, changing the ID is enough to read someone else's data. This is BOLA (broken object level authorization), one of the most commonly reported API vulnerabilities. Switching from sequential IDs to UUIDs makes guessing harder, but an ID leaked through a URL, a log, or a shared link works just the same. In a multi-tenant system where many companies share one table, a single query that forgets "WHERE tenant_id = ?" leaks other tenants' data.
tips.inDesign: In every handler that takes an ID, check that the caller owns the record or has rights to it. Make the data access layer always add the tenant ID, and layer the database's row-level security underneath as a last line of defense. Add automated tests, per endpoint, that try to fetch with someone else's ID.

tradeOffs.gain: Fine-grained rules per operation
tradeOffs.cost: Forgetting it in one place leaks data from there

tradeOffs.option: Always add the tenant ID in the data access layer
tradeOffs.gain: Prevents forgotten filters by construction
tradeOffs.cost: Cross-tenant work such as admin screens needs a separate, explicit path

tradeOffs.gain: Other tenants' rows stay hidden even when the app has a bug
tradeOffs.cost: Each connection must set the tenant, and its interplay with connection pools and performance needs checking

sources.title: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1: Broken Object Level Authorization

tips.title: Right after you revoke access, a cached authorization check still says yes (the new enemy problem)
tips.keyPoint: Saving an authorization revision such as a ZedToken with content and requiring checks at least that fresh prevents use of permissions predating that revision. It does not guarantee immediate later revocation for existing content.
tips.body: The paper on Zanzibar, Google's authorization system, named this failure the new enemy problem. Say Alice removes Bob from a shared folder, then puts a new document in it. If the check runs on data from before Bob was removed, Bob can read a document added after his removal. Permission checks are frequent and latency-sensitive, so they are usually served from caches or replicas and are slightly stale. The fix is not to make every check fresh. When a document is written, take a marker for the current permission version (a Zookie in Zanzibar, a ZedToken in SpiceDB), store it with the document, and on read require a check against data at least that new. Documents that have not changed keep the fast cached checks. This revision is a freshness lower bound. An old content token alone does not immediately enforce later revocation. Where immediate effect is required, pass the post-revocation revision or use the needed consistent read, with an appropriate cache invalidation policy.
tips.inDesign: If you cache permission checks, decide how stale a check may be and list the cases where a removal must take effect at once. Save the permission version marker when documents are created or updated, and pass it to the check on read. Fresh checks are slow, so limit them to where they matter, such as right after a permission change or for sensitive documents.

tradeOffs.option: Cache checks for a long time
tradeOffs.gain: Fast checks and little load on the authorization service
tradeOffs.cost: After a removal, stale grants keep coming back until the cache expires

tradeOffs.option: Store a permission version marker with each document
tradeOffs.gain: Avoids checks older than the content revision; immediate later revocation needs separate design
tradeOffs.cost: Every service that handles documents must store and pass the marker

tradeOffs.option: Check against the latest data every time
tradeOffs.gain: Removed access takes effect at once
tradeOffs.cost: Latency and database load rise sharply on every check

sources.title: Zanzibar: Google's Consistent, Global Authorization System (USENIX ATC 2019)

tips.title: A queued job may outlive the permission that allowed it
tips.keyPoint: Permissions and target state can change between enqueue and execution. If revocation must stop pending jobs, authorize the operation again when the job runs.
tips.body: An asynchronous job runs later in a separate worker. After acceptance, the requester might leave the organization or the target might move to another tenant. A worker service account having database access does not establish that the requester may operate on that data. Store the server-verified requester, tenant, and target in job metadata protected against tampering, and use them for execution-time authorization. Distinguish operations committed at acceptance from those governed by permissions at execution.
tips.inDesign: Ask: does removing permission also stop work that has not started? Where required, authorize before important reads or writes, and defer or deny execution if the check cannot be completed. For long jobs, define recheck boundaries and the treatment of side effects already completed. Test revocation after enqueue and attempts to substitute another tenant in job metadata.

tradeOffs.option: Check current permissions immediately before execution
tradeOffs.gain: Apply permission changes to work that has not started
tradeOffs.cost: Depend on the authorization system and define defer/deny and resume behavior when checks fail

tradeOffs.option: Split long jobs and recheck before important side effects
tradeOffs.gain: Provide boundaries for applying permission changes during execution
tradeOffs.cost: Handle partial output and interrupted work; completed effects are not automatically undone

tips.title: A feature that makes your server fetch URLs is a door into your internal network
tips.keyPoint: When the server fetches a user-supplied URL, as for link previews or webhook targets, it can reach internal services and cloud metadata that outsiders cannot. Check the resolved IP, connect to that IP, and keep outbound fetching on a separate network.
tips.body: SSRF is an attack that makes your server send requests to internal addresses. The server sits inside the firewall, so it reaches admin pages, internal APIs, and the cloud metadata service (169.254.169.254). The metadata service hands out the instance's credentials, and stolen ones let an attacker drive your cloud APIs. Checks on the URL string alone are easy to slip past: a redirect can bounce the request inward, a hostname can resolve to an internal IP after you checked it (DNS rebinding), and an IP can be written in decimal. Use an allow list, confirm the resolved IP is not private or link-local, connect to the IP you checked, and do not follow redirects.
tips.inDesign: Route outbound fetches through a dedicated proxy or network, and block traffic to internal addresses at the network level. In the app, layer allow lists, resolved-IP checks, and disabled redirects. On AWS, require IMDSv2, and give the fetching servers only minimal permissions.

tradeOffs.option: Restrict destinations to an allow list
tradeOffs.gain: The hardest to slip past
tradeOffs.cost: Cannot serve features that must fetch arbitrary URLs

tradeOffs.option: Check the resolved IP and connect to it
tradeOffs.gain: Handles arbitrary URLs while blocking internal targets
tradeOffs.cost: Needs an implementation that covers resolution, redirects, IPv6, and more without gaps

tradeOffs.option: Fetch from a network that cannot reach internal addresses
tradeOffs.gain: The network stops it even when the app has a bug
tradeOffs.cost: More to run: a proxy or a dedicated subnet

sources.title: OWASP — Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

tips.title: Limit credential lifetime and permissions to reduce exposure after leakage
tips.keyPoint: A long-lived access key, once leaked, works until someone notices. Give CI and servers credentials that last only a short time, through OIDC or roles, and allow only the operations they actually use (least privilege).
tips.body: Long-lived keys remain usable until revoked. In CI, use an OIDC identity token to obtain temporary cloud credentials. The OIDC token’s expiry and the resulting session’s expiry are different. AWS STS credentials remain valid until the configured session expiration; job completion alone does not revoke them. Restrict trust to repositories, branches, and environments, and use least privilege and short sessions.
tips.inDesign: Give neither people nor workloads long-lived access keys; use roles and temporary credentials. Tighten the conditions for assuming a role (repository, branch, environment). Do not start broad; narrow permissions from activity logs, and regularly remove unused ones. For any long-lived keys that remain, automate rotation and leak detection.

tradeOffs.gain: Simple, and usable from anywhere
tradeOffs.cost: A leaked key works until the next rotation, and rotation itself takes work

tradeOffs.option: Temporary credentials via OIDC or roles
tradeOffs.gain: No stored secret, and a leak expires quickly
tradeOffs.cost: Trust conditions need design, and some environments do not support it

tradeOffs.gain: Shrinks what a leaked credential can do
tradeOffs.cost: Rarely used operations that get dropped fail when they are finally needed

tips.title: Until you check the signature, you do not know who sent a Webhook
tips.keyPoint: Verify raw bytes and signed fields according to the sender’s protocol. Check freshness where signed timestamps exist. Couple deduplication with durable acceptance and effect boundaries so crashes do not lose work.
tips.body: Public endpoints can receive forged webhooks, so validate HMACs or signatures according to the sender. Stripe signs a timestamp with the raw body and supports a freshness tolerance. GitHub’s X-Hub-Signature-256 is a body HMAC; do not assume Stripe-style signed timestamps. Preserve raw bytes, use official verifiers and constant-time comparison, and handle replays and legitimate retries while deduplicating effects using event IDs or equivalent identifiers. Match defenses against replay attacks to each sender’s protocol.
tips.inDesign: After verification, atomically store the body and pending state in an inbox with a unique event ID, and acknowledge only after durable acceptance. Relay to another queue through an outbox or equivalent. Marking an event done before queueing can lose it on a crash between the two. Couple worker effects with a DB completion record or external API idempotency key and support recovery. Rotate secrets with an overlap period.

tradeOffs.gain: Confirms the sender is genuine and the body was not altered
tradeOffs.cost: Requires handling the raw body, and managing and rotating the secret

tradeOffs.option: Restrict by the sender's IP addresses
tradeOffs.gain: Stops unrelated senders at the network
tradeOffs.cost: Breaks when the sender's IPs change, and alone does not stop tampering with the body

tradeOffs.option: Re-fetch the state from the sender's API on each notification
tradeOffs.gain: Acts on the true state without trusting the notification's contents
tradeOffs.cost: An extra API call per notification, which can hit the sender's rate limits

sources.title: RFC 2104 — HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication
GitHub — Webhook best practices and delivery IDs

tips.title: Encrypt data with a data key, and have the KMS only wrap that key
tips.keyPoint: Do not send large data to the KMS to encrypt directly. Encrypt it locally with a data key you generate, have the KMS master key wrap only the data key, and store the wrapped key with the data (envelope encryption). The master key never leaves the KMS.
tips.body: A KMS stores keys safely and records who used them and when. But the data it can encrypt directly has a size limit, and every call costs a network round trip and counts against request quotas. With envelope encryption you create a data key for each write and encrypt the data locally. The KMS master key encrypts (wraps) the data key, and you store the wrapped data key next to the ciphertext. To read, the KMS unwraps the data key and you decrypt locally. Only the small data key goes to the KMS, so speed does not depend on data size. Replacing the master key means rewrapping data keys, not re-encrypting all the data.
tips.inDesign: Restrict and audit KMS unwrap permissions. Tenant-key crypto-shredding also requires expiring plaintext-key caches and removing plaintext or alternatively wrapped copies. Check disabling, scheduled deletion, final deletion, and waiting-period behavior. Deleting one key alone does not guarantee immediate unreadability of every copy.

tradeOffs.gain: Simple, and no plaintext key in your code
tradeOffs.cost: Size limits, plus a KMS round trip and quota use per item

tradeOffs.gain: Encrypts large data fast, and key replacement only rewraps data keys
tradeOffs.cost: Plaintext data keys must be handled correctly in your code and erased promptly

tradeOffs.gain: Fewer KMS calls and less latency
tradeOffs.cost: Plaintext keys stay in memory while cached, and one key protects more data

sources.title: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 — Recommendation for Key Management
AWS KMS — Deleting keys and waiting periods

tips.title: Keep tokens and complete request bodies out of diagnostic logs
tips.keyPoint: Log an allowlist of structured fields. Trace requests through IDs, outcomes, and duration, and check error paths for accidental secret exposure.
tips.body: Logging everything for debugging duplicates Authorization headers, cookies, passwords, and personal data into another store. Prefer an allowlist of structured log fields to saving whole payloads and attempting to redact them later. Useful fields include event, request_id, HTTP method, route template, status, duration_ms, and a safe error_code. Prefer `/users/:id` to `/users/123`, and omit queries that can contain secrets. Apply masking where needed, checking exception messages and nested objects too. Structured logging does not automatically remove secrets; define retention and viewing permissions as well.
tips.inDesign: Apply common rules to access, business, and exception logs. Send dummy secrets through validation and downstream failure paths and verify they do not reach logs or error collectors. Request IDs correlate events; they do not authenticate or authorize callers.

tradeOffs.option: Pass only allowed fields to the logger
tradeOffs.gain: Reduces accidental collection and gives consistent query fields
tradeOffs.cost: Requires choosing useful diagnostic fields in advance

tradeOffs.option: Add time-limited diagnostic fields when necessary
tradeOffs.gain: Adds focused information for a specific investigation
tradeOffs.cost: Requires sensitivity review, expiry, and removal management

sources.title: Django — Filtering Sensitive Error Report Information

tips.title: Map protected data and trust boundaries before building (threat modeling)
tips.keyPoint: Map entry points, data, and permissions, then ask who could abuse each path. Assign mitigations and checks, and revisit them when the feature changes.
tips.body: Threat modeling examines potential abuse paths during design. Identify protected assets such as personal data and credentials, actors, external services, and data flows. At each trust boundary, where permissions or trust assumptions change, consider impersonation, tampering, and disclosure. An internal network or an authenticated caller does not make every input trustworthy. Record a mitigation, owner, verification test, and residual risk for each threat. A diagram contributes to safety when its findings become implemented and verified controls.
tips.inDesign: Review new import jobs, administration features, and integrations. Decide where authentication, tenant membership checks, object authorization, input limits, and audit records are enforced. Assign an owner and review trigger to risks that remain.

tradeOffs.gain: Reveals permission and integration gaps before implementation
tradeOffs.cost: Requires time to keep diagrams and decisions current

tradeOffs.option: Combine with automated code and dependency checks
tradeOffs.gain: Repeatedly checks known dangerous patterns
tradeOffs.cost: Business authorization and design intent still require review

sources.title: OWASP — Multi-Tenant Security: tenant context and asynchronous work

tips.title: Track vulnerabilities through production remediation, beyond detection
tips.keyPoint: Inventory deployed components and versions. Prioritize using exploitation, reachability, and impact, then verify production deployment after merging a fix.
tips.body: Vulnerability management inventories direct and transitive dependencies, container operating systems, and exposed services. CVSS indicates technical severity; assess exploitation reports, whether untrusted input reaches the affected code, required privileges, and exposed data as well. Prefer a fixed version. If that is unavailable or delayed, assign an owner and expiry to temporary mitigations such as disabling the feature or restricting access. Verify the production version before considering remediation complete.
tips.inDesign: Map repositories to deployed artifacts and define owners and response targets by risk. Rescan when new advisories appear as well as during builds. Verify that temporary filters block the relevant exploit conditions and continue tracking the permanent fix.

tradeOffs.option: Update and redeploy the fixed version
tradeOffs.gain: Removes the known flaw from the component
tradeOffs.cost: Requires compatibility checks and updating all affected deployments

tradeOffs.option: Disable a feature or restrict its path until fixed
tradeOffs.gain: Can quickly reduce exposure when it blocks the exploit conditions
tradeOffs.cost: Disrupts functionality and may leave other paths exposed

tips.title: Design administrator access from granting through removal
tips.keyPoint: Use individual identities, multifactor authentication, and scoped, time-limited privileges. Include offboarding and emergency access checks in the lifecycle.
tips.body: Use individual accounts to attribute administrative actions. Centralize sign-in with SSO and require multifactor authentication (MFA). An access review removes unneeded administrators and contractor access; temporary elevation needs an expiry and audit record. Disabling SSO does not necessarily terminate existing service sessions or separately issued API keys. Verify those during offboarding. Emergency access for an SSO outage also needs protected storage, use alerts, and periodic checks.
tips.inDesign: Assign approvers and owners for expiry checks. Protect normal and emergency access with MFA and audit records, including recovery information. Avoid relying on shared accounts or standing administrator privileges for routine work.

tradeOffs.option: Centralize sign-in and offboarding with SSO
tradeOffs.gain: Consolidates identity entry points and administration
tradeOffs.cost: Requires checking each service’s sessions and keys and preparing for identity-provider outages

tradeOffs.option: Elevate administrator privileges only when needed
tradeOffs.gain: Limits privileges available during everyday compromise
tradeOffs.cost: Needs approval flows and emergency procedures that allow timely work

tips.title: Test that audit logging detects the operations you need to see
tips.keyPoint: Record who did what to which resource and when, then connect alerts to responders. Missing coverage or retention prevents absent logs from proving safety.
tips.body: An audit log helps trace privilege changes, administrative actions, and access to important data. Select events across identity, cloud, and application systems; align actor, resource, action, outcome, timestamp, and time zone. Exclude secret values and personal-data payloads. Protect storage against deletion by attackers or routine operators and restrict readers. Connect each detection rule to an owner, notification route, and investigation procedure. Test event generation through collection, alerting, and response, and detect collection failures.
tips.inDesign: Choose detections such as bulk reads, privilege escalation, and audit disablement. Management logging may not include data reads. Define coverage, retention, and cost, and verify storage and alert delivery. Injecting a sample alert alone does not test collection of the underlying real event.

tradeOffs.gain: Adds evidence for investigating impact, including reads
tradeOffs.cost: Requires log-volume, storage-cost, and access-control planning

tradeOffs.option: Alert immediately on high-confidence actions and investigate other patterns in aggregate
tradeOffs.gain: Helps responders prioritize notifications
tradeOffs.cost: Paths without immediate alerts still need regular investigation

tips.title: Rehearse incident contacts and decision authority before an incident
tips.keyPoint: Assign command, technical, and communication roles, escalation criteria, isolation authority, and alternative contacts. Rehearse decisions in a tabletop and test permissions separately.
tips.body: An incident response plan identifies reporting channels, escalation criteria, a commander and backup, technical responders, record keeping, and communications. Initial playbooks specify evidence storage and authority for disruptive actions. Prepare alternative communication channels if normal SSO or chat is unavailable or compromised. A tabletop exercise discusses decisions and responsibilities in a hypothetical incident. Discussion alone cannot validate tool permissions or successful operations, so test those in a controlled environment too.
tips.inDesign: Verify contacts for cloud providers, external responders, legal, and customer support, and keep them securely accessible. Include night-time and absent-owner scenarios and repeat exercises after procedure changes. Keep sensitive investigation details away from potentially compromised channels.

tradeOffs.option: Rehearse roles and decisions in a tabletop
tradeOffs.gain: Finds cross-team gaps with modest preparation
tradeOffs.cost: Does not verify actual tool behavior or permissions

tradeOffs.option: Rehearse operations in a controlled environment
tradeOffs.gain: Checks procedures, permissions, collection, and isolation
tradeOffs.cost: Requires a defined scope and preparation to avoid business impact

tips.title: Stop use of an exposed secret before relying on file cleanup
tips.keyPoint: Treat an exposed key as copied. Disable the original and revoke or restrict unauthorized derived sessions and additional keys. Replace it from a trusted environment and verify rejection of each affected access path.
tips.body: Removing a secret from Git can leave copies in clones, history, and logs. Notify responders, disable or restrict the key, and preserve evidence. Issuing a new key and disabling the old key are separate actions. Disabling the original does not necessarily stop sessions or additional keys created using it. Investigate activity to identify unauthorized derived access, then revoke sessions or restrict permissions using the service’s controls. Replace credentials from an uncompromised administrative environment. Allow for propagation delays and verify that both the old key and unauthorized derived access are rejected. Preserve evidence before cleaning history and storage, and investigate other compromise.
tips.inDesign: Deliver secrets from a dedicated store and combine local and server-side checks. Prepare reporting, revocation, replacement, and dependent-service recovery procedures. Routine rotation for continuity and urgent revocation during suspected abuse have different priorities.

tradeOffs.option: Immediately revoke a key suspected of abuse
tradeOffs.gain: Reduces time available for new actions using the old key
tradeOffs.cost: Can disrupt dependent services; recovery and stopping unauthorized derived access are also needed

tradeOffs.option: Automate and rehearse replacement and revocation
tradeOffs.gain: Can reduce response work and recovery time
tradeOffs.cost: Requires maintaining service-specific revocation behavior and exception handling

sources.title: AWS IAM — Disabling permissions for temporary security credentials
AWS IAM — Revoke IAM role temporary security credentials

tips.title: Contain a suspected compromise while preserving evidence
tips.keyPoint: Limit ongoing harm while retaining investigation records. Avoid blanket restart or deletion rules, and do not wait for all collection to finish while an attack continues.
tips.body: Containment can isolate resources, restrict credentials, or disable affected functionality. The commander weighs ongoing harm, business impact, and evidence loss while technical responders execute. Restarts and resets may destroy volatile evidence such as memory. Preserve logs, disks, and execution state before changes when feasible, while limiting active disclosure promptly. Evidence preservation includes recording actions, times, collection sources, collectors, evidence hashes, and transfers. Restrict access to and modification of original evidence.
tips.inDesign: Prepare permissions and storage for isolation and collection. A disk snapshot does not necessarily include memory. Observe containment effectiveness across existing connections and alternate paths instead of relying on a configuration change alone.

tradeOffs.gain: Limits abuse paths while retaining the resource
tradeOffs.cost: Can disrupt operations and requires checks for existing connections and alternate paths

tradeOffs.option: Shut down a resource when necessary
tradeOffs.gain: Can stop ongoing harm
tradeOffs.cost: May lose volatile evidence; weigh that against current damage

tips.title: Communicate verified impact separately from uncertain scope
tips.keyPoint: Trace identities, time windows, resources, and actions using evidence. Separate facts, hypotheses, and unknowns; involve stakeholders early and set the next update time.
tips.body: Establish incident scope beyond the detection timestamp to the earliest suspicious activity and possible intrusion window. Correlate identity, permission, data-operation, and endpoint evidence. Distinguish what an account could access from what evidence shows it actually did. Record time zones, coverage, and gaps. Public exposure does not prove every object was downloaded, and absent traces may not prove no disclosure. Revise scope as evidence develops.
tips.inDesign: Coordinate early through command and communications roles with leadership, security, legal, and customer support. Confirm applicable notification recipients and deadlines with the responsible teams. Share verified impact, actions, unknowns, and the next update time; exclude personal data and secrets from public notices.

tradeOffs.gain: Enables earlier protective decisions
tradeOffs.cost: Requires scheduled updates and corrections as findings change

tradeOffs.option: Keep detailed evidence in restricted investigation records
tradeOffs.gain: Preserves verifiability while limiting sensitive-data spread
tradeOffs.cost: Requires maintaining consistency between public messages and internal records

tips.title: Verify safe recovery by closing re-entry paths before restoring service
tips.keyPoint: Remove entry paths and unauthorized persistence, then restore into a trusted environment. Check data, permissions, and monitoring and return service in stages.
tips.body: Recovery after compromise must restore integrity as well as availability. Fix the entry path and investigate unauthorized accounts, credentials, startup settings, and jobs that enable persistence.
