BigQuery supports predicates such as constant ranges on the partition column, and a dry run can estimate bytes processed. If storage uses ingestion day while queries use event day, late arrivals may reside in other partitions. Excessively small partitions add metadata. Measure selected columns and joins too; scanned-byte ratios do not directly determine runtime or billing ratios.
tips.inDesign: Check partition filters using representative aggregation queries. Test late-arrival and reprocessing ranges, then compare estimated bytes with execution statistics.

tradeOffs.gain: Aligns date-range analytics and reprocessing units
tradeOffs.cost: Adds partitions and metadata for small datasets

tradeOffs.gain: Reduces overhead from tiny partitions
tradeOffs.cost: May read more data for short-range queries

tips.title: Choose reprocessing intervals by business time, not execution day
tips.keyPoint: Computing “yesterday” from the execution clock changes the target on later reruns. Define start and end in the business time zone and pass that interval explicitly.
tips.body: A data interval is the start-to-end scope processed by a run. A half-open interval includes its start and excludes its end, avoiding duplicate boundary membership across adjacent intervals. Find the business-day start and next-day start in the relevant time zone, then convert both to UTC instants for querying. Days in regions with daylight saving time are not always 24 hours. Airflow distinguishes data intervals from execution time, and manual-run intervals depend on the trigger path and timetable. Verify supplied intervals and record input versions when late arrivals can change the source.
tips.inDesign: Specify business dates, cutoffs, and time zones as requirements. Test boundary records, later reruns, and daylight-saving transitions to verify the same intended interval is reread.

tradeOffs.gain: Matches business cutoffs and reporting definitions
tradeOffs.cost: Requires verifying time-zone and daylight-saving boundaries

tradeOffs.option: Process fixed UTC intervals, then derive business-day aggregates
tradeOffs.gain: Simplifies a common ingestion time axis
tradeOffs.cost: Business-day queries may span multiple UTC intervals

tips.title: Decide whether historical revenue uses past or current attributes
tips.keyPoint: Joining historical orders to today’s customer master changes past breakdowns when attributes change. If reports need the historical attribute, keep history and select the version valid at the event time.
tips.body: SCD Type 2 preserves attribute history by adding a row when values change. Alongside the business key, store a version identifier and validity interval. Join historical orders using customer ID and the interval containing the order time. Overlapping intervals can create duplicate matches, so test overlaps and gaps. Distinguish business-effective time from ingestion observation time. Periodic snapshots do not capture every change between observations. Define how far back corrected history should trigger recomputation.
tips.inDesign: Clarify whether users need a historical breakdown or a restatement using today’s organization. Design the history source, timestamp meaning, overlap checks, and late-correction recomputation accordingly.

tradeOffs.gain: Makes it easy to restate all periods using current attributes
tradeOffs.cost: Cannot reproduce breakdowns by historical attributes

tradeOffs.gain: Builds historical breakdowns from available history
tradeOffs.cost: Requires history storage, interval validation, and late-correction recomputation

tips.title: "How would you generate IDs?"
tips.keyPoint: Compare sequences, UUIDs, and time-ordered IDs (Snowflake, UUIDv7) on ordering, collisions, and distribution, then choose.
tips.body: Database auto-increment is simple, but ID generation funnels through one node and collides across shards. UUIDv4 can be generated anywhere with negligible collision risk, but its randomness scatters inserts across a B-tree index and does not sort by creation time. IDs that start with a timestamp can be generated in a distributed way and sort roughly by creation time.
tips.inDesign: Whether you raise the requirements yourself: uniqueness, ordering, length, unguessability. And whether you avoid making ID generation a single point of failure and handle clocks moving backward in time-based schemes.

tradeOffs.gain: Short, ordered by creation, and simple
tradeOffs.cost: Numbering is centralized, collides across shards, and reveals counts

tradeOffs.gain: Generated anywhere with practically no collisions
tradeOffs.cost: 128 bits long, and random values scatter B-tree inserts and do not sort by creation

tradeOffs.gain: Generated in a distributed way and roughly ordered by creation
tradeOffs.cost: Need protection against clocks moving back, and reveal the creation time

tips.title: "What happens if the whole cache goes down?"
tips.keyPoint: Compute the database load from the hit rate, then explain how you protect it: redundancy, rate limiting, gradual recovery.
tips.body: The cache absorbs database load, so at a 95% hit rate, losing it multiplies database reads by 20 instantly. If the database cannot absorb that, a cache failure cascades into a database failure. Right after recovery the cache is empty, so the same surge happens again.
tips.inDesign: Whether you treat the cache not as a speed-up but as a component whose loss multiplies load. Whether you quantify the impact and cover both cache redundancy and database protection.

tradeOffs.gain: A single node failure does not lower the hit rate
tradeOffs.cost: Costs more, and does nothing against failures that take down the whole cache (a bad config)

tradeOffs.option: Rate-limit in front of the database and prioritize critical requests
tradeOffs.gain: The database survives a full cache outage
tradeOffs.cost: Some requests are rejected or slowed

tradeOffs.option: Warm the cache before restoring traffic, or ramp up gradually
tradeOffs.gain: Avoids the surge right after recovery
tradeOffs.cost: Recovery takes longer, and warming needs to be built

sources.title: AWS Builders' Library — Caching challenges and strategies

tips.title: "What if an entire region goes down?"
tips.keyPoint: Settle RPO (how much data you can lose) and RTO (how long you can be down) first, then pick the setup and cost that match.
tips.body: Multi-region setups are expensive and complex. First decide how much data loss (RPO) and downtime (RTO) you can tolerate. Regions are far apart, so replication between them is usually asynchronous, and failing over can lose the most recent writes.
tips.inDesign: Whether you avoid "make everything multi-region active/active" and instead derive the setup from requirements. Whether you explain data loss from asynchronous replication and how the failover decision is made, and by whom.

tradeOffs.option: Restore from backup in another region
tradeOffs.gain: Lowest cost
tradeOffs.cost: RTO of hours, and RPO equal to the backup interval

tradeOffs.option: Keep a standby (pilot light, warm standby)
tradeOffs.gain: RTO of minutes to tens of minutes
tradeOffs.cost: The standby costs money and failover needs drills; data within the async replication lag can be lost

tradeOffs.gain: Either region keeps serving immediately
tradeOffs.cost: Highest cost and complexity, and conflicting writes in both regions must be resolved

sources.title: AWS — Disaster recovery options in the cloud

tips.title: "Where is the single point of failure?"
tips.keyPoint: Walk the request path from the edge and answer "what if one of these dies?" for each component.
tips.body: A single point of failure (SPOF) is a component whose loss stops the whole service. App servers are easy to multiply, but a database primary, a lone queue, shared config or auth services, and concentration in one AZ are easy to overlook.
tips.inDesign: Whether you check systematically along the request path instead of listing whatever comes to mind. Whether you state failover times and what happens during them, such as failed writes or dropped connections.

tradeOffs.option: Add a standby with automatic failover (Multi-AZ)
tradeOffs.gain: A failed primary is replaced in one to two minutes
tradeOffs.cost: Roughly double the cost, and writes fail during failover

tradeOffs.option: Stay single and recover by runbook
tradeOffs.gain: Lowest cost
tradeOffs.cost: Writes stop for tens of minutes to hours until recovery

tradeOffs.option: Spread writes over several nodes (sharding, multi-writer)
tradeOffs.gain: One failure affects only part of the data
tradeOffs.cost: Much more complex to design and run

sources.title: Amazon RDS — Failing over a Multi-AZ DB instance

tips.title: "How do you deliver new messages in real time?"
tips.keyPoint: Compare polling, long polling, SSE, and WebSocket on latency, connection count, and direction, then choose.
tips.body: Short-interval polling is simple, but it sends requests even when nothing is new, costing connections × frequency. WebSocket keeps one connection open for two-way messages with no wasted requests, but servers must hold huge numbers of persistent connections and track which server owns which connection. Long polling has the server hold the response until something new arrives. SSE keeps an HTTP connection open and streams one way from the server.
tips.inDesign: Whether you go beyond "use WebSocket" to estimate connections, explain routing messages to the server holding each connection (pub/sub), and handle disconnects, reconnects, and missed messages.

tradeOffs.gain: Simple, using plain HTTP
tradeOffs.cost: Requests even when nothing is new, and delay up to the polling interval

tradeOffs.gain: Near-instant delivery over plain HTTP
tradeOffs.cost: Held connections raise concurrent connection counts, and SSE is server-to-client only

tradeOffs.gain: Two-way, with no wasted requests
tradeOffs.cost: Many persistent connections, routing to the server holding each one, and reconnect handling

tips.title: "How would you build a real-time leaderboard?"
tips.keyPoint: Redis sorted sets provide O(log N) updates and individual rank lookup, and O(log N + M) retrieval of the top M. A suitable RDB index can also make top-result retrieval efficient.
tips.body: Retrieving top results and computing one user’s exact rank are different access patterns. A suitable RDB index avoids a full ORDER BY sort, while rank needs counts or precomputation. Redis sorted sets support O(log N) updates and individual ranks; fetching the top M costs O(log N + M). Complexity describes growth, not an exact step count or latency guarantee.
tips.inDesign: Whether you choose based on data-structure complexity, and how you handle sets too big for one node, ties, per-period (daily, weekly) boards, and keeping the database in sync.

tradeOffs.option: `ORDER BY` in a relational database each time
tradeOffs.gain: No new system to run
tradeOffs.cost: An index can accelerate top results, while an arbitrary user’s exact rank needs counting or aggregation

tradeOffs.gain: Updates and rank lookups in O(log N)
tradeOffs.cost: Everything sits in memory, and it must be kept in sync with the database and rebuilt after failures

tradeOffs.gain: Cheapest reads, and works on a relational database
tradeOffs.cost: Rankings lag by the interval

tips.title: "How would you find nearby places?"
tips.keyPoint: Use geohash, H3, or another spatial index to cover the search region, then filter candidates by exact distance. Required cells depend on radius, latitude, and precision.
tips.body: Separate latitude and longitude indexes may leave many candidates for a radius search. Encoding position with geohash can gather candidates through several key ranges covering the circle. Nearby points can cross cell boundaries, so do not restrict to one prefix; perform a final exact-distance check.
tips.inDesign: Whether you can explain turning a 2D search into a 1D key, and cover misses near cell boundaries (check neighbors), cell size in dense versus sparse areas, and update load for moving objects such as ride-hailing drivers.

tradeOffs.option: Separate indexes on latitude and longitude
tradeOffs.gain: Works on the existing database
tradeOffs.cost: Slow, because one index yields many candidates the other must discard

tradeOffs.option: Cells such as geohash or H3
tradeOffs.gain: Maps spatial candidates into key-range searches
tradeOffs.cost: Neighboring cells must be searched for boundary cases, and cell size must suit density

tradeOffs.option: A spatial index (such as PostGIS GiST)
tradeOffs.gain: Accurate queries for any area or distance
tradeOffs.cost: Needs a database that supports it, and frequent location updates are costly

tips.title: "Why did you choose that database?"
tips.keyPoint: Justify the choice from access patterns, consistency, and scale, not from product names.
tips.body: Choose candidates from access patterns, consistency, and scale. Evaluate operational experience through maintenance, hiring, and incident-response constraints. Explain how familiarity lowers operational risk while meeting requirements. RDB versus NoSQL alone does not determine distribution capabilities; compare each product’s transactions, partitioning, replication, and cost.
tips.inDesign: Whether you explain in the order requirements → choice → trade-offs. Mentioning the strengths of the option you rejected and how hard it would be to migrate later is a plus. If horizontal partitioning is needed, explain product support and the partition key.

tradeOffs.gain: Flexible queries, transactions, and strong consistency
tradeOffs.cost: Single-writer designs have a writer limit; distributed SQL and automatic partitioning also exist. Compare distributed latency, cost, and operational requirements

tradeOffs.gain: Partitions horizontally and handles heavy writes for known access patterns
tradeOffs.cost: Weak at unplanned queries and joins; access patterns must be fixed up front

tradeOffs.gain: Stores data of varying shape flexibly
tradeOffs.cost: Weak at consistency and joins across documents

tips.title: "If traffic grew 10x, what breaks first?"
tips.keyPoint: Start with a linear first approximation of 10× load to find constraints. Validate nonlinear changes in caching, lock contention, and queueing through load tests. Scaling stateless tiers can expose DB limits.
tips.body: Senior interviews test less whether you can draw a design and more whether you know its limits. API servers can usually just be added, but each one adds database connections, writes, and lock contention. Components that do not grow by adding servers, such as a single primary or a connection limit, break first.
tips.inDesign: Can you multiply each component's current utilization by 10 and order them by when they exceed their limits? Instead of "just shard it," can you go from cheap fixes (a connection pooler, caching, spreading reads) upward, with numbers for when the next step becomes necessary? Can you also say why the components that survive 10x are fine? Multiplying utilization by ten is a first approximation; validate actual limits and their order with load tests.

tradeOffs.gain: Fixes the connection limit quickly and cheaply
tradeOffs.cost: One more hop to run and a little latency; pooling per transaction breaks features such as session variables

tradeOffs.option: Move reads to a cache and read replicas
tradeOffs.gain: Takes much of the load off the primary
tradeOffs.cost: Reads may be stale, and cache invalidation must be designed

tradeOffs.gain: Spreads writes too, raising the ceiling far
tradeOffs.cost: Cross-shard queries and transactions get hard, and migrating is a large effort

tips.title: "How would you monitor this system?"
tips.keyPoint: Define SLOs from SLIs and center paging on burn rate. Add preventive capacity alerts and synthetic checks, and use resource metrics for diagnosis too.
tips.body: "We watch CPU, memory, and disk and alert when they cross thresholds" says nothing about what affects users or who gets paged when. It is easier to explain if you split the roles: measure whether key user actions succeed (symptoms) and page on that, and use cause metrics after the page to narrow down the cause. Also, zero errors can mean requests are not arriving at all (DNS or entry-point failures), which internal metrics alone cannot see. Resource metrics also support preventive notifications for risks such as disk exhaustion before impact. Define actionable thresholds and recipients.
tips.inDesign: Can you start from key user actions and state SLIs and SLOs as numbers? Can you separate the paging condition (burn rate) from the metrics used to narrow things down (the four golden signals, queue age)? Can you cover asynchronous work and outages where traffic drops to zero, without gaps?

tradeOffs.option: Threshold alerts on many cause metrics
tradeOffs.gain: Early warning, with a hint at the cause
tradeOffs.cost: Fires when users are fine, and alert fatigue buries the pages that matter

tradeOffs.gain: Pages match user impact and urgency
tradeOffs.cost: SLIs must be designed first, and an outage where traffic drops to zero is not caught by this alone

tradeOffs.gain: Notices problems along the users' routes even with no traffic
tradeOffs.cost: Covers only the scripted routes, costs money to run, and needs upkeep whenever screens change

sources.title: Google SRE book — Monitoring Distributed Systems

tips.title: "Do you build timelines when a post is written, or when it is read?"
tips.keyPoint: Pushing each post to every follower makes reads fast, but posts from accounts with huge followings explode into writes. Answer with a mix: push for ordinary users, and merge posts from high-follower accounts at read time.
tips.body: Delivering one post to each follower's timeline is called fan-out. Fan-out on write inserts the post ID into each follower's cached timeline whenever someone posts. A read is a single cache lookup, so it is fast. In exchange, writes scale with followers: one post from an account with 10 million followers is 10 million writes and arrives late until they finish. It also writes for people who never log in, wasting storage. Fan-out on read gathers recent posts from everyone you follow and sorts them on each read. Writes happen once, and the ordering (ranking) can change on every read, but reads grow slower and heavier the more accounts someone follows. Most designs combine the two and merge only high-follower accounts at read time. Delivery volume is the sum of each author’s post count × actual recipients. Multiplying user averages can mislead when posting frequency and follower count are correlated.
tips.inDesign: Whether you estimate write volume from DAU, follow counts, and posts instead of just picking one side. Whether you cover high-follower accounts, inactive users, a cap on timeline length, and what a ranking change would cost.

tradeOffs.gain: A read is one fast cache lookup
tradeOffs.cost: Writes scale with followers, and celebrity posts arrive late

tradeOffs.gain: One write per post, and ranking is easy to change
tradeOffs.cost: Every read gathers and sorts posts from each followed account, so reads are slow and heavy

tradeOffs.gain: Ordinary posts read fast, and celebrity write storms are avoided
tradeOffs.cost: Two paths and a threshold make building and running it more complex
